body.p: J
JAAKAN
Esav’s (Esau’s) descendant and a son of Ezer the Hori (Horite) (1 Chr 1:42, nlt mg); alternately called Akan in Genesis 36:27. See Beeroth Bene-jaakan.
JAAKOBAH
Leader in Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) tribe (1 Chr 4:36).
JAALAH
Servant of King Shelomoh (Solomon) and head of a family who returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) with Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) after the Babylonian exile (Ezr 2:56; Neh 7:58).
JAALAM*
KJV form of Yaelam (Jalam), Esav’s (Esau’s) son, in Genesis 36:5, 14, 18 and 1 Chronicles 1:35. See Jalam.
JAANAI*
KJV form of Ya’anay (Janai), a Gadi (Gadite), in 1 Chronicles 5:12. See Janai.
JAAR

Most common word in Hebrew for “forest.” It refers to forests generally (Is 10:18) and to specific forests, such as the “forest of Efrayim (Ephraim)” (2 Sm 18:6) and the “forest of Heret (Hereth)” (1 Sm 22:5), both associated with King David. It also occurs as the name of one of Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) buildings, “the Palace of the Forest of Levanon (Lebanon)” (1 Kgs 7:2), apparently because of its extensive use of cedar. Only one occurrence of “Ya’ar (Jaar)” seems to be a proper name. Psalm 132:6 alludes to the transfer of the ark from Kiryat-Yearim (Kiriath-jearim) to Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Here it is called the field of Ya’ar (or “the wood,” kjv), perhaps a poetic abbreviation.
JAARE-OREGIM*
Textual corruption of Yair (Jair) in 2 Samuel 21:19. See Jair #3.
JAARESHIAH
Yeroham’s (Jeroham’s) son, a Benyamite (Benjamite) leader who lived in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (1 Chr 8:27).
JAASAU*
KJV spelling of Ya’asu (Jaasu), Bani’s son, in Ezra 10:37. See Jaasu.
JAASIEL
1. Warrior among David’s mighty men. He is called “the Metsovayah (Mezobaite)” (1 Chr 11:47).
2. Avner’s (Abner’s) son and the leader of Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe during David’s reign (1 Chr 27:21).
JAASU
Bani’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile (Ezr 10:37).
JAAZANIAH

1. Son of Hoshayah (Hoshaiah), who was a Ma’akati (Maacathite) and a leader in the armies of Yehudah (Judah) at the beginning of the exile. These troops received assurance of safety in return for loyalty to the Babylonians (2 Kgs 25:23). Ya’azanyah (Jaazaniah) is alternately called Yezanyah (Jezaniah) in Jeremiah 40:8 and Azaryah (Azariah) in Jeremiah 42:1 (nlt mg) and 43:2.

2. Son of Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) (not the prophet), who was taken by Yirmiyah the prophet into the Lord’s house, where he refused to drink wine because of the command of his ancestor Yonadav (Jonadab) the Recabite (Jer 35:3-11).
3. Shafan’s (Shaphan’s) son, who led a group of elders in worshiping idols in the temple (Ez 8:11).
4. Azur’s (Azzur’s) son and one of a group of 25 men seen by Yehezkel (Ezekiel) in a vision who gave bad counsel and plotted evil in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) near the time of the exile (Ez 11:1).
JAAZER*
KJV alternate form of Yazer (Jazer), an Amori (Amorite) city in Gilead, in Numbers 21:32 and 32:35. See Jazer.
JAAZIAH
Descendant of Merari in a list of family leaders among Levites assigned to temple duty in David’s reign (1 Chr 24:26-27).
JAAZIEL

One of the eight men appointed to play harps or lyres when the ark was brought up to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) by David (1 Chr 15:18-20; and probably 16:5a, “Yeiel (Jeiel),” which is most likely a copyist’s error). He is called Aziel in verse 20.
JABAL
Descendant of Kayin (Cain) and the first son of Lemek (Lamech) and Adah. He was the father of a nomadic people who dwelt in tents (Gn 4:20).
JABBOK

Eastern tributary of the Yarden (Jordan), the modern Nahr ez-Zerqa or Blue River. Its source is a spring near Amman, capital of modern Yarden (the Dekapolis (Decapolis) town of Filadelfeia (Philadelphia) in Hellenistic times). From its source the Yabok (Jabbok) loops northeast before swinging west and cutting a valley that, characteristic of the east Yarden tributary streams, deepens into a canyon. It emerges from this ravine near Tell Deir Alla, which may be the ancient Sukot (Succoth), quiets its flow, and joins the Yarden at ed-Damiyeh, the ancient Adam, some 15 miles (24 kilometers) north of the Dead Sea. The Yabok ranks next to the Yarmuk, its more northerly companion stream, in the extent of its watershed, a region of well-watered territory blessed with an average rainfall of some 30 inches (76 centimeters) per year. The Yabok has a fast, strong, perennial flow; over a large portion of its 60-mile (96.5-kilometer) course, the stream averages an 80-foot (24.4-meter) drop over each mile. The loop of the river north of Amman (biblical Rabah (Rabbah)) was an Amoni (Ammonite) frontier (Nm 21:24). The river separated the kingdoms of Sihon and Og (Jgs 11:19-22; cf. Dt 3:1-2, 8-10), land in Gilead that was later divided among the tribes of Gad, Re’uven (Reuben), and the half-tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh) (Dt 3:12, 16; Jos 12:2-6).
See also Jordan River.
JABESH (Person)
Shalum’s (Shallum’s) father. Shalum assassinated Zekaryah (Zechariah), king of Yisrael (Israel) (2 Kgs 15:10-14).
JABESH, JABESH-GILEAD (Place)

Town appearing in the closing chapters of the book of Judges (chs 19–21). This is a sad record of the division and degradation of the land, which tells of a base atrocity committed by the men of Giveah (Gibeah) against a Levite’s concubine, a sanguinary war against Benyamin (Benjamin) in consequence, and savage reprisals against Yavesh-Gilead (Jabesh-gilead), whose community had sent no contingent to the battle. Such is the first mention of the town. The town was repopulated by neighboring Giladim (Gileadites) and next appears in 1 Samuel 11. East of the Yarden (Jordan) River, Yavesh (Jabesh) was exposed to Amoni (Ammonite) attack, and Nahash of Amon (Ammon) forced Yavesh-Gilead to seek terms of surrender. The condition imposed by the barbarous Nahash was the loss of the right eye for all the inhabitants, a mutilation intended to humiliate Yisrael (Israel) and destroy the military potential of a border fortress. The sequel was Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) forced march, a fine piece of military prowess, and a tremendous boost for the new king’s prestige. Sha’ul gained in one swift blow the support of the Transjordanian tribes and the reduction of the frontier threat that a militarily powerful Amon would undoubtedly offer. The men of Yavesh-Gilead repaid their deep debt to Sha’ul when the king, now unbalanced and rejected, died on Mt Gilboa with his son Yonatan (Jonathan) in a last attempt to blunt the Pelishti (Philistine) drive to the north. The bodies of Sha’ul and Yonatan, hung headless over the walls of Beth-shan, were cut down and rescued by a commando force from Yavesh-Gilead, who made a forced march of nine miles (14.5 kilometers) each way to honor their onetime benefactor (1 Sm 31:8-13; 1 Chr 10:8-12). When David became king, he repaid the men of Yavesh-Gilead with gratitude.

The name Yavesh is preserved in that of the Wadi el-Yabis that runs into the Yarden directly south of the southern end of the Sea of Galil (Galilee). The town itself, according to Eusebius’s generally reliable topography, was about six miles (9.7 kilometers) south of Pella on the road to Gerasa. The twin tells of Tell el-Maqereh and Tell Abu Kharaz on the Wadi el-Yabis correspond with Eusebius’s location much better than the other site suggested: Tell el-Maqlub. Tell el-Meqereh and Tell Abu Kharaz are on the eastern rim of the Yarden Valley and fit the details of the historical record—Sha’ul’s forced march from Bezek, and the route of the Yavesh-Gilead raiding party to Beth-shan.
JABEZ (Person)
Member of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe who was noted for his godliness. He prayed for God’s protection, and his prayer was answered (1 Chr 4:9-10).
JABEZ (Place)
City that was probably located in Yehudah (Judah) and was inhabited by scribes (1 Chr 2:55).
JABIN
1. King of Hatsor (Hazor) who led a coalition against Yehoshua (Joshua) at Merom. Yavin (Jabin) and his allies were destroyed in the battle, and Hatsor was burned to the ground (Jos 11:1-14).

2. King of Hatsor during the period of the judges (Jgs 4). God allowed him to oppress Yisrael (Israel) for 20 years because of their wickedness. His army included 900 chariots of iron. Eventually, God delivered Yisrael through the prophetess Deborah and her captain, Barak, who defeated Sisera, the captain of Yavin’s army. While resting after his flight from battle, Sisera himself was killed by a woman. Yavin was no longer a threat after Sisera’s death and was soon killed (Jgs 4:24; Ps 83:9).
JABNEEL
1. Alternate name for the town Yavneh (Jabneh) in Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (Jos 15:11). See Jabneh.
2. Town of Galil (Galilee) near Tiberias, on Naftali’s (Naphtali’s) southern border (Jos 19:33). It was located south of modern Yavne’el (Jabneel).
JABNEH

Biblical city on the coastal plain between Yafo (Joppa) (modern Jaffa) and Ashdod, first mentioned as Yavne’el (Jabneel), on the northern border of the tribe of Yehudah (Judah) (Jos 15:11). It is mentioned together with the Pelishti (Philistine) cities Gat (Gath) and Ashdod, whose walls were breached by Uziyah (Uzziah), king of Yehudah (2 Chr 26:6). In the middle Bronze Age a harbor was established at Jabneh-yam, which is probably mentioned by Thutmose III in his list of conquered cities and in the Tell el-Amarna letters (Jabni-ilu). The remains of the harbor show evidence of all periods—from early Bronze Age down to the Byzantine period. In Hellenistic times Yavneh (Jabneh) was called Yavneh and was used as a base by foreign armies for subsequent attacks against the Yehudi (Judean) territory of the Maccabeans. After the destruction of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) in AD 70, a small community of learned refugees was located in Yavneh. Their leader was Yohanan (Johanan) ben Zakkai, a former member of the Sanhedrin, the supreme court of the Yehudim (Jews) in Yerushalem. He founded a school there. His successor was Gamliel (Gamaliel) II. Here the canon of the OT was defined. During the second Jewish war (Bar-Kochba Revolt, AD 132–135), Yavneh was deserted. The spiritual center of the Jewish life was removed to Galil (Galilee). The refugees settled down first in Zippori and later in Tiberias, where the Yerushalem Talmud was codified and the Masoretic Text of the OT was produced.
JACAN, JACHAN*
Member of Gad’s tribe who lived in Bashan during the reign of Yotam (Jotham), king of Yehudah (Judah) (1 Chr 5:13).
JACHIN*

1. Son of Shim’on (Simeon) and leader of the Jachinites, who immigrated to Mitsrayim (Egypt) with his grandfather Ya’akov (Jacob) (Gn 46:10; Ex 6:15; Nm 26:12). He is called Yariv (Jarib) in 1 Chronicles 4:24.
2. Priest who lived in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) after the exile (1 Chr 9:10; Neh 11:10). The name Yakin (Jachin) may possibly designate a family of priests of which Yakin was the head.
3. Descendant of Aharon (Aaron) and head of the 21st course of priests assigned to temple duty in David’s reign (1 Chr 24:17).
JACHIN AND BOAZ*

Names of two pillars Shelomoh (Solomon) set up before the temple vestibule. He named the south pillar Yakin (Jachin) and the north pillar Boaz (1 Kgs 7:21; 2 Chr 3:17). These hollow pillars were cast of bronze and measured about 27 feet (8.2 meters) in height and about 18 feet (5.5 meters) in circumference (nearly 6 feet, or 1.8 meters, in diameter). They were crowned with a capital (ornate cap or top) about 7½ feet (2.3 meters) high that consisted of cast lily work, chains, and 200 pomegranates each (1 Kgs 7:15-20; 2 Chr 3:15-16; 4:13).
JACHINITE*
Descendant of Yakin (Jachin), Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) son (Nm 26:12). See Jachin #1.
JACINTH
Precious stone mentioned in Revelation 21:20 as a foundation stone in the new Yerushalem (Jerusalem). See Stones, Precious.
JACKAL
Wolflike mammal known for its distinctive wail (Mi 1:8). See Animals.
JACKAL’S WELL

Unknown location along the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) wall between the Valley Gate and the Dung Gate visited by Nehemyah (Nehemiah) during his night inspection of the wall (Neh 2:13). It is also called Dragon’s Well or Serpent’s Well.
JACOB

1. Younger of twin sons born to Yitshak (Isaac) and Rivkah (Rebekah) (Gn 25:24-26). Yitshak had prayed for his barren wife, Rivkah, and she conceived the twins, who jostled each other in the womb. When she asked the Lord about this, he told her that she was carrying two nations and that the older son would serve the younger (v 23). Esav (Esau) was hairy and red (later he was called Edom, “red,” 25:30; 36:1), but Ya’akov (Jacob) was born holding the heel of his brother, so that he was named Ya’akov, “he takes by the heel” (cf. Hos 12:3), with the derived meaning “to supplant, deceive, attack from the rear.”
Personal History
Esav and Ya’akov were very different from each other. Esav was an outdoorsman, the favorite of his father, while Ya’akov stayed around the tents and was loved by his mother.

One day when Ya’akov was preparing red pottage, Esav came in famished and asked Ya’akov for some food. Ya’akov offered to sell Esav some stew in exchange for his birthright as firstborn, and Esav agreed, thus repudiating his birthright (cf. Heb 12:16). The significance of this episode of the red pottage is demonstrated by its association with Esav’s second name, Edom (“red”) (Gn 25:30).

Yitshak became old and blind. One day he asked Esav to take his weapons and get some wild game, of which Yitshak was very fond (Gn 27:6-7; cf 25:28), so that he could eat and then confer his blessing upon Esav. Rivkah overheard this, so she called Ya’akov and told him to go to the flock and select two good kids. She would prepare a dish that would pass for the game while Esav was out hunting. Ya’akov feared that Yitshak would detect the deception, for Esav was very hairy, but Rivkah had everything planned. She placed the skins of the kids on Ya’akov’s hands and neck to give the impression of hairiness (27:16) and clothed him in Esav’s best garments, which had the smell of the outdoors on them. Although Yitshak recognized the voice of Ya’akov, his other senses failed him, and he was deceived by the feel of the skins and the smell of the garments. He proceeded to give the blessing to Ya’akov (vv 27-29).

No sooner had Ya’akov left than Esav arrived with the game he had cooked. Ya’akov’s ruse was discovered, but the deed could not be undone (Gn 27:33), for, as the Nuzi tablets show, an oral blessing had legal validity and could not be revoked. Esav was heartbroken (cf. Heb 12:17). Yitshak gave him a blessing inferior to the one given to Ya’akov (Gn 27:39-40).

The animosity between the brothers deepened, and Esav plotted to kill Ya’akov after the death of their father. Rivkah learned of this, so she instructed Ya’akov to flee to her brother Lavan (Laban) in Haran (Gn 27:42-45). Esav’s Hiti (Hittite) wives, meanwhile, had been making life miserable for Rivkah; she complained to Yitshak, who called Ya’akov and sent him to Lavan to marry one of his uncle’s daughters (27:46–28:4).

Ya’akov set out for Haran. Using a stone for a pillow, he dreamed one night of a ladder reaching up to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending on it. God spoke to Ya’akov and gave to him the promise he had given to Avraham (Abraham) and Yitshak concerning the land and descendants. The next morning Ya’akov took his stone pillow and set it up as a pillar, anointing it with oil. He named the place Beyt-El (Bethel) (“house of God”) and made a vow that if the Lord would be with him and provide for him, he would give a tithe to the Lord (Gn 28:10-22).

When Ya’akov reached the area of Haran, he met shepherds who knew Lavan. Rahel (Rachel), Lavan’s younger daughter, arrived with her father’s flock, and Ya’akov rolled the large stone from the mouth of the well and watered the sheep for her (Gn 29:1-10). When Rahel learned that Ya’akov was from their own family, she ran to tell her father, who greeted Ya’akov warmly. After staying with them for a month, Ya’akov was hired to tend Lavan’s flocks. When wages were discussed, Ya’akov proposed to work seven years to earn Rahel as his wife (vv 15-20).

At the end of seven years Ya’akov was set to claim his wages, but on the night of the wedding feast, Lavan gave his older daughter, Le’ah (Leah), to Ya’akov; Ya’akov did not discover the substitution until morning. He felt cheated and protested to Lavan, but Lavan insisted that according to custom the older daughter must marry first and proposed that Ya’akov work another seven years for Rahel. Ya’akov agreed to this and put in his time (Gn 29:21-30).

Genesis 29 and 30 relate the births of most of Ya’akov’s children. Le’ah bore Ya’akov four sons: Re’uven (Reuben), Shim’on (Simeon), Levi, and Yehudah (Judah) (Gn 29:31-35). She named her first son Re’uven (“see, a son”) since she felt that her husband would love her because she bore a son. Shim’on is derived from the root “hear,” since Le’ah thought that God had given her this son because he had heard that she was hated. Levi is related to the verb “join,” for Le’ah thought that her husband would be joined to her because of this third son. Yehudah means “praise,” for she praised the Lord at the birth of her fourth son.

Rahel had not conceived any children, so she gave her maid Bilhah to Ya’akov (Jacob). She bore him Dan and Naftali (Naphtali) (Gn 30:1-8). Rahel named the first son Dan (“he judged”) because God had judged, that is, vindicated her. Naftali means “my struggle, my wrestling,” for Rahel said she had wrestled with and overcome her sister.

Thereupon Le’ah gave her maid Zilpah to Ya’akov as a wife; she brought forth Gad and Asher (Gn 30:11). Gad means “fortune”; Le’ah said, “Good fortune,” when he was born. Asher (“happy”) was so named because Le’ah said, “Now the women will call me happy.”

Re’uven found some mandrakes in the field, and Le’ah traded them to Rahel for Ya’akov’s services. Le’ah then bore sons five and six, Yisakar (Issachar) and Zevulun (Zebulun), followed by a daughter, whom she named Dinah (Gn 30:14-21). Yisakar perhaps means “reward,” for Le’ah said that God had rewarded her for giving her maidservant to her husband. Zevulun probably means “honor”; Le’ah thought that now her husband would honor her.
At last Rahel herself conceived and bore her first child, a son whom she named Yosef (Joseph). “Yosef” means “he will add” or “may he add,” for Rahel wanted God to add another son to her.

Ya’akov wanted to leave and go back to Kena’an (Canaan), but Lavan wanted him to stay, for through divination he had learned that the Lord had blessed him because of Ya’akov (Gn 30:27). They discussed the matter of wages, and Ya’akov proposed that every speckled and spotted sheep and goat and every black lamb become his (vv 32-33). Lavan agreed to this, but he quickly removed all the animals marked in that fashion and put them under the care of his sons, some three days’ distance from the rest of the flocks (vv 35-36).

Ya’akov also contrived to gain an advantage; he tried to influence the genetics of the animals by putting speckled and streaked wooden rods by the water troughs when the best animals were breeding. The Lord blessed Ya’akov and he became rich in flocks and herds (Gn 30:37-43).

The sons of Lavan (Laban) became very bitter toward Ya’akov, and Lavan’s attitude toward him changed also. Ya’akov noticed this, and now the Lord spoke to Ya’akov and told him to return to Kena’an (Gn 31:3-16). Ya’akov held a family council with his two wives and told them how God had blessed him, even though their father had cheated him and had changed his wages ten times. Ya’akov organized his caravan while Lavan was away shearing sheep. Rahel stole her father’s household gods, for their possession would make the holder heir to Lavan’s estate (see Nuzi Tablets). The party took off, crossed the Perat (Euphrates), and headed for Gilead. Lavan and his relatives pursued them, but God spoke to Lavan in a dream, warning him not to say anything to Ya’akov.

When Lavan caught up with Ya’akov, he upbraided him for sneaking away and inquired about his household gods. Ya’akov did not know what Rahel had done, so he said that the one found with the gods should be put to death (Gn 31:32). Rahel had hidden them in a camel saddle and was sitting on the saddle when her father searched the tent. Lavan did not find the idols. After this, Ya’akov became angry and complained that he had served Lavan for 20 years and that Lavan had reduced his wages ten times.
Lavan suggested a covenant of peace, so the two men gathered stones to make a monument and called it “heap of witness.” Early the next morning Lavan said his farewells and returned home.

As Ya’akov and his household journeyed on, he was met by the angels of God (“God’s camp,” Gn 32:2), so he named that place Mahanayim (Mahanaim), “the two camps.” Ya’akov sent messengers ahead to inform Esav (Esau) of his return. They came back with the news that Esav was approaching with 400 men. Ya’akov was afraid and sought the Lord’s protection. To win Esav’s favor, Ya’akov sent ahead gifts of animals, and that night he sent his family and possessions across the ford of the Yabok (Jabbok) River. Ya’akov was left alone, and “a man” wrestled with him throughout the night. Toward dawn the man touched Ya’akov’s thigh, and his hip was dislocated, but Ya’akov would not give up until the “man” blessed him. Here the Lord changed Ya’akov’s name to Yisrael (Israel) (“he strives with God”), and Ya’akov named the place Peniel (“face of God”) because he had seen God face to face and lived (Gn 32:30).

Esav was getting near, so Ya’akov arranged his family and went forward, bowing low before his brother. But Esav was gracious and forgiving and the meeting was a happy one (Gn 33:4). Esav was surprised at Ya’akov’s large family and property and made every gesture of friendship. Esav returned to Se’ir (Seir), and Ya’akov moved on to Shekem (Shechem), where he bought a piece of land from Hamor, the father of Shekem. Ya’akov built an altar there and named it El-Elohey-Yisra’el (El-Elohe-Israel), “God, the God of Yisrael” (v 20).

Acting on the Lord’s instructions, Ya’akov (Jacob) moved to Beyt-El (Bethel) and expelled the foreign gods from his household. At Luz (Beyt-El) the Lord again met him and reaffirmed his new name, renewing his promise of land and descendants (Gn 35:9-15). As they journeyed south, Rahel (Rachel) died while giving birth to her second son (vv 16-20). She named him Ben-Oni (Ben-oni) (“son of my sorrow”), but Ya’akov changed his name to Benyamin (Benjamin) (“son of the right hand”). Ya’akov went on to Hevron (Hebron) and found that Yitshak (Isaac) was still living. Yitshak died at age 180 and was buried by Esav and Ya’akov.

Although the story of Ya’akov continues in the book of Genesis, the central figure of chapters 37–50 is Yosef, Ya’akov’s favorite son, the firstborn of Rahel. Ya’akov showed this favoritism so openly that the other sons became jealous of Yosef. They plotted to kill Yosef but instead sold him to a caravan of traders on their way to Mitsrayim (Egypt) (Gn 37:9-28). They took Yosef’s coat, dipped it into the blood of a goat, and took it to their father, telling him that they had found the robe. Ya’akov recognized the coat he had given his son and concluded that he was dead. Ya’akov was heartbroken and would not be comforted.

When a famine hit Kena’an, Ya’akov sent his sons to Mitsrayim to buy grain (Gn 42:1-5), keeping Benyamin at home. When the brothers returned to Kena’an, they reported to Ya’akov that the governor (who was really Yosef) had kept Shim’on (Simeon) as a hostage and demanded that they bring Benyamin with them when they came again for grain. The famine continued, and Ya’akov again sent his sons to Mitsrayim for grain. Very reluctantly, he permitted Benyamin to go with them, also sending a gift for the Mitsri (Egyptian) governor (43:11-14).

The next news Ya’akov received was that Yosef (Joseph) was alive in Mitsrayim and wanted his father and all his family to join him (Gn 45:21-28). Ya’akov went first to Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba) and made offerings to the Lord. The Lord spoke to Ya’akov, telling him to go down to Mitsrayim and confirming once more the promises he had previously made. Ya’akov and his descendants who were in Mitsrayim numbered 70, including the two sons of Yosef.

When Ya’akov reached Goshen, Yosef came to meet him, and there was a joyous reunion (Gn 46:28-30). Yosef reported the arrival of his father and brothers to the pharaoh (47:1) and took five of the brothers and his father to meet the ruler. Yisrael settled in the area of Goshen and prospered there. Ya’akov spent 17 years in Mitsrayim and reached the age of 147.

When Ya’akov sensed his death was near, he called Yosef and made him swear that he would bury him with his forebears in Kena’an (Canaan). Yosef took his two sons, Menasheh (Manasseh) and Efrayim (Ephraim), to his father for the patriarchal blessing. He presented the boys so that Menasheh, the firstborn, would be on Ya’akov’s right and Efrayim on his left. Ya’akov, however crossed his hands and gave the younger son the greater blessing (48:13-20). Ya’akov prophesied that his people would return to Kena’an, and he gave Yosef a double portion of the land. Then Ya’akov called for all his sons and gave to each of them a blessing (49:1-28). Yehudah (Judah) received the place of preeminence, and it is he who appears in the genealogies of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) (vv 8-12). The blessing of Yosef shows the mark of special favor (vv 22-26). Ya’akov also charged his sons to bury him in the cave of Makpelah (Machpelah) near Hevron, then he drew his feet up on the bed and died.

Yosef summoned the physicians to embalm his father according to Mitsri practice; there were 40 days for embalming and 70 days for the period of mourning (Gn 50:1-3). Arrangements were made to go to Kena’an to bury Ya’akov as Yosef had promised, and a large funeral procession, including many Mitsri officials as well as the family of Ya’akov, went up from Mitsrayim. The company mourned for seven days at the threshing floor of Atad; then the sons of Ya’akov buried him in the cave of Makpelah as he had requested. The entire group returned to Mitsrayim, and Yosef assured his brothers that he had no intention of avenging the wrong they had done him. God had meant the whole episode for good (vv 15-21).
Ya’akov as the Nation Yisrael
God made the same promises concerning the land and the nation to Avraham (Abraham), Yitshak, and Ya’akov, but it is by Ya’akov’s God-given name, Yisrael, that the nation is known.

The name Ya’akov is used for the nation about 100 times (e.g., Nm 24:5, 19; Dt 32:9; Ps 59:13). It is often found as a parallel to Yisrael (Israel) (e.g., Nm 23:7; Dt 33:10; Is 14:1). “Ya’akov” is also used specifically of the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Am 7:2, 5). In Isaiah 41:21 “the King of Ya’akov” refers to God himself.
See also Genesis, Book of; Israel, History of; Patriarchs, Period of the.

2. Father of Yosef, the husband of Maria (Mary) and earthly father of Yeshua according to Matay’s (Matthew’s; Grk. Matthaios’) genealogy (Mt 1:16). Lukas (Luke), however, names Eli (Heli) as Yosef’s father (Lk 3:24). See Genealogy of Jesus Christ (The Relationship between the Two Records).
JACOB’S LADDER*

When Ya’akov (Jacob) left home after deceiving his father, Yitshak (Isaac), into giving him the blessing that Yitshak had intended for Esav (Esau) (Gn 27:6-40), he was not only desirous of finding a wife from among the daughters of his mother’s brother, but he was also literally fleeing for his life, because Esav had determined to kill him (v 41). When he stopped to rest for the night in the open countryside, the Lord appeared to him in a dream and blessed him (28:10-22). In the vision Ya’akov saw a ladder reaching from the earth to heaven with angels ascending and descending upon it. At the top of the ladder stood the Lord himself, who confirmed to Ya’akov the promise previously given to Avraham (Abraham) (12:2-3, 7), and repeated to Yitshak (26:3-5). In the context it seems clear that the ladder with the ascending and descending angels depicts God reaching out to Ya’akov and making a way for Ya’akov to have a relationship with him. The communion that was to exist between God and Ya’akov is symbolized in the ladder and the movement of the angels. This communication between heaven and earth appears to be the same point that is made in John 1:50 when Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) says to Netanel (Nathanael) and his other disciples, “You will all see heaven open and the angels of God going up and down upon the Son of Man” (nlt). Ya’akov was so overwhelmed by God’s grace in revealing himself to him in this way that he named the place at which this took place Beyt-El (Bethel)—the House of God.
JACOB’S WELL

Place mentioned only in Yohan’s (John’s; Grk. Yoannes’) Gospel (Jn 4:5-29). It was here that Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) sat and talked with the unnamed woman of Shomron (Samaria), who readily accepted Yeshua’s words. This well is located in a plot of ground acquired by the patriarch Ya’akov (Jacob), about 300 yards (274 meters) southeast from the traditional tomb of Yosef (Joseph) (Gn 33:19; Jos 24:32; Jn 4:5-6). The site is about two miles (3.2 kilometers) southeast of modern Nablus, 600 yards (549 meters) southeast of the site of ancient Shekem (Shechem) (modern Balata), and 1,000 yards (914 meters) south of Sukar (Sychar) (modern Askar). Towering over the site on the northwest is Mt Eyval (Ebal) (at the foot of which lies Askar), and on the southwest Mt Gerizim, mountains of cursing and blessing, respectively (Dt 27:12-13; Jos 8:30-33). Near here Avraham (Abraham) built his first altar, and Ya’akov his second (Gn 12:6-7; 33:18-20). Thus the site is one of the most ancient and sacred in the Holy Land.

The well is about 100 feet (30.5 meters) in depth and one yard (.9 meter) in diameter, cut through limestone. Fed by subterranean streams from the adjacent mountain slopes, the water is pure and plentiful, the pride of the villagers. A church has existed on the site from at least AD 380. The Greek Orthodox Church acquired the site in 1885 and built a structure on the site. Access to the well is by steps leading from either side of the church altar to the well curb below.
JADA
See Jade.
JADAH
Variant of Yeho’adah (Jehoaddah) (1 Chr 8:36) and Yaerah (Jarah) (1 Chr 9:42). See Jehoadah, Jehoaddah.
JADDAI
Nevo’s (Nebo’s) descendant, who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era (Ezr 10:43).
JADDUA
1. Leader who set his seal on Ezra’s covenant during the postexilic era (Neh 10:21).

2. Elyashiv’s (Eliashib’s) descendant and a contemporary of Nehemyah (Nehemiah) (Neh 12:11, 22). Yadua’s (Jaddua’s) father, Yonatan (Jonathan) (v 11), is mentioned in the Elephantine papyri as Yohanan (Johanan) (see also v 22).
JADE*
Onam’s son from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 2:28, 32).
JADON

Workman on the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) wall after the return from exile. Yadon (Jadon) worked on the section near the Old Gate of the city with men from Giveon (Gibeon) and Mitspah (Mizpah). He was a Meronoti (Meronothite) (Neh 3:7).
JAEL

Wife of Hever (Heber). Though her husband was from the Keyni (Kenite) tribe, a longtime ally of Yisrael (Israel), he had chosen to side with Yavin (Jabin), the Kena’ani (Canaanite) king. Ya’el (Jael) demonstrated her loyalty to Yisrael, Yavin’s enemy, however, by inviting Sisera, Yavin’s general, into her tent, giving him milk instead of water, providing him a place to sleep, and then driving a tent peg into his temple (Jgs 4:17-18, 21-22). Deborah, the inspired poetess, reflecting on the God-given victory over the Kena’anim (Canaanites), praises Ya’el for this deed (5:6, 24-31).
JAGUR
Place in the extreme southern part of Yisrael (Israel), near Edom, inherited by Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe soon after the Conquest (Jos 15:21).
JAH*

Abbreviation of the covenant name of God, Yahweh (YHWH) or Yahweh (“Jehovah,” kjv; “Yahweh,” most modern translations). The fragment is often used in words and names (e.g., Hallelujah, Yah (Jah)aziel). See God, Names of.
JAHATH
1. Reayah’s (Reaiah’s) son and the father of Ahumay (Ahumai) and Lahad, Tsor’atim (Zorathites) from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 4:2).
2. Gershoni (Gershonite) Levite (1 Chr 6:20), whose descendant Asaf (Asaph) was appointed by King David to serve as a musician in the temple (v 43).
3. A descendant of Shimei, who was a descendant of Gereshon (Gershon) from Levi’s tribe (1 Chr 23:10-11).
4. Shelomit’s (Shelomith’s) son from Levi’s tribe (1 Chr 24:22).
5. Merari (Merarite) Levite, who was one of the supervisors of the temple repairs under Yoshiyah (Josiah) (2 Chr 34:12).
JAHAZ

Town east of the Dead Sea (in modern Yarden (Jordan)) where the Israelis (Israelites) defeated Sihon, king of the Amorim (Amorites), when he refused to permit them to pass through his land (Nm 21:23; Dt 2:32; Jgs 11:20). According to Joshua 13:18, Mosheh (Moses) gave the town to Re’uven’s (Reuben’s) tribe as part of its allotment. The town with its surrounding pasturelands was given to the Merari (Merarite) Levites (Jos 21:36; 1 Chr 6:78).

In later times, in prophetic oracles by both Yeshayah (Isaiah) (Is 15:4) and Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) (Jer 48:21), it is referred to as a city in the land of Moav (Moab). This may indicate that it was taken from Yisrael (Israel) by Moav (to whom it apparently belonged before Sihon conquered it). The town is mentioned on the Moavi (Moabite) Stone (known as the Divon (Dibon) Stele and dating to c. 845 BC) as the place where Meysha (Mesha), king of Moav, had lived while at war with Yisrael. According to Meysha, he took Yahats (Jahaz) from Yisrael and added it to his own territory.
JAHAZA*, JAHAZAH*
KJV spellings of Yahats (Jahaz). See Jahaz.
JAHAZIAH*
KJV rendering of Yahzeyah (Jahzeiah), Tikvah’s son, in Ezra 10:15. See Jahzeiah.
JAHAZIEL

1. Warrior from Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe who joined David at Tsiklag (Ziklag) in his struggle against King Sha’ul (Saul). Yahaziel (Jahaziel) was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers (1 Chr 12:4).

2. One of the two priests David appointed to blow trumpets before the ark as it was brought into the tent in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), where it remained until the completion of the temple by Shelomoh (Solomon) (1 Chr 16:6).
3. Levite belonging to the Kohatite (Kohathite) division appointed by David to temple duties (1 Chr 23:19; 24:23).

4. Levite of the sons of Asaf (Asaph) who encouraged Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) and the army of Yehudah (Judah) not to be dismayed by the size of Moavi (Moabite) and Amoni (Ammonite) armies coming against them but to stand still and see the victory of the Lord (2 Chr 20:14). Yehoshafat’s response exemplified a godly king encouraging his people to have faith in the Lord their God (vv 18-21).
5. Shekanyah’s (Shecaniah’s) father. Shekanyah returned to Yerushalem with Ezra after the exile (Ezr 8:5).
JAHDAI
Kalev’s (Caleb’s) descendant from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 2:47).
JAHDIEL

One of the family heads of Menasheh’s (Manasseh’s) tribe dwelling east of the Yarden (Jordan) following the allotment of the land (1 Chr 5:24). He was noted as one of the mighty warriors in his tribe.
JAHDO

Gadi (Gadite), son of Buz and a forefather of a number of valiant men who were registered during the reigns of King Yarov’am (Jeroboam) of Yisrael (Israel) (793–753 BC) and King Yotam (Jotham) of Yehudah (Judah) (750–735 BC; 1 Chr 5:14).
JAHLEEL, JAHLEELITE
Zevulun’s (Zebulun’s) son (Gn 46:14) and the founder of the Yahle’eli (Jahleelite) family (Nm 26:26).
JAHMAI
Tola’s son from Yisakar’s (Issachar’s) tribe (1 Chr 7:2).
JAHZAH*
Alternate form of Yahats (Jahaz), a town east of the Dead Sea, in 1 Chronicles 6:78 (nlt mg) and Jeremiah 48:21 (nlt mg). See Jahaz.
JAHZEEL, JAHZEELITE
Naftali’s (Naphtali’s) son (Gn 46:24; 1 Chr 7:13) and founder of the Yahtse’eli (Jahzeelite) family (Nm 26:48).
JAHZEIAH

Tikvah’s son and one of the persons named in connection with the divorce proceedings between the Israelis (Israelites) and their foreign wives (Ezr 10:15). Opinions differ as to whether he was for or against the proceedings. While the Hebrew text can be justifiably read either way, the grammar favors the interpretation that Yahzeyah (Jahzeiah) opposed the proceedings (see nlt).
JAHZERAH

Ancestor of a priest who returned to Yehudah (Judah) after the Babylonian exile (1 Chr 9:12). He is called Ahzay (Ahzai) in Nehemiah 11:13. Little else is known about him except that he was a great-grandson of a priest named Imer (Immer) who lived in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) before the exile.
See also Ahzai.
JAHZIEL*
Alternate spelling of Yahtse’el (Jahzeel), Naftali’s (Naphtali’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 7:13 (nlt mg). See Jahzeel, Jahzeelite.
JAIR

1. Descendant of Menasheh (Manasseh) (Nm 32:41), who at the time of the Conquest took several villages in the Argov (Argob) region of Bashan and Gilead and called them after his own name, Havot-Ya’ir (Havvoth-jair), meaning “Towns of Yair (Jair)” (Dt 3:14; cf. Jos 13:30; 1 Kgs 4:13; 1 Chr 2:23).
See also Havoth-jair, Havvoth-jair.
2. One of the judges of Yisrael (Israel). He judged Yisrael 22 years. His being a Giladi (Gileadite) makes it probable that he was a descendant of #1 above (Jgs 10:3-5).
3. Father of Elhanan, who killed Lahmi, Galyat’s (Goliath’s) brother (1 Chr 20:5). In 2 Samuel 21:19 he is called Ya’are-Oregim (Jaare-oregim).

4. Father of Mordekai (Mordecai) (Est 2:5). Because of the time lapse from the capture of Yekaneyah (Jeconiah), king of Yehudah (Judah) (597 BC), to the beginning of the reign of Ahashverosh (Xerxes), king of Paras (Persia) (486 BC), Yair was either the one taken captive with Yekaneyah or his father, Shimei, was, in which case Yair would have been born during the Captivity.
JAIRITE
Descendant of Yair (Jair) from Menasheh’s (Manasseh’s) tribe (2 Sm 20:26). See Jair #1.
JAIRUS

Leader of the synagogue, perhaps at Kafarnaoum (Capernaum). Yair (Jairus) sought Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) among the crowds and petitioned him to come and heal his critically ill daughter. While delayed by another healing, Yeshua learned that Yair’s daughter had died. Encouraging Yair not to fear but to believe, Yeshua went on to the leader’s house, dismissed the mourners, and brought the child back to life (Mk 5:22, 35-42; Lk 8:41, 49-55).
JAKAN*
KJV spelling of Ya’akan (Jaakan), Esav’s (Esau’s) descendant, in 1 Chronicles 1:42. See Jaakan.
JAKEH
Agur’s father. Agur authored a series of proverbs addressed to Itiel (Ithiel) and Ukal (Ucal) (Prv 30:1).
JAKIM
1. Shimei’s descendant from Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe (1 Chr 8:19).
2. Family leader of the 12th group of Aharon’s (Aaron’s) descendants assigned to temple duty in David’s time (1 Chr 24:12).
JAKIN
See Jachin.
JAKIN AND BOAZ
See Jachin and Boaz.
JAKINITE
See Jachinite.
JALAM
Esav’s (Esau’s) son and chief of an Edomi (Edomite) clan (Gn 36:5, 14, 18; 1 Chr 1:35).
JALON
Ezra’s (Ezrah’s) son from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 4:17).
JAMBRES
Enemy of Mosheh (Moses), who, along with Yannes (Jannes), is used by Paulos (Paul) as an example of the type of person to avoid (2 Tm 3:8-9). See Jannes and Jambres.
JAMBRI

Ancestor of an Aravi (Arab) tribe. During the Hasmonean (Maccabean) wars when Yonatan (Jonathan) was ruler, the Jambrites captured a baggage train of the Yehudim (Jews) when it was being sent to the Nabateans for safekeeping (1 Macc 9:36).
JAMES (Person)
1. Ya’akov (James), brother of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus); leading elder in the church at Yerushalem (Jerusalem); author of the epistle bearing his name.

The only two references to Ya’akov in the Gospels mention him with his brothers Yosef (Joseph) (Greek Yoseh (Joses)), Shim’on (Simon), and Yehudah (Judas; Grk. Yudas) (Mt 13:55; Mk 6:3). This Ya’akov may have been, after Yeshua, the oldest of the brothers. The question has been raised about whether these were indeed full brothers of Yeshua by Maria (Mary), for such a situation has created difficulty for those who cannot square it with their views on the perpetual virginity of Maria. But there seems to be no good reason to challenge the fact from Scripture. As with the other brothers, Ya’akov apparently did not accept Yeshua’s authority during his earthly life (Jn 7:5).

There is no specific mention of Ya’akov’s conversion; it may have dated from Yeshua’s appearance to him and the others after Yeshua’s resurrection (1 Cor 15:7). He became head of the church at Yerushalem (Acts 12:17; 21:18; Gal 2:9). Although Yeshua had always taught the relative subordination of family ties (Mt 12:48-50; Mk 3:33-35; Lk 8:21), it is hard to believe that Ya’akov’s authority was not somehow enhanced because of his relationship to the Master.

Ya’akov was regarded as an apostle (Gal 1:19), although he was not one of the Twelve. Some suggest he was a replacement for the martyred son of Zavday (Zebedee); others infer his apostleship by widening the scope of that term to embrace both “the Twelve” and “all the apostles” (see the two separate categories cited in 1 Cor 15:5, 7).

Tradition stated that Ya’akov was appointed the first bishop of Yerushalem by the Lord himself as well as the apostles. What is certain is that he presided over the first Council of Yerushalem, called to consider the terms for admission of Gentiles into the Christian church, and he may have formulated the decree that met with the approval of all his colleagues and was sent to the churches of Antiokeia (Antioch), Aram (Syria), and Kilikia (Cilicia) (Acts 15:19-20). Ya’akov evidently regarded his own special ministry as being to the Yehudim (Jews), and his was a mediating role in the controversy that arose in the young church around the place of the law for those who had become Christians, from both Gentile and Jewish origins.

That he continued to have strong Jewish-Christian sympathies is apparent from the request made to Paulos (Paul) when the latter visited Yerushalem for the last time (Acts 21:18-25). This was also the last mention in Acts of Ya’akov’s career. His name also occurs in the NT as the traditional author of the Epistle of Ya’akov, where he describes himself as “a slave of God and of the Lord Yeshua Christ” (Jas 1:1).

According to Hegesippus (c. 180), Ya’akov’s faithful adherence to the Jewish law and his austere lifestyle led to the designation “the Just.” It seems clear that Ya’akov suffered martyrdom. Josephus places it in the year 61, when there was a Jewish uprising after the death of Festos (Festus) the procurator and before his successor had been appointed.
2. Ya’akov, son of Halfay (Alphaeus); one of the 12 apostles.

Ya’akov, son of Halfay, is always listed as one of the 12 apostles (Mt 10:3; Mk 3:18; Lk 6:15; Acts 1:13), but nothing is known for certain about him. Levi (also known as Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios)) is also described as the son of Halfay (Mk 2:14), but it is improbable that he and Ya’akov were brothers. Many scholars have identified him with the one called “Ya’akov the less” or “Ya’akov the smaller.” The description “the less” seems to have been given to distinguish him from the son of Zavday, and it may signify that he was either smaller or younger than Zavday’s son (the Greek word can cover both interpretations).
3. Ya’akov, son of Zavday. One of the 12 apostles; the first of them to be martyred (AD 44).

Ya’akov was a Galili (Galilean) fisherman whose circumstances we can suppose to have been comfortable (Mk 1:19-20) and who was called to be one of the disciples at the same time as his brother Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) (Mt 4:21; Mk 1:19-20). It is reasonable to assume that he was older than Yohan, both because he is nearly always mentioned first and because Yohan is sometimes identified as “the brother of Ya’akov” (Mt 10:2; 17:1; Mk 3:17; 5:37).

Ya’akov (James), Yohan, and Shim’on Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros), who were part of a fishing partnership that included Andreas (Andrew), Shim’on’s brother (Lk 5:10), were a trio who attained in some sense a place of primacy among the disciples. They are found at the center of things—for example, when Yair’s (Jairus’) daughter was raised (Mk 5:37; Lk 8:51), at the Transfiguration (Mt 17:1; Mk 9:2; Lk 9:28), on the Mount of Olives (Mk 13:3), and in the Garden of Gethsaimanai (Gethsemane) (Mt 26:37; Mk 14:33). It was Ya’akov and Yohan, moreover, who had earlier accompanied Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) to the home of Shim’on and Andreas (Mk 1:29).

Ya’akov and Yohan were given by Yeshua the nickname Thunder Brothers (Boanerges), or “sons of thunder” (Mk 3:17), when they were rebuked by the Lord for impetuous speech and for having totally misconceived the purpose of his coming. This may have been the consequence of the suggestion made by them that they should pray for the destruction of the Shomroni (Samaritan) village, the inhabitants of which had rejected the Lord’s messengers (Lk 9:54; cf. Mk 9:38; Lk 9:49).

The presumptuous and ill-considered thinking of the two brothers was obvious also when, after asking with his brother for a place of honor in the kingdom, Ya’akov was corecipient of the prophecy that they would drink the cup their Master was to drink (Mk 10:35-40; cf. Mt 20:20-23). The two sons of Zavday are also assumed to have been present with the other disciples when the risen Christ appeared by the Sea of Galil (Galilee) (Jn 21:1), though curiously Ya’akov’s name is nowhere mentioned in the fourth Gospel.

We know nothing about Ya’akov’s career subsequently until about the year 44, when Yeshua’s prophecy was fulfilled: Ya’akov was killed “by the sword” by Herodes (Herod) Agrippas (Agrippa) I, and thus became the first of the Twelve whose martyrdom was referred to in the NT (Acts 12:1-2).

The wife of Zavday (Zebedee) was Salome (Mt 27:56; Mk 15:40), who may have been a sister of the Lord’s mother (Jn 19:25). If this were so, it would mean that Ya’akov and Yohan were first cousins of Yeshua and that they may have considered themselves to have been in a privileged position.
JAMES, Letter of
First letter of the General Epistles.
Preview

• Date, Origin, and Destination
• Purpose of Writing and Theological Teaching
• Content
Author

According to the salutation, this letter was written by “Ya’akov (James), a slave of God and of the Lord Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ” (Jas 1:1, nlt). But who was this Ya’akov? Of the several mentioned in the NT, only two have ever been proposed as the author of this letter—Ya’akov the son of Zavday (Zebedee), and Ya’akov the Lord’s brother.

The Ya’akov who wrote this epistle was probably not Ya’akov the son of Zavday, for he was martyred too early (AD 44) to have written it (see Acts 12:1-2). Most scholars have identified this Ya’akov as Yeshua’s brother (Mk 6:3; Gal 1:19), the prominent elder of the church in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Acts 15:13, 19; 21:17-25; Gal 2:12). The whole character of the epistle coincides with what we know of this Ya’akov’s legalism and Jewishness.

As an elder of Yerushalem writing to the 12 tribes of the dispersion (which came as a result of the persecution noted in Acts 11:19), Ya’akov set forth the gospel in its relation to the law, which the Yehudim (Jews) revered. As Paulos’s (Paul’s) epistles are a commentary on the doctrines flowing from the death and resurrection of Christ, so Ya’akov’s epistle has a close connection with Christ’s teaching during his life on earth, especially his Sermon on the Mount. In both the Sermon on the Mount and the Epistle of Ya’akov, the law is represented as fulfilled in love, and the very language is remarkably similar (cf. Jas 1:2 with Mt 5:12; Jas 1:4 with Mt 5:48; Jas 1:5 and 5:14-15 with Mt 7:7-11; Jas 2:13 with Mt 5:7 and 6:14-15; Jas 2:10 with Mt 5:19; Jas 4:4 with Mt 6:24; Jas 4:11 with Mt 7:1-2; Jas 5:2 with Mt 6:19). The whole spirit of this epistle breathes the same gospel-righteousness that the Sermon on the Mount inculcates as the highest realization of the law. Ya’akov’s own character as “the Just” suited this coincidence (cf. Jas 1:20; 2:10; 3:18 with Mt 5:20). It also fitted him for presiding over a church still zealous for the law (Acts 21:18-24; Gal 2:12). If any could win the Yehudim to the gospel, he was the most likely one because he presented a pattern of OT righteousness, combined with evangelical faith (cf. also Jas 2:8 with Mt 5:44, 48).
Date, Origin, and Destination

Many scholars confirm an early date for Ya’akov’s epistle, even as early as AD 45–49, because the whole orientation of the epistle fits the early history of the church, an era in which many Jewish Christians had not made a complete severance from Youdaismos (Judaism). Thus, Ya’akov uses the terms “the twelve tribes” (Jas 1:1) and “the synagogue” (2:2, Greek); he speaks as an OT prophet (5:1ff.) and as one fond of OT proverbs (cf. Jas 1:5 with Prv 2:6; Jas 1:19 with Prv 29:20; Jas 3:18 with Prv 11:30; Jas 4:13-16 with Prv 27:1; and Jas 5:20 with Prv 10:12). Ya’akov’s message, as was noted earlier, closely follows Yeshua’s sermons. His message does not deal with the Jewish/Gentile problems that arose in the 50s and 60s. Moreover, he, unlike Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros), Yehudah (Jude; Grk. Yudas), and Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) (in their epistles), did not deal with false teachings. All these facts point to an early date. This date is probably before AD 50, when the first Yerushalem Council assembled to discuss the Jewish/Gentile problem (Acts 15:1ff.). Also, the date is probably after AD 44, the time of the persecution instigated by Herodes (Herod) Agrippas (Agrippa) (12:1). This persecution would have caused many Jewish Christians to leave Yerushalem and thereby be “the dispersed” (Jas 1:1). Thus, Ya’akov should be dated AD 45–49. As such, the Epistle of Ya’akov was the first NT book to be written. If these dates are not accurate, then we are, at least, sure that it was written before AD 61 or 62, the time of Ya’akov’s martyrdom, according to Josephus.

Although a number of suggestions have been made from time to time about the origin of the book, there can be little doubt that the letter was written in Palestine. The author makes allusions that are Near Eastern generally and Palestinian particularly (cf. “the early and late rain,” 5:7; the spring of brackish water, 3:11; the fig, olive, and vine, 3:12; and the “scorching heat,” 1:11).

The contents of the letter indicate clearly that Ya’akov was writing to Jewish Christians. They are called “the twelve tribes,” a title of Yisrael (Israel) (1:1); their Christianity is assumed in 2:1; their place of meeting is called a synagogue (2:2); and they are told about the compassion of “the Lord Almighty” (5:4)—a name for God used in the OT. In the shorter, disconnected passages of the letter, it is impossible to discover anything about the readers’ circumstances. Most of these exhortations are general and relate to social and spiritual conditions one might find among any group of Christians in any age. The more extended passages that deal with social conditions (2:1-12; 5:1-11) do provide information about the readers’ situation. Ya’akov is addressing poor Christians who are employed as farm laborers by wealthy landowners. A few rich may be included among his Jewish Christian readers (cf. 4:13-17), but Ya’akov is primarily concerned with the poor. His statements denouncing the rich are reminiscent of the OT prophets, especially Amos.
Purpose of Writing and Theological Teaching

The letter of Ya’akov was written (1) to strengthen Jewish Christians undergoing trial (Jas 1:2-4, 13-15; 5:7-11); (2) to correct a misunderstanding of the Pauline doctrine of justification by faith (2:14-26); and (3) to pass down to first-generation Christians a wealth of practical wisdom.

Ya’akov’s theology is not dogmatic; it omits the great theological themes that dominate Paulos’s writings and play such an important role in the rest of the books of the NT. Ya’akov makes no mention of the Incarnation, and the name of Christ appears only twice (1:1; 2:1). No mention is made of Christ’s sufferings, death, or resurrection.

Ya’akov’s (James’) theology is practical and has a decided Jewish flavor. The distinctive Christian features, of course, are there. Ya’akov has simply mingled the two to produce a Jewish-Christian document.
The outstanding theological themes of the letter are as follows:
Temptations and Trials

The typically Jewish teachings—joy in trials and the use of trials for the building and perfecting of character—are both found in the letter (1:2-4). Ya’akov also discusses the origin of temptation (vv 13-15). Here the author comes into conflict with contemporary Jewish theology. The rabbinical solution to the problem of the origin of sin was that there was an evil tendency in man that enticed man to sin. The rabbis reasoned that since God is the Creator of all things, including the evil impulse in people, they are not responsible for their sins. No, says Ya’akov. “And remember, no one who wants to do wrong should ever say, ‘God is tempting me.’ God is never tempted to do wrong, and he never tempts anyone else either. Temptation comes from the lure of our own evil desires” (vv 13-14, nlt).
Law

The entire letter is concerned with ethical teaching; there is no mention of the central gospel truths of Christ’s death and resurrection. Ya’akov presupposes the gospel and presents the ethical side of Christianity as a perfect law. He seems to be reassuring his Jewish-Christian readers that for them there is still law (the priceless possession of every Yehudi (Jew)).

The law (ethical teaching of Christianity) is a perfect law (1:25) because it was perfected by Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ. It is also a law of freedom—that is, a law that applies to those who have freedom, not from law, but from sin and self through the “word of truth.” Thus “law” is a Palestinian-Christian Yehudi’s way of describing the ethical teaching of the Christian faith, the standard of conduct for the believer in Yeshua Christ.

This tendency to describe Christian ethical teaching as law is found in 2:8-13, a passage that arises out of a rebuke against the favoritism that Ya’akov’s readers were showing toward the rich. This favoritism was being condoned by an appeal to the law of love to one’s neighbor. So Ya’akov writes, “It is good when you truly obey our Lord’s royal command” (2:8, nlt). The “royal command” is for those who are of God’s kingdom; it is the rule of faith for those who have willingly subjected themselves to God’s rule. The identification of law with the ethical side of Christianity runs through the entire letter.
Faith and Works

Faith plays an important role in the theology of Ya’akov. The basic element of piety (1:3; cf. 2:5) is belief in God—not merely belief in his existence but belief in his character as being good and benevolent in his dealings with mankind (1:6). Faith includes belief in the power of God and in his ability to perform miraculous acts; it is closely associated with prayer (5:15-16; cf. 1:6). Ya’akov has a dynamic concept of faith and clearly goes beyond Youdaismos (Judaism) when he speaks of faith directed toward the Lord Yeshua Christ (2:1).

Similarities exist between the concept of faith in Ya’akov and that concept in the teachings of Yeshua. For the Lord Yeshua, also, faith meant gaining access to the divine power and is often associated with healing (cf. Mt 21:22; Mk 5:34; 11:24).

The best-known passage in which faith is mentioned is James 2:14-26, where it is contrasted with works. From a close study of this passage, it can be determined that Ya’akov (James) is not contradicting Paulos (Paul). For both Ya’akov and Paulos, faith is directed toward the Lord Yeshua Christ; such faith will always produce good works. The faith of which Ya’akov speaks is not faith in the Hebraic sense of trust in God that results in moral action. This is not recognized as true faith by Ya’akov (cf. “if a man says he has faith,” 2:14), and Paulos would agree with him.

Ya’akov’s use of the word “works” differs significantly from Paulos’s. For Ya’akov, “works” are works of faith, the ethical outworking of true spirituality and include especially the “work of love” (2:8). (Paulos would probably call such works “the fruit of the Spirit.”) When Paulos uses the word “works,” he usually has in mind the works of the law whereby people attempt to establish their own righteousness before God. It is against such theological heresy that Paulos’s strongest polemics are addressed in the letters to the Galatians and Romans.
Wisdom

Ya’akov’s concept of wisdom also reveals the Jewish background of the letter. Wisdom is primarily practical, not philosophical. It is not to be identified with reasoning power or the ability to apprehend intellectual problems; it has nothing to do with the questions how or why. It is to be sought by earnest prayer and is a gift from God (Jas 1:5). Both of these ideas find their roots in the Wisdom Literature of the Yehudim (Jews) (cf. Prv 2:6; Wisd of Sol 7:7; Ecclus 1:1). The wise man demonstrates his wisdom by his good life (Jas 3:13), whereas the wisdom that produces jealousy and selfishness is not God’s kind of wisdom (vv 15-16).
Doctrine of the End Time
Three important end-time themes are touched upon in the letter.
The Kingdom of God

Mention of the kingdom of God grows out of a discussion of favoritism in the first half of chapter 2. No favoritism is to be shown to the rich, for Ya’akov asks, “Hasn’t God chosen the poor in this world to be rich in faith? Aren’t they the ones who will inherit the kingdom God promised to those who love him?” (2:5, nlt). This echoes our Lord’s teaching in Luke 6:20: “God blesses you who are poor, for the Kingdom of God is given to you” (nlt). The kingdom is the reign of God partially realized in this life but fully realized in the life to come (cf. “promised,” Jas 2:5).
Judgment

This is a dominant end-time theme of the letter. In 2:12, the readers are admonished to speak and act, remembering that they will be judged under the law of liberty, and they are reminded that judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. In other words, judgment will be administered according to “works of love.” In 3:1, Ya’akov addresses teachers and reminds them that privilege is another basis on which God judges.

The theme of judgment again appears in 5:1-6, and here the author reaches prophetic heights. God’s judgment will fall on the wealthy landowners who have lived self-indulgent, irresponsible lives. Not only have they cheated their poor tenant farmers; they have even “condemned and killed good people who had no power to defend themselves against you [the landowners]” (5:6, nlt). All this has made them ripe for judgment (“your hearts are nice and fat, ready for the slaughter”—v 5, nlt).

The final passage on judgment (5:9) is addressed to those who are exploited or suffering. Ya’akov’s (James’) word of exhortation is that they are not to grumble against each other. Judging is God’s business, and the Judge is close at hand.
The Second Coming

The hope of Christ’s coming is presented as the great stimulus for Christian living. Every kind of suffering and trial must be endured because the coming of Christ is at hand (5:8). This expectancy is powerful and immediate—like that found in the Thessalonikai (Thessalonian) letters.
Content

In the true spirit of Wisdom Literature, Ya’akov touches upon many subjects. His short, abrupt paragraphs have been likened to a string of pearls—each is an entity in itself. Some transitions exist, but they are often difficult to find and Ya’akov moves quickly from one subject to another.

The author begins by identifying himself as the “slave of God and of the Lord Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ,” and his readers as the “twelve tribes in the dispersion” (see nlt mg)—that is, the Jewish Christians who left Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and Yisrael (Israel) due to persecution.

His first word is one of encouragement. Trials are to be counted as joy because they are God’s way of testing the believer, and they produce spiritual maturity. If the reason for a trial is not clear, God can and will give the answer. He is a lavish giver of wisdom to those who really want it (1:5-8).

A poor Christian should be proud of his exalted position in Yeshua Christ, and a rich Christian should be glad that he has discovered there are more important things than wealth. Riches are transitory, like quickly wilting flowers under the hot Palestine sun (1:9-11).

God promises life to those who endure trials. One must not blame God for temptation, for it is contrary to his very nature either to be tempted or to tempt people. Temptation has its origin in people’s selfish desire—a desire that, when brought to full fruition, produces death (1:12-15). God is not the origin of temptation but the source of all good. He has given people his best gift, the gift of new life, and this has come through the gospel (vv 16-18).

The proper attitude toward the Word of Truth is receptivity, not anger, and effective listening to that word involves spiritual preparation of heart and mind. Such a reception of the word brings salvation (1:19-21). The word is to be acted upon, not merely listened to. To be a passive hearer is to be like a man who sees himself in a mirror, and because he takes such a fleeting glance, forgets what he sees. An active hearer, one who takes a long look in the mirror of God’s Word, will become a doer, and God will bring great blessing into his life (vv 22-25).
True religion is an intensely practical thing. It involves such things as controlling one’s tongue, looking after the needs of orphans and widows, and adopting a nonworldly lifestyle (1:26-27).

Favoritism and faith in Yeshua Christ do not go together. It is wrong to show favoritism to a rich man when he comes into the assembly and to ignore a poor man. God has chosen poor people to be heirs of his kingdom. Furthermore, to show favoritism to the rich does not make sense, since they are the very ones who drag Christians into court and blaspheme the name of Christ (2:1-7). If, by showing deference to the rich, the royal law—to love one’s neighbor as oneself —is fulfilled, well and good. But to show favoritism is sin, and such sin will be judged by God. In order to be a lawbreaker one has only to break a single law (vv 8-13).

Can a faith that does not produce works save a person? What good is a faith that does not respond to human need? Such a faith is dead. Someone will object by saying that there are “faith Christians” and there are “works Christians.” But this is not so. True faith is always demonstrated by works. It is not enough to have orthodox beliefs. Even the demons are theologically orthodox! Avraham (Abraham), by offering up Yitshak (Isaac), is an example of how true faith and works go together. Even Rahav (Rahab) the prostitute demonstrated her faith by protecting the spies at Yeriho (Jericho). So faith and works are inseparable (2:14-26).

Not many people should become spiritual teachers, because of the awesome responsibility involved. All of us are subject to mistakes, especially mistakes of the tongue, because the tongue is almost impossible to control. It is like a destructive blaze set by hell itself. The tongue is also inconsistent; it is used both to praise God and to curse men. Such inconsistency ought not to be (3:1-12).
True wisdom will always evidence itself in ethical living, whereas false wisdom produces jealousy and selfish ambition (3:13-18).

Strife and conflict arise out of illegitimate desires. Failure to have what one wants arises either from not asking God for it or from asking for the wrong thing. To be a friend of the world is to be an enemy of God, for God is a jealous God and will brook no rivals. He also opposes the proud but offers abundant grace to the humble (4:1-10).

To speak against a brother or sister, or to judge them, is to speak against God’s law and to judge it. The Christian’s proper role is to be a doer of the law, not a judge. The role of judge belongs to God alone (4:11-12).

Life is uncertain. Therefore, plans for traveling or doing business should be made with the realization that all are subject to the will of God. To do otherwise is to be boastful and arrogant. When what is right is clearly known and one fails to do it, that is sin (4:13-17).

Judgment is coming to the rich because they are hoarding their wealth instead of using it for good purposes. God is not unmindful of the cries of the poor whom the rich have cheated and unjustly condemned. He is preparing the selfish, unscrupulous rich for a day of awful judgment (5:1-6).

In the midst of suffering and injustice, the poor are to be patient for Christ’s coming, as the farmer must be patient as he waits for God to send the rains to cause his crops to grow and ripen. The return of Christ is at hand and therefore complaining and judging one another must cease. Iyov (Job) is a good example of patience and endurance in suffering. One need not use oaths to guarantee the truthfulness of his statements. A single yes or no is sufficient (5:7-12).

Suffering should elicit prayer, cheerfulness, and praise. When believers are sick, they should call the elders of the church to pray for them and anoint them with oil. God has promised to answer such prayers. If the sickness is due to personal sin, and if that sin is confessed, God will forgive. Eliyah (Elijah) is a classic example of how the prayer of a righteous man has powerful results (5:13-18).

If a Christian sees that another Christian has strayed from the truth and is able to bring him or her back into fellowship with Christ and his church, the consequences will be (1) that the sinner will be saved from death, and (2) that God will forgive the erring Christian (5:19-20).
See also Brothers of Jesus; James (Person).

JAMINITE

JAMNIA

JANAI

JANIM

JANNES AND JAMBRES

Two of Par’oh’s (Pharaoh’s) magicians, who opposed Mosheh (Moses) and tried to show that they were as effective as he at working miracles (Ex 7–9). Jewish legend regarded Yannes (Jannes) and Yambres (Jambres) (somewhat improbably) as sons of Bil’am (Balaam), the Midyanite (Midianite) prophet of Numbers 22–24. Curiously, the Exodus chapters do not identify them by name. The only biblical reference to them appears in the NT. The apostle Paulos (Paul) saw similarity between Yannes and Yambres and the false teachers of debased intellect who were enemies of the truth in his day (2 Tm 3:6-8).

Much speculation has arisen about the two names. They are apparently Semitic, but their precise derivation is unclear. They are referred to in the Qumran documents and in late Jewish, pagan, and early Christian literature. Variations include “Yohanneh and his brother” (Qumran), “Yohane and Mamre” (Babylonian Talmud), and “Mambres” (the translation in most Latin and some Greek manuscripts of 2 Tm 3:8). The names appear also in the writings of Pliny (first century AD) and of Apuleius and Numenios (Numenius) (both second century), though both names are not always cited.

Origen, an Alexandria (Alexandrian) church father, twice referred to an apocryphal work entitled The Book of Yannes and Yambres, suggesting that it was the source of Paulos’s words in 2 Timotheos (Timothy). A Latin church document called the Gelasian Decree (fifth or sixth century?) mentions Penitence of Yannes and Yambres, possibly the work mentioned by Origen.
JANOAH
1. City defining the eastern border of Efrayim’s (Ephraim’s) territory, located southeast of Shekem (Shechem) and northeast of Shiloh (Jos 16:6-7). It has been identified with modern Khirbet Yanun.

2. Town (modern Yanuh) of Naftali’s (Naphtali’s) tribe captured by Tiglat-Pileser (Tiglath-pileser), king of Ashur (Assyria), during the reign of King Pekah of Yisrael (Israel) in 732 BC (2 Kgs 15:29).
JANOHAH*
KJV spelling of Yanoah (Janoah), a town in Efrayim’s (Ephraim’s) territory, in Joshua 16:6-7. See Janoah #1.
JANUM*
KJV spelling of Yanum (Janim), a town in Yehudah’s (Judah’s) territory, in Joshua 15:53. See Janim.
JAPHETH

One of Noah’s three sons (Gn 5:32; 7:13; 9:18, 23, 27; 10:1-5; 1 Chr 1:4-5) who, along with his wife, was among the eight human survivors of the great Flood. Because Yefet (Japheth) and his brother Shem acted with respect and modesty in covering their father’s nakedness while he was in a drunken condition (Gn 9:20-23), they were both blessed in Noah’s prophetic pronouncement of Genesis 9:26-27. Of Yefet, Noah said, “God enlarge Yefet, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem; and let Kena’an (Canaan) be his slave” (rsv). There are two interpretations of the meaning of this prophecy. Some understand the enlargement of Yefet to be a reference to a great increase in numbers of descendants. “To dwell in the tents of Shem” is understood as Yefet’s sharing in the blessing of Shem. According to this view, there is to be a time when God will work primarily with Shem (the people of Yisrael (Israel)), but then, at a later time, Yefet will be brought into connection with the faith of Yisrael and share in its promises. In this view fulfillment is found in the opening of the gospel to the Gentiles at the inception of the NT church. Others understand the “enlargement of Yefet” to refer to territorial enlargement, and the “dwelling in the tents of Shem” as the conquest of Shemite territory by Japhethites. In this view, fulfillment is found in the Greek and Roman conquests of Palestine.

In the “table of nations” in Genesis 10:2, Yefet is listed as the father of Gomer, Magog, Maday (Madai), Yavan (Javan), Tuval (Tubal), Meshek (Meshech), and Tiras. These are the ancestors of peoples who lived to the north and west of Yisrael and who spoke what today are classified as Indo-European languages.
See also Nations; Noah #1.
JAPHIA (Person)

1. King of Lakish (Lachish) who joined an alliance of four other Amori (Amorite) kings to punish Giveon (Gibeon) for its treaty with the Yehudim (Jews). Yehoshua (Joshua) dealt a total defeat to the Amorim (Amorites) at the battle of Beyt-Horon (Beth-horon) (aided by hailstones and the sun standing still). Yafia (Japhia) and the four kings hid in a cave at Makedah (Makkedah) but were discovered and hung by Yehoshua (Jos 10:3-27).
2. Son born to David while he was king in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (2 Sm 5:15; 1 Chr 3:7; 14:6).
JAPHIA (Place)

Town described as part of the southern border of Zevulun’s (Zebulun’s) territory (Jos 19:12). It has been identified with modern Yafa, about two miles (3.2 kilometers) southwest of Nazaret (Nazareth).
JAPHLET

JAPHLETITES
People occupying an area that marked part of the southern border of Efrayim’s (Ephraim’s) territory in the vicinity of Beyt-Horon (Beth-horon) (Jos 16:3).

JAREB*

Name used by Hoshea (Hosea) to designate an Assyrian king (Hos 5:13). Because no such name is to be found in the Assyrian king lists, some have conjectured that it designated Sargon, but this is mere speculation. In all probability Hoshea chose this name (which in Hebrew means “contentious”) to describe the opposition that Efrayim (Ephraim) and Yehudah (Judah) would encounter from a contentious king in Ashur (Assyria) because of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) sin (10:6).
JARED
Mahalalel’s son and a descendant of Shet (Seth). He was the father of Hanok (Enoch) (Gn 5:15-20; 1 Chr 1:2; Lk 3:37). See Genealogy of Jesus Christ.
JARESIAH*
KJV rendering of Ya’areshyah (Jaareshiah), Yeroham’s (Jeroham’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 8:27. See Jaareshiah.
JARHA
Mitsri (Egyptian) servant of Sheshan, Yerahme’el’s (Jerahmeel’s) descendant, who was given his master’s daughter in marriage. Sheshan did this because he had no sons (1 Chr 2:34-35).
JARIB
1. Alternate name for Yakin (Jachin), Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 4:24. See Jachin #1.
2. Man who assisted Ezra in securing temple servants before the return to Palestine from exile (Ezr 8:16).
3. From Yeshua’s (Jeshua’s) family, a priest who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile (Ezr 10:18).
JARMUTH

1. Fortified city in the northern part of the Shefelah (Shephelah) given to Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe for an inheritance (Jos 15:35). It was one of five Amori (Amorite) cities that banded together to attack Giveon (Gibeon) after they had made peace with Yehoshua (Joshua) and Yisrael (Israel) (10:3-5). Yarmut (Jarmuth) was reinhabited after the exile by people of Yehudah (Neh 11:29), and possibly maintained a population throughout the Dispersion. It is identified with Khirbet Yarmuk, 18 miles (29 kilometers) southwest of Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Archaeological evidence suggests that the area of the Bronze Age city was six to eight acres (2.4 to 3.2 hectares) and had a population of about 1,500 to 2,000 people. It is mentioned in the Amarna letters as receiving aid from Lakish (Lachish).

2. One of four cities of Yisakar (Issachar) given to the Levites for their inheritance (Jos 21:28-29). It is apparently identifiable with Ramot (Ramoth) in 1 Chronicles 6:73 and Remet (Remeth) in Joshua 19:21. A stele of Par’oh (Pharaoh) Seti I was found at Beth-shan, referring to the whole area as Mt Yarmut.
See also Levitical Cities.
JAROAH
Gilead’s son from Gad’s tribe (1 Chr 5:14).
JASHAR, Book of

This was an ancient Hebrew writing that is no longer extant. It was probably a national songbook containing songs praising the exploits of Hebrew heroes. It is mentioned in the OT account of Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) command to the sun and moon to stand still during the battle with the five kings (Jos 10:13) and in the account of David’s lament over Sha’ul (Saul) and Yonatan (Jonathan) (2 Sm 1:17-27). It is also possible that Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) words of dedication of the temple (1 Kgs 8:12-13) were included. According to the Septuagint (Greek translation of the OT), the writer of that passage uses the same language as in Joshua 10:12-13 and asks rhetorically if Shelomoh’s statement were written in the book of “Song.” Some scholars believe that this question may have accidentally dropped out of the Hebrew text since the whole quotation appears in the Septuagint following Shelomoh’s prayer of 1 Kings 8:14-53. It is also likely that some Hebrew letters may have been transposed so that the Septuagint reads “Song” instead of “Jashar.” If one accepts these assumptions, then 1 Kings 8:12-13 would have been part of the Book of Jashar.

It is also possible that the Septuagint rendering, “Book of Song,” is the more correct title. All of the quotations are poetry; the term “Jashar” has never been explained satisfactorily; and “Jashar” has similarities to various Hebrew root forms meaning “to sing.” Hence, some scholars believe that “Book of Song” is a more correct title.

The nature of the book cannot be determined with certainty except to say that it probably contained a wide variety of songs. This is evident as one considers the types of materials contained in the three passages mentioned above. One is an appeal for the prolonging of daylight in order for Yisrael (Israel) to complete a military victory; one is an example of David’s literary skill and an expression of the national importance and close friendship of the persons involved; and one is an exclamation extolling God’s supremacy over ritual and nature.

The origin of the Book of Jashar is more clouded in obscurity than is its content. Some believe that it was a written collection of songs dating to the days before the monarchy. Some think that it was an oral tradition dating approximately from the time of Shelomoh. Others suggest that it was a vital instrument in the establishment of literary archives during the monarchy to preserve the notable events of Israelis (Israelites). This has led to the suggestion that the Song of Miryam (Miriam) (Ex 15:21) and the Song of Deborah (Jgs 5) may have been part of the collection.
The book has long interested many people, and this interest has led to various false imitations, false identifications, and false reproductions of it.
JASHEN

One of David’s 30 mighty men (2 Sm 23:32). The Hebrew text reads “the sons of Yashen (Jashen),” and 1 Chronicles 11:34 reads “the sons of Hashem the Gizoni (Gizonite).” Scholars are generally agreed that the phrase “the sons of” is dittographic and repeats the last three letters of the preceding word. The reading in the original text probably was either “Yashen the Gizoni” or “Hashem the Gizoni,” making him, and not his son, the mighty man of David’s army.
JASHOBEAM

1. Zavdiyel’s (Zabdiel’s) son who was put in charge of David’s “Three” mightiest men (1 Chr 11:11) and also appointed chief of a division (24,000 soldiers) on duty in the first month of the year (1 Chr 27:2). He is the same person as Yoshev-Bashevet (Josheb-basshebeth), the Tahkemonite (2 Sm 23:8, nlt mg). Yashaveam (Jashobeam) gained renown by killing 300 men, according to 1 Chronicles 11:11, or 800, according to 2 Samuel 23:8.
2. One of the ambidextrous warriors who joined David at Tsiklag (Ziklag) (1 Chr 12:6).
JASHUB
1. Yisakar’s (Issachar’s) third son (1 Chr 7:1; alternately called Iob in Gn 46:13), and founder of the Yashuvi (Jashubite) family (Nm 26:24).
2. Bani’s descendant, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile (Ezr 10:29).
JASHUBI-LEHEM
Mentioned along with Moav (Moab) in 1 Chronicles 4:22.
JASHUBITE
Descendant of Yashuv (Jashub), Yisakar’s (Issachar’s) third son (Nm 26:24). See Jashub #1.
JASIEL*
