JASON

1. Jewish high priest (174–171 BC) who brought about the decline of the priesthood by Hellenizing Yerushalem (Jerusalem), making her inhabitants “citizens of Antiokeia (Antioch)” (2 Macc 4:9ff.). He was deposed by his cousin Honyo (Onias) Menelaos (Menelaus), but when a false report told of the death of Antiokos (Antiochus) Epifanes (Epiphanes), Yason (Jason) attacked Yerushalem without mercy for his own people. Antiokos, returning from an aborted attack on Mitsrayim (Egypt), retook Yerushalem and Yason was forced to flee to Transjordan and thence from city to city. Second Maccabees reports that at his death, “[Yason] who had cast out many to lie unburied had no one to mourn for him; he had no funeral of any sort and no place in the tomb of his fathers” (5:10, rsv).

2. Jewish Christian at Thessalonikai (Thessalonica) who hosted Paulos (Paul) and Silas (Acts 17:1, 5-9). He and others were called before the city officials on charges of harboring seditionists. He was released when he put up bail.
3. Christian at Korinthos (Corinth) who, along with Paulos, sent greetings to the church at Romai (Rome) (Rom 16:21).
JASPER
Variety of green quartz. See Stones, Precious.
JATHAN*
One of the sons of Shemayah (Shemaiah), who had accompanied Tovi (Tobit) to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to worship (Tb 5:14, nlt mg).
JATHNIEL
Fourth son of Meshelemyah (Meshelemiah) the Korhi (Korahite) and doorkeeper of the temple in David’s time (1 Chr 26:2).
JATTIR

Town in the hill country of Yehudah (Judah) given to the Levites (Jos 15:48; 21:14; 1 Chr 6:57). David sent spoils from his victory over the Amalekim (Amalekites) to Yatir (Jattir) (1 Sm 30:27). It is identified with modern Khirbet ‘Attir, 13 miles (21 kilometers) southeast of Hevron (Hebron).
JAVAN (Person)
Yefet’s (Japheth’s) son whose seafaring descendants migrated to the north and west of Kena’an (Canaan) (Gn 10:2-4; 1 Chr 1:5-7).
JAVAN* (Place)

Location commonly identified with Yavan (Greece). The name is linguistically associated with Ionia, a region in westernmost Asia Minor that was colonized by Greeks. By extension, Yavan came to be applied to Yavan itself. In most occurrences in the Greek translation of the Bible, Yavan appears as “Hellas,” Yavan.

Some hints as to its location are given as early as the “table of nations,” where Yavan appears as the fourth son of Yefet (Japheth) (Gn 10:2; cf. 1 Chr 1:5); moving west from Gomer, this tends to place it in Europe. Yefet is also said to be the father of Elishah, Tarshish, Kitim (Kittim), and Dodanim or Dodanim (Rodanim) (Gn 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). The connections of these areas or peoples is well known.

Most of the references to Ionia (Yavan) are in the prophetic books. In Isaiah 66:19 Yavan is named along with Tarshish, Put, Lud, and Tuval (Tubal) as places to which the glory of the Lord will be declared. These are taken as a representative of the distant nations.

In a lengthy prophecy against Tsor (Tyre), Yehezkel (Ezekiel) refers to Yavan, Tuval, and Meshek (Meshech) as those who traded slaves and bronze vessels for the merchandise of Tsor (Ez 27:13), while in Joel 3:6 Tsor is condemned for having sold the people of Yehudah (Judah) and Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to the Greeks. In Ezekiel 27:19 the Hebrew text reads “Vedan and Yavan from Uzal.” This is translated as “Greeks from Uzal” in the nlt (see also mg). The nasb states, “Vedan and Yavan paid for your wares from Uzal”; the kjv reads “Dan also and Yavan.” The rsv (see also mg) follows the Greek translation: “wine from Uzal.”

The references to Yavan in Daniyel (Daniel) clearly mean Yavan. The he-goat who represents the king of Yavan (Dn 8:21) is Alexandros (Alexander) the Great, whose empire was divided among his four generals upon his death. The prince of Yavan in Daniel 10:20 is parallel to the prince of Paras (Persia) in Daniel 10:13, 20. It has been suggested that “prince” means guardian angel, but the prince of Paras’s opposition to the archangel Mika’el (Michael) makes it evident that “prince” is a demonic spirit of high rank (cf. Eph 6:12). Conflict between Paras and Yavan is predicted in Daniel 11:2, while the following verse tells of the success of Alexandros the Great and the breakup of his empire.
See also Greece, Greek.
JAVELIN
Light, short, spearlike weapon. See Armor and Weapons.
JAZER

Town east of the Yarden (Jordan) River in southern Gilead, taken with its surrounding villages by the Israelis (Israelites) under Mosheh (Moses) (Nm 21:32). The tribes of Gad and Re’uven (Reuben) asked for the lands of Yazer (Jazer) and Gilead. They had large flocks and herds and saw that the east side of the Yarden was fertile and best suited for livestock grazing (32:1-5). They promised to build protection for their women and children, then go with the other tribes to fight in Kena’an (Canaan) (vv 6-27). Yazer became a border point marking the inheritance of Gad (Jos 13:25) and was given to the Levites (Jos 21:39; 1 Chr 6:81). When Yoav (Joab) was sent to number the people, he reached the city of Yazer in Gad (2 Sm 24:5). This town was later recognized during a search for “capable men” under King David (1 Chr 26:31). Just over 200 years later, however, it was occupied by Moav (Moab) (Is 16:6-9; Jer 48:32).
JAZIZ
One of David’s royal stewards in charge of the flocks (1 Chr 27:30-31).
JEALOUSY*, Ordeal of

Numbers 5:11-28 contains a provision by which a man who suspected his wife of adultery could bring her to the priest to determine her guilt or innocence. She had to appear with a grain offering, take an oath, and then drink “bitter” water mixed with dust taken from the tabernacle floor. As the woman drank the water, the priest offered the jealousy offering. If she were guilty, “her abdomen [would] swell and her thigh [would] waste away” (Nm 5:27, nlt mg), and she would be a curse among the people. If she were innocent, no ill effects would result. See Bitterness or Jealousy, Water of.
JEARIM, Mount

Mountain on the northwest border of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) territory between Beyt-Shemesh (Beth-shemesh) and Kiryat-Yearim (Kiriath-jearim). Kesalon was located on its northern slope (Jos 15:10). It is associated with Mt Se’ir (Seir) and Mt Efron (Ephron).
See also Kesalon.
JEATERAI*, JEATHERAI
Zerah’s son, a Gershoni (Gershonite) Levite (1 Chr 6:21), called Etni (Ethni) in 1 Chronicles 6:41.
JEBERECHIAH*, JEBEREKIAH
Father of Zekaryah (Zechariah) the scribe. Zekaryah, with Uriyah (Uriah) the priest, witnessed Yeshayah’s (Isaiah’s) prophecy of the Assyrian conquest of Yisrael (Israel) (Is 8:2).
JEBUS, JEBUSITE

Walled city, lying on the boundary between Yehudah (Judah) and Benyamin (Benjamin), conquered by David; thereafter, it was known as the “city of David,” or ancient Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Its occupants were Yevusim (Jebusites) (Jos 18:16). They were one of the several clans or tribes collectively known as Kena’anim (Canaanites) (Gn 10:15-16). Their land, along with that of their neighbors, was repeatedly promised to the Israelis (Israelites) (Ex 3:8; 13:5; 23:23; 33:2; 34:11; Nm 13:29; Dt 7:1; 20:17). This promise was partially fulfilled early in the campaign under Yehoshua (Joshua) (Jos 3:10; 12:8; 18:16; cf. 24:11). It is said that the men of Yehudah fought against Yerushalem and took it (18:28). “The Benyamites (Benjamites), however, failed to dislodge the Yevusim, who were living in Yerushalem; to this day the Yevusim live there with the Benyamites” (Jgs 1:21, niv). Apparently the city was captured by the men of Yehudah, but its inhabitants were not destroyed and they later reoccupied the site.

Yevus (Jebus) (or Yerushalem) lay on the borderline between two tribes, and this may account for its survival until the time of David. The borders of Yehudah and Benyamin are thus defined: “The boundary then passed through the valley of the son of Hinom (Hinnom), along the southern slopes of the Yevusim, where the city of Yerushalem is located. Then it went west to the top of the mountain above the valley of Hinom, and on up to the northern end of the valley of Refaim (Rephaim)” (Jos 15:8, nlt); “it then goes down the valley of Hinom, south of the shoulder of the Yevusim, and downward to Eyn-Rogel (En-rogel)” (Jos 18:16, rsv). The two accounts agree: the survey of Yehudah follows a westerly direction; the survey of Benyamin moves eastward; both indicate that Yevus lay on the southern slope of the “mountain” north of the valley of Hinom, the site of East Yerushalem today.

The city’s survival was assured by a constant supply of water, the spring of Gihon, and by strong natural defenses. It was easily defended by steep valleys on three sides: the Kidron on the east, the Hinom on the south and west. The Yevusim therefore considered their city impregnable. This gave them a certain arrogance and complacency. After the death of Sha’ul (Saul), when David was seeking to consolidate the kingdom, the Yevusim scornfully challenged David to capture their stronghold (2 Sm 5:6; cf. 1 Chr 11:5). As the last remaining Kena’ani (Canaanite) stronghold in the area, it presented a unique challenge. Yoav (Joab) apparently led the attack up the water shaft and succeeded where previous attempts had failed (2 Sm 5:8).

For political as well as strategic reasons, David decided to move his capital from Hevron (Hebron) to Yevus. Politically, it lay in neutral territory between Yehudah and Benyamin and thus aroused no jealousy. Strategically, it was easily defended and more centrally located. The choice proved a wise one. In spite of the fact that Jebus-Jerusalem lies on no waterway or major highway, it has become through the centuries the spiritual capital of the world. Under David and Shelomoh (Solomon), it became Yisrael’s (Israel’s) religious center, and today it is of prime importance to the three major monotheistic religions of mankind.
See also Jerusalem.
JECAMIAH*
KJV spelling of Yekamyah (Jekamiah), King Yehoyakin’s (Jehoiachin’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 3:18. See Jekamiah #2.
JECHOLIAH*
KJV spelling of Yekaleyah (Jecoliah), King Azaryah’s (Azariah’s) mother, in 2 Kings 15:2. See Jecoliah.
JECHONIAH*
Alternate form of Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin), a Yehudi (Judean) king, in Matthew 1:11-12. See Jehoiachin.
JECHONIAS*
KJV form of Yekaneyah (Jechoniah), an alternate name of Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin), king of Yehudah (Judah), in Matthew 1:11-12. See Jehoiachin.
JECOLIAH
Mother of King Azaryah (Azariah), or Uziyah (Uzziah) (2 Kgs 15:2; 2 Chr 26:3).
JECONIAH*
Alternate name for King Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin) of Yehudah (Judah), who was carried into Babylonian exile (1 Chr 3:16-17; Jer 24:1). See Jehoiachin.
JEDAIAH
1. Shimri’s son and the father of Alon (Allon). He is listed in the genealogical tables of the Simeonites who settled in the valley of Gedor in Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) time (1 Chr 4:37).
2. Harumaf’s (Harumaph’s) son, who helped repair the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) wall after the exile (Neh 3:10).

3. Aharon’s (Aaron’s) descendant and head of the second of the 24 priestly divisions for temple service in David’s time (1 Chr 24:7). His descendants are listed among the returned exiles (1 Chr 9:10; Ezr 2:36; Neh 7:39). The individuals and families listed below are probably a part of this priestly line, but their exact relationships are difficult to determine.
4. Provincial priest who agreed to resettle in postexilic Yerushalem (Neh 11:10; cf. v 2).
5. Priest who returned with Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) after the exile (Neh 12:6-7). In the next generation this was the name of a family (v 21).

6. One of the exiles taken by Zekaryah (Zechariah) as witness to the symbolic crowning of Yehoshua (Joshua) (nlt “Yeshua (Jeshua)”). He may be the same as #4 or #5 above. He came back from captivity bringing gifts for the temple in the days of the high priest Yehoshua (Zec 6:10-14).
JEDIAEL
1. Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) son (1 Chr 7:6, 10-11), whose descendants were warriors, numbering 17,200 by David’s time. Some suggest that he is identifiable with Ashbel, also Benyamin’s son (Gn 46:21).
See also Ashbel, Ashbelite.
2. Shimri’s son, listed among David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:45).
3. One who deserted Sha’ul (Saul) to join David at Tsiklag (Ziklag) (1 Chr 12:20). He may be the same as #2 above.
4. Member of the Levitical family of Korah, appointed a doorkeeper of the temple during David’s reign (1 Chr 26:2).
JEDIDAH
Adayah’s (Adaiah’s) daughter, the wife of King Amon of Yehudah (Judah) and the mother of King Yoshiyah (Josiah) (2 Kgs 22:1).
JEDIDIAH
Name meaning “beloved of Yahweh [Yahweh].” God told Natan (Nathan) the prophet to give Shelomoh (Solomon), David’s second son by Bat-Sheva (Bathsheba), this name soon after his birth (2 Sm 12:24-25).
JEDUTHUN

Member of the Levitical family of Merar who, along with Asaf (Asaph) and Heyman (Heman), presided over the music in the sanctuary in David’s reign (1 Chr 25:1; 2 Chr 5:12; called “Eytan (Ethan)” in 1 Chr 6:44; 15:17). Yedutun (Jeduthun) is mentioned in the titles of Psalms 39, 62, and 77. Some of his sons were set apart to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals (1 Chr 25:1-3), apparently following the example of their father, who was called “the king’s seer” (2 Chr 35:15). In 1 Chronicles 16:38 and 42, he is listed as Oved-Edom’s (Obed-edom’s) father.
JEEZER*, JEEZERITE*
KJV forms of I’ezer (Iezer) and Iezeri (Iezerite), contractions of Aviezer (Abiezer) and Abiezerite, the names of Gilead’s son and his descendants (Nm 26:30). See Abiezer #1.
JEGAR-SAHADUTHA

Aramaic name given by Lavan (Laban) to the heap of stones that he and Ya’akov (Jacob) piled up as a memorial to their covenant; Ya’akov called it “Gal’ed (Galeed)” (Gn 31:47). The name means “heap of witness.”
See also Galeed.
JEHALLELEL
1. Descendant of Yehudah (Judah) who had four sons (1 Chr 4:16).
2. Levite of the family of Merari whose son Azaryah (Azariah) participated in the cleansing of the temple in Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) time (2 Chr 29:12).
JEHDEIAH
1. Shuvael’s (Shubael’s) son, a Levite in David’s time (1 Chr 24:20).
2. Royal steward from Meronoth who was in charge of David’s donkeys (1 Chr 27:30).
JEHEZKEL
Levite assigned to temple duty in David’s time; leader of the 20th division (1 Chr 24:16).
JEHIAH
Levite who, along with Oved-Edom (Obed-edom), was appointed as doorkeeper for the ark when David brought it to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (1 Chr 15:24).
JEHIEL
1. KJV spelling of Yeiel (Jeiel), King Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) ancestor, in 1 Chronicles 9:35. See Jeiel #2.
2. KJV spelling of Yeiel, Hotam’s (Hotham’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 11:44. See Jeiel #3.

3. A Levite musician who, along with other Levites appointed by David, played a psaltery at the removal of the ark to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (1 Chr 15:18-20). Afterward, he was appointed to a permanent ministry of music in the sanctuary (1 Chr 16:5).

4. Levite of the family of Gereshon (Gershon); a chief of the house of Laedan (Ladan) (1 Chr 23:8, nlt mg). He was in charge of the temple treasury during David’s reign—an office that seems to have continued in the family (29:8)—and founder of a priestly family called Yehiel (Jehieli) or Jehielites (26:21-22).
5. Hakmoni’s (Hacmoni’s) son who, with David’s uncle Yonatan (Jonathan) (a counselor and a scribe), was appointed to take care of the king’s sons as a tutor and adviser (1 Chr 27:32).

6. Son of King Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) of Yehudah (Judah), placed by his father over one of the fortified cities of Yehudah (2 Chr 21:2). He and five brothers were slain by Yehoram (Jehoram) when Yehoram became king.

7. One of the Kohatite (Kohathite) Levites from the family of Heyman (Heman) who assisted in King Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) reforms (2 Chr 29:14, rsv “Yehiel”). He may be the same Levite who was assigned to oversee the reception and distribution of the sacred offerings (2 Chr 31:13).
8. One of the chief officers of the temple at the time of Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) religious reformation (2 Chr 35:8); he contributed many sacrifices for the great Passover service.
9. Father of Ovadyah (Obadiah) from Yoav’s (Joab’s) house; he returned with Ezra from Bavel (Babylon) (Ezr 8:9).

10. One of the sons of Eylam (Elam) and father of Shekanyah (Shecaniah). He was associated with Ezra’s marriage reforms (Ezr 10:2) and was perhaps the same Yehiel who was among those who divorced their foreign wives (v 26).
11. Priest who was among those Ezra persuaded to divorce their foreign wives (Ezr 10:21).
JEHIELI*, JEHIELITE*
Alternate spelling of Yehiel (Jehiel), a Levite and founder of the Jehielite family, in 1 Chronicles 26:21-22. See Jehiel #4.
JEHIZKIAH
Shalum’s (Shallum’s) son and a chief of Efrayim (Ephraim) during the reign of Ahaz in Yehudah (Judah). He opposed the enslavement of the men of Yehudah by victorious Yisrael (Israel) (2 Chr 28:12).
JEHOADAH*, JEHOADDAH*
Ahaz’s son and a descendant of King Sha’ul (Saul) through Yonatan’s (Jonathan’s) line (1 Chr 8:36); alternately called Yaerah (Jarah) in 1 Chronicles 9:42.
JEHOADDAN*, JEHOADDIN
Mother of Amatsyah (Amaziah), king of Yehudah (Judah) (2 Kgs 14:2; 2 Chr 25:1).
JEHOAHAZ

1. Twelfth king of Yisrael (Israel), succeeding his father, Yehu (Jehu), and ruling from 814 BC to 798 BC. Because he was an evil king, God punished Yisrael by subjecting them to the Aramean kings Hazael and his son Ben-Hadad (Ben-hadad). The military force in Yisrael was reduced to 50 cavalrymen, 10 chariots, and 10,000 infantrymen. The oppression became so severe that Yehoahaz (Jehoahaz) prayed to God, who listened to him and delivered Yisrael from the Arameans, but not until the reign of Yoash (Joash) (Yehoash (Jehoash)) (2 Kgs 13:2-7, 25). During Yehoahaz’s reign, relations between Yehudah (Judah) and Yisrael seem to have been fairly good, since Yehoahaz (14:1, “Yo’ahaz (Joahaz)”) named his son Yoash after his contemporary, Yoash king of Yehudah (2 Kgs 13:1, 9; 14:1).

2. Seventeenth king of Yehudah, ruling three months in 609 BC. The people chose him to succeed his father, Yoshiyah (Josiah), who was killed in the battle of Megidon (Megiddo). His mother’s name was Hamutal. Yehoahaz was 23 years old at his coronation. He is also called Shalum (Shallum) (1 Chr 3:15), and Yehoahaz may well be a throne name. He is characterized as an evil king before God. His rule ended when Par’oh (Pharaoh) Nekoh (Neco) imprisoned him at Rivlah (Riblah) in Hamat (Hamath). Later he was taken to Mitsrayim (Egypt), where he died (2 Kgs 23:30-34). Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) prophesied that Yehoahaz would never return to Yisrael but would die in the land of his captivity (Jer 22:11-12).

3. Another form of the name of Ahazyah (Ahaziah), the sixth king of Yehudah, who ruled in 841 BC (2 Chr 21:17; cf. 22:1). Both forms of the name have the same meaning. The difference is the placement of the divine name. In Yehoahaz it comes first, “Jeho-” and in Ahazyah it comes last, “-iah” (-yah). See Ahaziah #2.
4. Full name of Ahaz, the 12th king of Yehudah, according to an inscription of Assyrian king Tiglat-Pileser (Tiglath-pileser) III. See Ahaz #1.
See also Israel, History of.
JEHOASH

Name of two OT kings, occurring only in the book of 2 Kings. The name means “Yahweh is strong” or “Yahweh hath bestowed.” Yoash (Joash), the shorter form of the name, frequently appears in the Kings and Chronicles narratives.

1. Son of Ahazyah (Ahaziah) and seventh king of Yehudah (Judah) (835–796 BC). Yehoash (Jehoash) ascended the throne after the wicked Atalyah (Athaliah) had been killed at the command of Yehoyada (Jehoiada) the priest. As an infant, he was hidden by his aunt Yehosheva (Jehosheba) in the temple and thus survived the slaughter of the king’s household by Atalyah (2 Kgs 11:1-3; 2 Chr 23:10-12). After remaining six years within the temple precinct, Yehoash was declared king at the age of seven and ruled for 40 years (2 Kgs 11:21–12:1; 2 Chr 24:1-3).

His major activity during his reign was the renovation of the temple (2 Kgs 12:4-5; 2 Chr 24:4-5). When, by his 23d year, little progress had been made (2 Kgs 12:6), he revised the taxation schedule, commanded the people of Yehudah to bring their contributions directly to the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) temple, and soon restored the Lord’s house to its proper condition (2 Chr 24:13).

After the death of the priest Yehoyada, Yehoash and Yehudah forsook the Lord and served the Asherim and the idols (2 Chr 24:15-18). Not heeding the prophetic warning of divine judgment (v 20), Yehoash and his people were conquered by the Arameans. Though Yehoash had once been able to avert a siege of Yehudah by paying tribute to Hazael (2 Kgs 12:17-18), the same strategy did not work a second time. The Arameans plundered Yehudah and Yerushalem, sending the spoil to Hazael in Damesek (Damascus) (2 Chr 24:23-24). Yehoash was assassinated by his servants Yozakar (Jozacar) (Yozavad (Jozabad)/Zavad (Zabad)) and Yehozavad (Jehozabad) while recuperating from wounds incurred in battle with the Arameans (2 Kgs 12:20-21; 2 Chr 24:25-26).

2. Son of Yehoahaz (Jehoahaz) and 13th king of Yisrael (Israel) (798–782 BC). Yehoash enjoyed a measure of military success that had eluded his father. No longer subject to punitive military exploits from Hazael of Aram, he was able to establish political stability in the northern kingdom. In fact, he subjugated the southern kingdom of Yehudah while Amatsyah (Amaziah) was king in Yerushalem (796–767 BC). The conflict between Amatsyah and Yehoash was precipitated mainly by Amatsyah. Overconfident with his victories in Edom, Amatsyah initiated a military conflict with Yisrael (2 Chr 25:17-19). The battle was fought near Beyt-Shemesh (Beth-shemesh) in the Yehudi (Judean) Shefelah (Shephelah). King Yehoash routed the army of Yehudah, captured Amatsyah, and moved on to Yerushalem. Destroying the outer wall from the Efrayim Gate (Ephraim Gate) to the Corner Gate, he entered the capital city and plundered the treasures of both the palace and the temple (vv 21-24). He was apparently used as an instrument of the Lord to subdue Yehudah (v 20).

A contemporary of Yehoash was Elisha the prophet. In spite of the pervasive wickedness in Yisrael and the apostasy of the king himself (2 Kgs 13:10-11), Yehoash still sought the counsel of this prophet of the Lord. While Elisha was on his deathbed, Yehoash sought the prophet’s blessing (v 14). Elisha assured the king that the Arameans would be defeated by Yisrael at Afek (Aphek) and that Yisrael would enjoy three decisive victories over this same enemy (vv 15-19). During his 16-year reign, Yehoash achieved political stability in the northern kingdom. Though considered an evil king, he was used as an instrument of judgment against Amatsyah of Yehudah and enjoyed the blessing of Yahweh against Aram.
See also Israel, History of.
JEHOHANAN
1. Korhi (Korahite) Levite who was a gatekeeper of the sanctuary during David’s reign (1 Chr 26:3).
2. Commander of thousands in King Yehoshafat’s (Jehoshaphat’s) army (2 Chr 17:15).
3. Father of Yishmael (Ishmael), commander of a unit of soldiers who helped the priest Yehoyada (Jehoiada) overthrow the wicked queen Atalyah (Athaliah) of Yehudah (Judah) (2 Chr 23:1).

4. Elyashiv’s (Eliashib’s) descendant who owned a chamber into which Ezra retired to pray, fast, and mourn for his people (Ezr 10:6). He is possibly the same as Yohanan (Johanan), a grandson of Elyashiv the high priest (Neh 12:22-23, nlt), and Yonatan (Jonathan) (a textual variant), Yoyada’s (Joiada’s) son, in Nehemiah 12:11.
5. One of Bevay’s (Bebai’s) four sons, who was exhorted by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife (Ezr 10:28).

6. Son of the Amoni (Ammonite) official Toviyah (Tobiah) and a contemporary of Nehemyah (Nehemiah). He married a Jewish woman whose father, Meshulam (Meshullam), had helped repair the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) wall (Neh 6:18; kjv “Yohanan”).
7. Priest and family leader in postexilic Yerushalem during the time Yoyakim (Joiakim) was high priest (Neh 12:13).
8. One of the priests who participated as a singer in the dedication of the rebuilt Yerushalem wall (Neh 12:42).
JEHOIACHIN

King of Yehudah (Judah) for a very brief time (598–597 BC). He was the son of Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) and Nehushta, the daughter of Elnatan (Elnathan) of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (possibly the Elnatan mentioned by Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), cf. Jer 26:22; 36:12, 25). The name Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin) means “Yahweh will uphold,” and variations include Konyah (Coniah) (Jer 22:24, 28; 37:1), Yekaneyah (Jeconiah) (1 Chr 3:16-17; Est 2:6; Jer 24:1; 27:20; 28:4; 29:2), and Yekaneyah (Mt 1:11-12; kjv “Yekonias (Jechonias)”). Yehoyakin was 18 years old when he was installed as king upon his father’s death, and he ruled for only three months and ten days in Yerushalem (2 Kgs 24:8; cf. 2 Chr 36:9, nlt mg). He inherited a vassal kingdom in revolt. Besieged by the armies of the Babylonian overlord Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar), Yehoyakin had little choice but to capitulate in the face of insurmountable odds. According to the Babylonian Chronicle, records based on the official annals of the Babylonian kings, Nevukadnetsar entered Syro-Palestine in December of 598 BC and took Yerushalem on March 16, 597. The Babylonians plundered the palace and temple treasuries. Along with Yehoyakin, his family, prominent military leaders, royal officials, and artisans were taken prisoner and led away to exile in Bavel (Babylon). Before returning to Bavel, the victorious king placed Yehoyakin’s uncle Matanyah (Mattaniah), now named Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah), on the throne in Yerushalem (2 Kgs 24:12-17; cf. 2 Chr 36:10).

According to Yirmiyah, the trauma caused by the Babylonian invasion of Yehudah, and the consequent political upheaval prompted by a succession of three kings in four months, had little impact on the people spiritually (Jer 37–38). This same prophet of God forecast Yehoyakin’s exile and predicted he would have no descendants succeeding him on the throne (22:24-30). In contrast, the false prophet Hananyah (Hananiah) prophesied Yehoyakin would be restored to the throne of Yehudah within two years (28:3-4, 11; cf. vv 12-17).

Yehoyakin’s continuing royal status as the legitimate claimant to the Judahite kingship was reflected in the fact that Yehezkel’s (Ezekiel’s) oracles are dated to the year of Yehoyakin’s exile, not Tsidkiyah’s reign (Ez 1:2; 8:1; 20:1; etc.). Babylonian records confirm this recognition of Yehoyakin’s former position; he retained his title of king and received favorable treatment from the Babylonians. He is certainly the “Yaukin, king of the land of Yahuda” listed in one of the cuneiform tablets; this tablet contains inventories of rations of oil and barley for the king and his five sons and implies they were not imprisoned but living a fairly normal life in Bavel. At some point Yehoyakin must have been imprisoned, however, because later, during the reign of Evil-Merodak (Evil-merodach), he was released from prison and granted dining privileges with the Babylonian king (c. 562 BC; cf. 2 Kgs 25:27-30; Jer 52:31-34). Whether he was imprisoned for attempting to escape or because of Yehudah’s rebellion against Bavel under Tsidkiyah is unclear.

Yehoyakin’s name appears in Matay’s (Matthew’s; Grk. Matthaios’) genealogy of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ (Mt 1:11-12), and some contend that this contradicts Yirmiyah’s oracle of judgment against the king’s descendants (Jer 22:30). Yet it is possible to understand Hagay’s (Haggai’s) blessing of Zerubabbel (Hg 2:20-23) as a reversal of Yirmiyah’s curse and the reinstatement of Yehoyakin’s line on the Davidic—and ultimately messianic—throne (cf. Is 56:3-5).
See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Diaspora of the Jews; Israel, History of.
JEHOIADA

1. Father of Benayah (Benaiah), a high military officer during the reigns of David and Shelomoh (Solomon). Yehoyada (Jehoiada) was a priest (1 Chr 27:5) who joined forces with David at Hevron (Hebron) and was identified with the house of Aharon (Aaron) (12:27). See Benaiah #1.

2. High priest in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) who organized and led the coup that overthrew Queen Atalyah (Athaliah) of Yehudah (Judah), together with the Ba’al (Baal) cult she supported, and established his nephew Yoash (Joash) (Yehoash (Jehoash)) on the throne (2 Kgs 11:4-21; 2 Chr 23:1-15). As long as he lived, Yehoyada kept the king true to the Lord (2 Kgs 12:1-16; 2 Chr 23:16–24:14). He died at the age of 130 and was buried in the city of David among the kings.
3. Benayah’s son, who succeeded Ahitofel (Ahithophel) as King David’s counselor (1 Chr 27:33-34); he was probably a grandson of #1 above, although some believe these to be the same.
4. KJV spelling of Yoyada (Joiada), Paseah’s son, in Nehemiah 3:6. See Joiada #1.
5. Alternate name for Yoyada, son of Elyashiv (Eliashib) the high priest, in Nehemiah 13:28. See Joiada #2.
6. Priest during the time of Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) who was succeeded by Tsefanyah (Zephaniah) as overseer of the temple (Jer 29:26).
JEHOIAKIM

Second son of Yoshiyah (Josiah) by Zevidah (Zebidah) (2 Kgs 23:36; 1 Chr 3:15; 2 Chr 36:4) who became king of Yehudah (Judah) in 609 BC. He replaced his younger brother Yehoahaz (Jehoahaz) as king when he was deposed and exiled by Par’oh (Pharaoh) Nekoh (Neco) after a three-month reign (2 Kgs 23:31-35). Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) was installed as king at age 25, and he ruled for 11 years in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). His given name, Elyakim (Eliakim), means “God will establish.” Upon enthroning him, Nekoh changed his name to Yehoyakim, meaning “Yahweh will establish” (2 Kgs 23:34), perhaps seeking to claim Yahweh’s support for his action.

Nekoh laid a heavy tribute on Yehudah, which Yehoyakim raised by levying a tax on the whole land (2 Kgs 23:35; cf. Jer 22:13-17, where the woe oracle against Yehoyakim implies that he appropriated some of these funds for personal use). Yehoyakim remained subservient to the Mitsrim (Egyptians) until the battle of Karkemish (Carchemish) in 605 BC, when Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) and the Neo-Babylonians routed Nekoh. Yehudah then became a vassal state of Bavel (Babylon) for three years (2 Kgs 24:1-2). After Nevukadnetsar’s failure to completely subdue Nekoh in a second fierce battle in 601 BC, Yehoyakim seized the opportunity to throw off the Babylonian yoke when the Babylonian king returned home to reorganize his army. This ill-advised decision proved costly, as Nevukadnetsar invaded Yehudah in 598 BC to punish the rebellious vassal king (2 Kgs 24:3-7). The expected help from Mitsrayim (Egypt) never came, and the Babylonians destroyed the important Judahite cities of Devir (Debir) and Lakish (Lachish), seized control of the Negev, and deported several thousand of Yehudah’s ablest citizens. This no doubt crippled the economy and left Yehudah virtually leaderless. Yehoyakim died during the Babylonian siege (probably late in 598 BC). His son Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin) was placed on the throne.

Although the details of Yehoyakim’s death are not reported, the biblical historian does pass judgment on this reign as one that perpetuated the evils of his fathers (see 2 Kgs 23:37; 2 Chr 36:5, 8; cf. Jer 22:18-19 and 36:27-32, which predicted that Yehoyakim’s dead body would be cast on the ground outside of Yerushalem without proper burial and he would have no descendants upon the throne). Presumably the reference to “fathers” is to his predecessors Menasheh (Manasseh), Amon, and Yehoahaz. Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) specifies the evils that characterized Yehoyakim’s rule, including idolatry, social injustice, robbery of the wage earner, greed, murder, oppression, extortion, and forsaking of the covenant of the Lord (Jer 22:1-17). Despite Yirmiyah’s extensive activity during his reign (chs 25–26, 36), Yehoyakim remained disobedient, unrepentant, smug, and self-sufficient in his ill-gotten prosperity (22:18-23).
See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Diaspora of the Jews; Israel, History of.
JEHOIARIB
1. Alternate form of Yoyariv (Joiarib), a priestly family in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), in 1 Chronicles 9:10. See Joiarib #1.
2. Priest in the time of King David, assigned to head the first of 24 divisions of priests for annual temple duty (1 Chr 24:7).
JEHONADAB
Alternate name for Yonadav (Jonadab), Recab’s son. See Jonadab #2.
JEHONATHAN
1. KJV spelling of Yonatan (Jonathan), Uziyah’s (Uzziah’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 27:25. See Jonathan #7.
2. One of the Levites appointed by Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) to travel about Yehudah (Judah) teaching the law to the people as part of his national religious reform (2 Chr 17:8).
3. Head of Shemayah’s (Shemaiah’s) priestly house in postexilic Yerushalem (Jerusalem) during the days of Yoyakim (Joiakim) the high priest (Neh 12:18).
JEHORAM

1. Yehoshafat’s (Jehoshaphat’s) son and Yehudah’s (Judah’s) fifth king (853–841 BC; also called Yoram (Joram)). Prior to the rule of the Omride dynasty in the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel) (885–841 BC), the relationship between Yehudah and Yisrael had been strained. The political influence and economic stability of the united monarchy had long since vanished. Power and wealth had been diminished by Mitsri (Egyptian) overlordship under Shishak (2 Chr 12) and by civil war: the unsuccessful Shekem (Shechem) conference (ch 10); Rehav’am (Rehoboam) of Yehudah versus Yarov’am (Jeroboam) of Yisrael (12:15); Aviyah (Abijah) of Yehudah versus Yarov’am of Yisrael (13:1-22); and Asa of Yehudah versus Baesha (Baasha) of Yisrael (16:1-4). The Omride dynasty in the mid-ninth century BC, however, cast aside familial rivalry and sought to forge a new alliance between the two nations.

The two kingdoms of Yehudah and Yisrael were increasingly threatened by the surrounding peoples—the Amonim (Ammonites), Moavim (Moabites), Edomim (Edomites), Aramim (Syrians), Pelishtim (Philistines), Arabs, and Assyrians. In response to this threat Ahav (Ahab), the second king of the Omride dynasty, secured diplomatic relations with Foinikai (Phoenicia) (1 Kgs 16:31) and Yehudah (22:4). During this time, joint military expeditions by Yisrael and Yehudah were not infrequent (1 Kgs 22; 2 Kgs 3; 8:28), though these political alliances were not without their liabilities. The intrusion of the worship of Ba’al (Baal) and Asherah led to religious apostasy in Yehudah and Yisrael (1 Kgs 16:31-33; 2 Kgs 3:2; 2 Chr 21:11). It was within this political-religious context that Yehoram (Jehoram) reigned over Yehudah.

Though he may have served as co-regent as early as 853 BC, Yehoram was the sole ruler for eight years (848–841 BC). His reign was marked by unnecessary internecine fighting and religious apostasy. His father had generously provided for his six brothers, a decision that Yehoram quickly reversed once he had secured the throne (2 Chr 21:2-3). He executed not only his brothers but also several Israeli (Israelite) princes, thereby removing any political threat to himself (v 4). In addition, he reverted to the idolatrous practices that his father had tried to eliminate by restoring forbidden worship sites, “the high places” (v 11). Yehoram had apparently fallen under the influence of his wife, Atalyah (Athaliah), the daughter of Izevel (Jezebel) (2 Kgs 8:18). As her mother had done in Yisrael, Atalyah imported Ba’al worship into Yehudah. As a result, Eliyah (Elijah) the prophet pronounced judgment on Yehoram and the people of Yehudah—a curse that brought a great plague upon Yehoram’s people, children, wives, and possessions, and a gross intestinal disorder upon the king himself. In spite of this pervasive wickedness in Yehudah, the Lord did not destroy the southern kingdom, because of his promise to David (2 Kgs 8:19; cf. 2 Sm 7:12-16).

Politically, Yehudah was vulnerable, having lost its control of Edom (2 Chr 21:9) and having sustained attacks by the Pelishtim and the Arabs. Yehoram was left bereft of possessions, wives, and sons except for Yehoahaz (Jehoahaz) (Ahazyah (Ahaziah)), his youngest (vv 16-17). At his death Yehoram was not honored and was deprived of burial in the tomb of the kings within the city of David (vv 19-20).
See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Israel, History of.

2. Ahav and Izevel’s son, and Yisrael’s tenth king (852–841 BC; also called Yoram). He succeeded his brother Ahazyah, whose premature death led to Yehoram’s ascension to the throne in Shomron (Samaria) (2 Kgs 1:2, 17); he was a contemporary of the Yehudi (Judean) kings Yehoshafat, Yehoram, and Ahazyah.

Yehoram was preoccupied with the political resurgence of the two neighboring kingdoms of Moav (Moab) and Aram (Syria). When Moav withheld its annual tribute to Yisrael, he sought assistance from both Yehoshafat and Yehudah’s vassal kingdom, Edom. Yehoram and Yehoshafat joined forces with the king of Edom but were halted in their attack on Moav when they encountered a serious lack of water. Hesitant to advance with their troops, they summoned Elisha the prophet and asked him to inquire of the Lord’s will regarding the expedition. Because of the high regard that Elisha held for Yehoshafat, the prophet sought the Lord on their behalf, gaining both the Lord’s blessing and an abundance of water. The account of the battle records the slaughter of the Moavim as well as the horrible incident of a human sacrifice by the Moavi (Moabite) king. Having won the battle, Yisrael withdrew (2 Kgs 3:4-27).

Yehoram’s conflict with Aram was less successful because the Israeli king sustained a battle wound. Retreating from Ramot-Gilead (Ramoth-gilead) in Transjordan to his palace in Yizre’el (Jezreel) (2 Kgs 8:29), he found his problems compounded when one of his generals, Yehu (Jehu), led an insurrection against him. Commissioned by the Lord and declared to be king of Yisrael, Yehu confronted Yehoram and his nephew, Ahazyah, king of Yehudah. The incident culminated in the death of the two reigning monarchs of Yisrael and Yehudah (2 Kgs 9:14-24, 27). While Ahazyah was buried in the tomb of the kings in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (v 28), Yehoram’s corpse was cast into Navot’s (Naboth’s) field outside the city of Yizre’el. His end was the appropriate judgment against the last king of the wicked Omride dynasty (vv 25-26).
3. Levite member of a traveling group of scholars who taught the people from the Book of the Law during the reign of Yehoshafat (2 Chr 17:7-9).
See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Israel, History of.
JEHOSHABEATH*
Alternate name for Yehosheva (Jehosheba), daughter of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) King Yehoram (Jehoram), in 2 Chronicles 22:11. See Jehosheba.
JEHOSHAPHAT (Person)
1. The fourth king of Yehudah (Judah) (872–848 BC), son and successor of Asa (910–869 BC).

Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) was 35 years of age when he began his reign; he ruled 25 years, during which time he maintained the stability of the Davidic dynasty (1 Kgs 22:41-42). He was contemporary with King Ahav (Ahab) of Yisrael (Israel) (874–853 BC), since his first year on the throne corresponds with the fourth year of the reign of Ahav (v 41). He was also contemporary with Ahazyah (Ahaziah) (853– 852 BC), son of Ahav, and his brother Yehoram (Jehoram) (852–841 BC), who succeeded Ahazyah when he died childless (2 Kgs 1:17).

Yehoshafat is held in high esteem by the Chronicler, along with Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) and Yoshiyah (Josiah). His successful rule was due to his religious policy. He continued the religious reformation initiated by his father; therefore, the Lord firmly established the kingdom under his control. Everyone in Yehudah brought tribute to Yehoshafat, so that he had great riches and honor (2 Chr 17:1-5). The Chronicler praised Yehoshafat’s courageous heart, evidenced in his removing the high places and the Asherim from Yehudah (v 6). Yehoshafat is also reported to have closed all the temples of prostitution (1 Kgs 22:46).

The biblical record informs us that Yehoshafat reversed his father’s foreign policy. During his reign, Asa warred against Baesha (Baasha) of Yisrael (908–886 BC), who exterminated the house of Yarov’am (Jeroboam) I (930–909 BC) and usurped the throne for himself, keeping it for nearly a quarter of a century. The two kingdoms engaged in warfare over the boundaries between the kingdoms. Yehoshafat, however, discontinued this war and made peace with the king of Yisrael (1 Kgs 22:2). To confirm this state of peace, he made an alliance with Ahav and married his son and successor, Yehoram, to Ahav’s daughter Atalyah (Athaliah) (2 Kgs 8:18; 2 Chr 18:1-2). In accordance with this alliance Yehoshafat fought on the side of Ahav in his battle against Aram, which took place at Ramot-Gilead (Ramoth-gilead) (1 Kgs 22; 2 Chr 18). He also was an ally of Yehoram, the younger son of Ahav, against Meysha (Mesha) the king of Moav (Moab) (2 Kgs 3:4-27).

In his domestic reforms Yehoshafat sent Ben-Hayil (Ben-hail), Ovadyah (Obadiah), Zekaryah (Zechariah), Netanel (Nethanel), and Mikayah (Micaiah) to teach the law in the cities of Yehudah (2 Chr 17:7-9). He is also reported to have organized the use of tribute paid to Yehudah. The surrounding nations, observing the strength of Yehoshafat and recognizing the presence of the Lord with him, not only refrained from attacking Yehudah but even brought tribute to him. He used this tribute to fortify the cities of Yehudah (vv 10-13). Yehoshafat also reorganized the army and made arrangements for the defense of the kingdom. He had a standing army in the capital as well as garrisons in the fortified cities. It is evident that the organization centered about the tribal association of Yehudah and Benyamin (Benjamin) (vv 14-19).

A prophet by the name of Yehu (Jehu) rebuked Yehoshafat for his alliances with Ahav (2 Chr 19:1-3). Evidently, Yehoshafat took this rebuke to heart and ruled Yehudah wisely. He swept most of the Asherim from the land and determined in his mind to seek God. He is reported to have gone regularly among the people from Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba) to Mt Efrayim (Ephraim) to convert them to the Lord. He appointed judges in each of the fortified cities of Yehudah and admonished them to judge as the Lord’s representatives. He also appointed Levites, priests, and family heads to handle cases pertaining to the worship of the Lord and to make decisions in disputes arising among citizens (vv 4-11).

In addition to the fortified cities in Yehudah, Yehoshafat placed military forces in the cities of Efrayim that his father, Asa, had taken (2 Chr 17:1-2). Though his alliances with Foinikai (Phoenicia) and Yisrael were not approved by the prophets and proved dangerous in the long run, they still brought relative peace and temporary prosperity to his realm. He was held in high esteem by the neighboring Pelishtim (Philistines) and the Arabs (vv 10-13), and it is also evident that Edom submitted to him. He won victory over the Moavim (Moabites), Amonim (Ammonites), and Meunim (Meunites) at Eyn-Gedi (En-gedi) (20:1-30). Wishing to emulate Shelomoh (Solomon), he constructed ships at Etsyon-Gever (Ezion-geber) to go to Tarshish, but this did not prove a successful venture (vv 35-37).

Yehoshafat died when he was about 60 years of age and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His son Yehoram became king in his place (2 Chr 21:1). His name is listed in Matay’s (Matthew’s; Grk. Matthaios’) genealogy of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ (Mt 1:8).
See also Israel, History of.

2. Son of Ahilud who held the position of “recorder” (the Hebrew word may imply an official historian or a spokesman for the king) in the days of David and Shelomoh (2 Sm 8:16; 20:24; 1 Kgs 4:3; 1 Chr 18:15).

3. Son of Paruah and one of Shelomoh’s 12 administrative officials who requisitioned food from the people for the king’s household. Each of them arranged provisions for one month of the year. Yehoshafat was the officer assigned for the tribe of Yisakar (Issachar) (1 Kgs 4:7, 17).
4. Son of Nimshi and the father of Yehu, who exterminated the dynasty of Omri and became king of Shomron (Samaria) around 842–815 BC (2 Kgs 9:2, 14).
5. KJV spelling of Yoshafat (Joshaphat) in 1 Chronicles 15:24, a priest during David’s reign. See #2 (above).
JEHOSHAPHAT, Valley of

Valley mentioned in prophecy as the place of future judgment (Jl 3:2, 12), sometimes called the valley of decision (v 14). Its exact location is disputed. Some (notably Jerome) identify it with the Kidron Valley, east of Yerushalem (Jerusalem), pointing to early Christian tradition; others prefer the valley of Hinom (Hinnom), south of Yerushalem. This tradition may be traced back through Eusebius to the book of 1 Hanok (Enoch) (1 Hanok 53:1). Still others say the name is symbolic and refers only to coming judgment, not to a specific place.
JEHOSHEBA

Daughter of King Yehoram (Jehoram) of Yehudah (Judah) (853–841 BC) and Queen Atalyah (Athaliah), sister of King Ahazyah (Ahaziah) (841 BC), and wife of Yehoyada (Jehoiada) the high priest. Upon Ahazyah’s death, Atalyah attempted to kill all the remaining royal heirs to the throne; Yehosheva (Jehosheba), however, hid young Yoash (Joash), Ahazyah’s son, in a temple bedroom for the duration of Atalyah’s reign (841–835 BC; 2 Kgs 11:2). Yehosheva is alternately spelled Yehoshav’at (Jehoshabeath) in 2 Chronicles 22:11.
JEHOSHUA*, JEHOSHUAH*
Alternate kjv names for Yehoshua (Joshua), son of Nun, in Numbers 13:16 and 1 Chronicles 7:27, respectively. See Joshua (Person) #1.
JEHOVAH*

Name for God formed by adding the vowels of the Hebrew word ’Adonai to the consonants of the Hebrew divine name, YHWH. Out of their respect for God and their fear of defiling his name, the postexilic Yehudim (Jews) refused to pronounce the divine name when reading Scripture. Instead, they substituted ’Adonai, a word meaning “my Lord.” Prior to the sixth century AD, the Hebrew text had no vowels. These were supplied during the reading of the Scripture by one who was familiar with the language. When vowel points were added to the text (AD 660–700), the vowels of ’Adonai were placed below the consonants of YHWH to indicate that ’Adonai should be read.

It is thought that about AD 1520 Petrus Galatinus conceived the idea of combining the two names, thus creating the new form YeHoWaH, from which the English term Jehovah comes. Although this form was foreign to the Hebrew language, it gained wide acceptance and was included as the translation for God’s name in various verses in the kjv and asv. Biblical scholars now agree that the original pronunciation of the divine name was Yahweh or Jahveh.
See also God, Names of.
JEHOVAH-TSIDKENU*

Name of the righteous king of David’s line who God promised would rule over his people (Jer 23:5-6). The name means “Yahweh (Yahweh or Jehovah) is our righteousness.” It was also applied to the king’s subjects, who will profit by his reign (33:16). To Christians, God’s promise finds its fulfillment in Christ, who is Lord of all and the believer’s righteousness.
JEHOZABAD

1. Shomer’s son, who was a servant of King Yoash (Joash) and later, with another assailant, murdered the king at Milo (Millo) (2 Kgs 12:21). In a parallel passage, Yehozavad (Jehozabad) is called the son of Shimrit (Shimrith) the Moavit (Moabitess) (2 Chr 24:26). King Amatsyah (Amaziah), Yoash’s son, eventually executed Yehozavad for the murder (25:3).
2. Oved-Edom’s (Obed-edom’s) second son and a member of a Levitical Korhi (Korahite) family appointed by King David to be gatekeepers in the temple (1 Chr 26:4).
3. Benyamite (Benjamite) military commander who served under King Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) of Yehudah (Judah) and commanded 180,000 men in his army (2 Chr 17:18).
JEHOZADAK
Alternate name for Yotsadak (Jozadak), Serayah’s (Seraiah’s) son. See Jozadak.
JEHU

1. Prophet and son of the “seer” Hanani (2 Chr 16:7), who denounced Baesha (Baasha) for following in the ways of Yarov’am (Jeroboam) (1 Kgs 16:1-7). In addition to continuing the heretical worship of the golden calves at Beyt-El (Bethel) and Dan, Baesha also assassinated Nadav (Nadab), the son of Yarov’am (15:25-32).

Yehu (Jehu) later rebuked Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat), king of Yehudah (Judah), for helping Ahav (Ahab) the king of Yisrael (Israel) in his wars against the Arameans (2 Chr 19:1-2). The writings of this prophet were included in one of the records of the reign of Yehoshafat, The Book of the Kings of Yisrael (2 Chr 20:34).

2. Important army officer during the reigns of Ahav and Yehoram (Jehoram) (2 Kgs 9:25), who in reaction to the economic and religious abuses of the house of Omri was anointed as king of the northern kingdom of Yisrael (1 Kgs 19:16-17). In the following revolution he exterminated the royal house of Yisrael, the king of Yehudah, and a royal party from the south (2 Kgs 9–10). He executed the worshipers of Ba’al (Baal) in order to revive true worship in Yisrael. As king, he ruled in Shomron (Samaria) 28 years (841–814 BC) and began a dynasty that lasted some 100 years.

In the time of Yehu the prophets were engaged in a religious equivalent of war with the adherents of the Tsori (Tyrian) Ba’al. Eliyah (Elijah) met and defeated the Kena’ani (Canaanite) priests on Mt Karmel (Carmel) (1 Kgs 18:17-40). Later he and then Elisha were commissioned to anoint Yehu as king. The prophets waited until the time was right (2 Kgs 9:1-10), at which time Elisha sent a “son of the prophets” to Ramot-Gilead (Ramoth-gilead) to designate Yehu as the monarch.

Yehu left his siege of Ramot-Gilead in northern Transjordan to meet the king of Yisrael in Yizre’el (Jezreel). There he killed King Yehoram and Ahazyah (Ahaziah), the king of Yehudah (2 Kgs 9:17-28). His bloody ways continued as he extinguished the royal house of Ahav (10:1-17) and 42 ambassadors of goodwill from Yehudah (apparently without provocation, vv 12-14). Yisrael’s bloodbath finally ended in Shomron. There Yehu cunningly vowed to serve Ba’al with a zeal greater than that of Ahav. Unsuspecting devotees of Ba’al gathered in great numbers to join in a festival sacrifice. Instead, the devotees themselves became the sacrifice, and the house of Ba’al in Shomron was destroyed and desecrated by turning its ruins into a latrine (vv 18-27).

Political and economic problems also contributed to the unrest. Under the reign of Ahav and Izevel (Jezebel), justice was corrupted. The poor lost their land in the drought and their property rights were ignored (1 Kgs 18:5-6). Yehu threw the body of Yehoram into the field of Navot (Naboth) the Yizre’eli (Jezreelite) (2 Kgs 9:25-26) as justice for the crime of Ahav and Izevel (1 Kgs 21:19; cf. v 13). But religious passions dominated the cause. Yehu called his slaughter of the house of Omri his “zeal for the Lord.” Yehonadav (Jehonadab), a Recabite, joined Yehu as he traveled toward Shomron (2 Kgs 10:15-17). Recabites opposed social and economic developments that took place in the northern kingdom under Ahav. They followed a strict moral code and lived a simple life (Jer 35). Since Recabites represented the most conservative elements of Yahwism, they became natural allies for the reform of Yehu.

Yehu’s revolution seriously weakened the worship of Ba’al. Although not all of the adherents were eliminated, Baalism no longer remained the official religion of the state (2 Kgs 10:28). Rather, Baalism united with Yahwism to form the sinister syncretistic religion that was denounced by Hoshea (Hosea).

Politically, the revolt of Yehu was disastrous. The triple alliance between Tsor (Tyre), Yisrael, and Yehudah was shattered by the atrocities. Yisrael, now isolated, became easy prey for Ashur (Assyria) and Aram (Syria). Yehu attempted to buy some help from Ashur by paying tribute to Shalmaneser III. That event is pictured on the Black Obelisk in a relief from the campaign of 841 BC. An inscription names “Yehu, son of Omri,” as the one kneeling before Shalmaneser.

After the Assyrian threat dissipated in 838 BC, Hazael, king of Aram-Damascus, conquered all of Israeli (Israelite) Transjordan as far as the Arnon (2 Kgs 10:32-33). In a second campaign in 815 BC, Hazael moved across the Yarden (Jordan) River, through the Yizre’el plain, and down the coast, conquering the land as far as Gat (Gath) in the northern Shefelah (Shephelah). There the son of Yehu, Yehoahaz (Jehoahaz), paid tribute to Hazael (12:18). The revolution weakened Yisrael both politically and economically.

Later generations spoke of the massacre of the house of Omri with horror (Hos 1:4). Yehu did not destroy the golden calves of Yarov’am, and so continued the syncretistic worship at Beyt-El and Dan. In the final analysis the revolution, which was meant to purge Yisrael of oppression and false religion, succeeded in doing neither.
3. Member of Yehudah’s tribe, the son of Oved (Obed) and Azaryah’s (Azariah’s) father (1 Chr 2:38).

4. Prince of Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) tribe, and the son of Yoshivyah (Joshibiah), who, along with others, migrated from the approaches to the valley of Gedor eastward in search of good pasture (1 Chr 4:35).

5. One of the skilled warriors who joined David at Tsiklag (Ziklag). Interestingly, he was of Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) tribe, Benyamin (Benjamin), and from Anatot (Anathoth), to which Evyatar (Abiathar) of the priests of Eli was later banished (1 Chr 12:3).
See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Israel, History of.
JEHUBBAH*
Shemer’s son from Asher’s tribe (1 Chr 7:34).
JEHUCAL

Son of Shelemyah (Shelemiah) who was sent by King Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah) to request Yirmiyah’s (Jeremiah’s) prayers for Yehudah (Judah) (Jer 37:3; 38:1). Later he tried to kill Yirmiyah, who continued to prophesy the invasion of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) by the Babylonians, thereby undermining the confidence of the people and the army (38:1-6).
JEHUD

One of the towns given to Dan’s tribe after the Conquest (Jos 19:45). It has been variously identified with the village of el-Yehudiyeh, about seven miles (11.3 kilometers) southeast of Yafo (Joppa), and with Yazur, about five miles (8 kilometers) southeast of Yafo.
JEHUDI

Son of Netanyah (Nethaniah) and a messenger of King Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) of Yehudah (Judah). He was sent by a number of princes to summon Baruk (Baruch) to read Yirmiyah’s (Jeremiah’s) scroll privately to them. Later, Yehoyakim ordered Yehudi (Jehudi) to read the same scroll publicly before him and all the court, after which the writing was burned (Jer 36:14-23).
JEHUDIJAH*
Not a proper name; kjv mistranslation for “Jewish,” a descriptive term distinguishing Mered’s Jewish wife from his other wife, who was an Mitsri (Egyptian) princess (1 Chr 4:18).
JEHUSH*
KJV spelling of Ye’ush (Jeush), Eshek’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:39. See Jeush #3.
JEIEL
1. Chief in Re’uven’s (Reuben’s) tribe (1 Chr 5:7).
2. Benyamite (Benjamite) who lived at Giveon (Gibeon) and an ancestor of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) first king, Sha’ul (Saul) (1 Chr 8:29; 9:35).
3. One of David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:44). He is perhaps identical with #1 above.
4. Levite gatekeeper in the sanctuary. He seems to have served as a musician also (1 Chr 15:18, 21; 16:5b). The Yeiel (Jeiel) of 1 Chronicles 16:5a is probably a different musician.
5. Levite descended from Asaf (Asaph) and an ancestor of a prophet named Yahaziel (Jahaziel) (2 Chr 20:14).
6. Secretary for King Uziyah’s (Uzziah’s) army, who kept or made military “rolls” or “musters” of the king’s troops (2 Chr 26:11).
7. KJV and nlt spelling of Ye’uel (Jeuel), Elitsafan’s (Elizaphan’s) descendant, in 2 Chronicles 29:13. See Jeuel #2.
8. Levite leader who contributed Passover offerings during King Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) reign (2 Chr 35:9).
9. KJV spelling of Ye’uel, Adonikam’s descendant, in Ezra 8:13. See Jeuel #3.
10. Nevo’s (Nebo’s) descendant who was encouraged to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era (Ezr 10:43).
JEKABZEEL
Alternate name for Kavtse’el (Kabzeel), a city in southern Yehudah (Judah), in Nehemiah 11:25. See Kabzeel.
JEKAMEAM
Hevron’s (Hebron’s) son from the Kohatite (Kohathite) division of Levi’s tribe (1 Chr 23:19; 24:23).
JEKAMIAH
1. Shalum’s (Shallum’s) son from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 2:41).
2. One of King Yehoyakin’s (Jehoiachin’s) sons (1 Chr 3:18).
JEKUTHIEL
Zanoah’s father from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 4:18).
JEMIMAH
First of the three daughters born to Iyov (Job) when he was restored after his affliction (Jb 42:14).
JEMUEL
Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) first son (Gn 46:10; Ex 6:15). He is called Nemuel in 1 Chronicles 4:24 and is the founder of the Nemueli (Nemuelite) family (Nm 26:12).
JEPHTHAH

Illegitimate son of Gilead (Jgs 11:1) and a leader in the period of the judges. The son of a harlot, Yiftah (Jephthah) was dispossessed by his father’s other sons and refused a share in their father’s home. He moved to the land of Tov (Tob), a small Aramean state east of the Yarden (Jordan) River (Jgs 11:3-5), and became leader of a band of malcontents and adventurers who went raiding with him.

When war broke out between the Israelis (Israelites) and the Amonim (Ammonites), the leaders of Gilead begged Yiftah to return and lead their army. At first he refused because of their previous mistreatment of him. When they promised to make him Gilead’s ruler, he accepted and became commander in chief and ruler (Jgs 11:4-10). The agreement was ratified before the Lord at a general assembly of the people at Mitspah (Mizpah) (v 11) in Gilead, probably just south of the Yabok (Jabbok) River.

After diplomatic negotiations with the king of Amon (Ammon) failed, Yiftah waged war against the Amonim. Before the fighting started, he vowed to the Lord that if he was victorious, on his return home he would sacrifice to God whoever met him at the door of his house. Then he successfully led his army against the Amonim, destroying them with a terrible slaughter (Jgs 11:29-33).

When Yiftah returned home, he was shocked to find that the first person to meet him was his only child, his daughter, playing a tambourine and dancing for joy. When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, “Alas, my daughter! you have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me; for I have opened my mouth to Yahweh, and I cannot take back my vow” (Jgs 11:35, rsv). She submitted to her destiny but begged that it might be postponed for two months so that she and her companions could retreat to the mountains and lament that she must die a virgin (vv 34-38). A woman in ancient Yisrael (Israel) could suffer no greater disgrace than to die unmarried and childless. When she returned, her father fulfilled his vow (vv 38-39).

Yiftah also led Gilead against the Efrayimim (Ephraimites), who were resentful that they had not been included in the fight against Amon. They had been given a previous chance to ally with Gilead but had refused. Yiftah captured the fords of the Yarden behind the Efrayimim and prevented their escape by an ingenious strategy. Giladi (Gileadite) guards put fugitives to a test, demanding that they say “Shibboleth.” If they could not pronounce the “sh,” they were revealed as Efrayimim and killed. The account says that 42,000 Efrayimim died at that time (Jgs 12:1-6).

Yiftah was judge over Gilead for six years (Jgs 12:7), and when he died, he was buried in one of the cities of Gilead. In the Letter to the Hebrews, Yiftah is named with Gid’on (Gideon), Barak, and others as a hero of faith (Heb 11:32).
See also Judges, Book of.
JEPHUNNEH

1. Father of Kalev (Caleb), one of the 12 spies sent by Mosheh (Moses) to search out the land of Kena’an (Canaan) (Nm 13:6; 14:6; 26:65; 1 Chr 4:15; 6:56). He is identified variously as a Judahite and a Kenizi (Kenizzite) (Jos 14:6).
2. Yeter’s (Jether’s) son from Asher’s tribe (1 Chr 7:38).
JERAH

Son of Yaketan (Joktan) and nephew of Peleg, during whose lifetime the earth was divided, probably a reference to the dispersion following Bavel (Babel). Yerah (Jerah) is likely also the name of an Aravi (Arabian) tribe or district (Gn 10:25-26; 1 Chr 1:20).
JERAHMEEL

1. Firstborn of Hetsron’s (Hezron’s) three sons, the father of six sons and a descendant of Yehudah (Judah) through Perets’s (Perez’s) line (1 Chr 2:9-42). He was the founder of the family of Yerahme’elim (Jerahmeelites), who in David’s time lived in the Negev region and occupied a number of cities (1 Sm 27:10; 30:29).
2. Kish’s son and a Levite family leader who served in the sanctuary during David’s reign (1 Chr 24:29).
3. Son of King Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) of Yehudah and one who, with Shelemyah (Shelemiah) and Serayah (Seraiah), was ordered by the king to seize Baruk (Baruch) and Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) (Jer 36:26).
JERAHMEELITE
Yerahme’el’s (Jerahmeel’s) descendant from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Sm 27:10; 30:29). See Jerahmeel #1.
JERED
1. KJV spelling of Yered (Jared) in 1 Chronicles 1:2. See Jared.
2. Ezra’s (Ezrah’s) son from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 4:18).
JEREMAI
Hashum’s son who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his foreign wife after the exile (Ezr 10:33).
JEREMIAH (Person)
1. Prophet to Yehudah (Judah) before its fall in 586 BC; his name is also spelled “Yirmiyah (Jeremias)” (Mt 16:14) and “Yirmiyah” (Mt 2:17; 27:9) in the kjv.

Yirmiyah was born in the village of Anatot (Anathoth), about three miles (4.8 kilometers) northeast of Yerushalem (Jerusalem). His father’s name was Hilkiyah (Hilkiah), and he belonged to the tribe of Benyamin (Benjamin). His call came in the 13th year of King Yoshiyah (Josiah) (640–609 BC). He refers to himself as “a child” when called (Jer 1:6), but the Hebrew word is not the same as used in Jeremiah 30:6 and 31:8 and cannot be limited to preadolescence. He was probably referring to his inexperience rather than to his age. Yirmiyah was born about 657 BC during the reign of the wicked king Menasheh (Manasseh), while the great Ashurbanipal, who had shaken the world by sacking the ancient Mitsri (Egyptian) city of No (Thebes) in 663 BC, ruled a world empire from Ashur (Assyria).

God informed Yirmiyah that he had consecrated and appointed him before birth (Jer 1:4-5). Yirmiyah first shrank with a sense of inadequacy and fear: “O The master Yahweh, . . . I can’t speak for you! I’m too young!” (v 6, nlt). God would not allow Yirmiyah to excuse himself. He was assured that words would be given him to speak, and guidance given for the way (v 7). He was promised protection (v 18) and deliverance (v 8) despite opposition (v 19). God touched his mouth, signifying divine inspiration of his words, and gave the sign of a branch from an almond tree, explaining that the Lord is watching (see nlt mg). The third sign was the boiling pot (v 13) facing from the north, picturing the source and fury of impending disaster.
Thus the tone of Yirmiyah’s life ministry was set: judgment, disaster, danger, defeat, and impending death for the nation.
Early Ministry

The messages given by Yirmiyah during his first five years of ministry may have been instrumental in the great revival of 622 BC. Those cooperating with King Yoshiyah in the reformation and friendly with Yirmiyah included Ahikam and his father, Shafan (Shaphan) (Jer 26:24); Gedalyah (Gedaliah), Ahikam’s son (39:14), who later became governor; Acbor, son of Mikayah (Micaiah), also called Avdon (Abdon), whose son Elnatan (Elnathan) joined the opposition (26:22) but later repented (36:25); and Asayah (Asaiah) (2 Chr 34:20). The prophets Nahum and Tsefanyah (Zephaniah) also influenced the reform movement, which must have climaxed under the preaching of Havakuk (Habakkuk) and Yirmiyah, the priestly ministry of Hilkiyah, and the prophecies of Huldah the prophetess. During the reign of King Yoshiyah, Yirmiyah spoke without the fear of persecution that plagued his later ministry. Though the content of the book of Yirmiyah sometimes appears to be fragmentary, most of chapters 1–19 date to the time of Yoshiyah.

The finding of the lost Book of the Covenant in the temple debris may be the reason for the words in Jeremiah 15:16: “Your words are what sustain me. They bring me great joy and are my heart’s delight” (nlt). The words “So be it, Yahweh” (Jer 11:5) in a context recalling the words of Mosheh (Moses) in the Torah may be Yirmiyah’s response after hearing King Yoshiyah read the newly found book.

Small towns and rural areas, including his hometown, heard Yirmiyah’s denunciation of high places and idolatry. They sought to kill the young prophet, or at least to intimidate him (11:21). Instead of being silent, Yirmiyah asserted that his motivation was for their good and condemned their resistance to the truth as their greatest danger.

Shortly after Yirmiyah began his ministry, a number of world-changing events took place. Ashurbanipal died and the Assyrian Empire rapidly declined. Nabopolassar began a 21-year reign in Bavel (Babylon), leading an expansion that culminated in his son Nevukadnetsar’s (Nebuchadnezzar’s) subjugation of the known world. As the world news filtered in, Yirmiyah turned more toward Yerushalem. His first temple speeches (chs 7–10) may have been uttered at this time.

Nabopolassar felt his strength sufficient to launch an attack against Assyrian territory in 616 BC, but he advanced cautiously because Psamtik I (Psammetichus) of Mitsrayim (Egypt) appeared ready to aid Ashur. Cyaxares of Media pounced on Ashur when Bavel hesitated and took its most sacred city, Ashur, in 614 BC. Bavel joined Media, along with Scythia, and waged an assault against Nineveh, which fell late in the summer of 612 BC. The Assyrian Empire had shriveled to two small holdings, Haran and Karkemish (Carchemish).

Nabopolassar took Haran in 610, and Ashuruballit, having escaped, appealed to Mitsrayim for help at Karkemish. Nekoh (Neco), who had become pharaoh within the year, responded immediately. He marched through Yehudah without giving Yoshiyah prior notice and asked that the Yehudim (Jews) not bother him in view of his haste to go northward (2 Chr 35:21). Ignoring the request, Yoshiyah pursued them to Megidon (Megiddo) and was wounded in the ensuing battle; he died in Yerushalem.
Ministry during the Reign of Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim)

In place of Yehoahaz (Jehoahaz), Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) fourth son, who reigned only three months, Par’oh (Pharaoh) Nekoh enthroned Yehoyakim (Elyakim (Eliakim)). Nekoh demanded heavy indemnity payments from Yehudah (Judah) and took Yehoahaz prisoner as collateral to assure payment (2 Kgs 23:31-33).

Early in the reign of Yehoyakim, Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), moved by God’s Spirit, delivered his third temple speech (Jer 26) on the occasion of one of the annual Jewish feasts. He called for the people to repent and to act on the basis of the revelation they had heard repeatedly from the Book of the Law. The barb of the sermon came in the warning: “This is what Yahweh says: If you will not listen to me and obey the law I have given you, and if you will not listen to my servants, the prophets—for I sent them again and again to warn you, but you would not listen to them—then I will destroy this Temple as I destroyed Shiloh, the place where the Tabernacle was located. And I will make Yerushalem (Jerusalem) an object of cursing in every nation on earth” (26:4-6, nlt). Shiloh had been the heart of Jewish worship from Yehoshua (Joshua) to Shmuel (Samuel), but after being destroyed by the Pelishtim (Philistines), it never revived. It served as an example of complete desolation following God’s judgment in the days of Eli.

Crowds gathered rapidly and reacted angrily against Yirmiyah. Priests and princes hurried to the New Gate, where a court was established to bring order and to control violence. Yehoyakim would be no help to Yirmiyah, for he had refused to listen to God’s messages (Jer 22:21). The priests and false prophets spoke against Yirmiyah, calling him a traitor. Then some of the elders spoke to the people about Uriyah (Uriah), who had prophesied the same message. Rather than risk disaster, Ahikam persuaded the court to spare Yirmiyah.

Mitsrayim controlled Palestine and Aram (Syria) after the decay of the Assyrian Empire. In 606 BC Mitsrayim succeeded in annihilating a garrison city of Babylonian soldiers south of Karkemish and then reoccupied Karkemish to await the return blow from Bavel. This Mitsri (Egyptian) victory meant persecution for Yirmiyah, who was often accused of false prophecy (cf. Jer 20).

Yirmiyah never had confidence in Mitsrayim. Each time a Jewish leader would call for a new alliance with Mitsrayim, Yirmiyah repeated God’s message against it. Whenever a Jewish group fled to Mitsrayim for security, Yirmiyah warned of worse things in that land of false refuge (see Jer 44:26-27). Yirmiyah’s ode and prophecy in chapter 46 poetically describe Mitsrayim’s defeat at Karkemish, when Nabopolassar sent his son Nevukadnetsar to destroy them (605 BC). After smashing the Mitsri army at Karkemish, Nevukadnetsar pursued the enemy through Yehudah. “Not a single man escaped to his own country,” reads the exaggerated Babylonian record. His father’s death, however, prevented him from invading Mitsrayim, and he returned to Bavel to assume the throne. The following year Nevukadnetsar, now king of Bavel, returned to accept the homage of the rulers of Yehudah, Aram, and Foinikai (Phoenicia). On this occasion God gave Yirmiyah his great 70-year prophecy (Jer 25:11-12), which became the basis of Daniel 9:2, 24-27.

A year after the decisive battle at Karkemish, Baruk (Baruch), Yirmiyah’s scribe, finished recording all the dictated words of Yirmiyah and was reading from this scroll at the temple. A report reached the king, who sent Yehudi (Jehudi), a servant, to fetch the scroll and read it to him. When this was done, Yehoyakim burned the scroll in spite of his counselors, who pleaded that the king not do it (Jer 36:23-25). God’s message, soon rewritten, added a promise of fearful judgment on Yehoyakim (vv 27-31).

Ambitious young Nevukadnetsar determined to add Mitsrayim to his dominion. In 601 BC he led his forces through Yehudah again, but Nekoh had advance warning and was prepared for the onslaught. In the desert of Shur, Nevukadnetsar suffered defeat. Encouraged by this display of Mitsri defensive strength, the pro-Egyptian parties in Yehudah asserted themselves, persuading Yehoyakim to lead them to freedom from Bavel by making an alliance with Mitsrayim (2 Kgs 24:1). But help from Mitsrayim did not come (v 7).

In 599 BC, Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) armed those surrounding the rebel Jewish kingdom to harass the Yehudim, which they willingly did (2 Kgs 24:2). Evidently Yehoyakim lost his life in one of these raids. Since the people despised him, his body was thrown out without honorable burial, as Yirmiyah had predicted (Jer 22:19).
Ministry during the Reign of Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah)

Nevukadnetsar’s siege of Yerushalem in 598 BC lasted only a short time because the new king, Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin), crowned at age 18, knew resistance was useless. He gave himself up, with all his family and court, in March of 597 BC, after serving as king about three months. The Babylonian Chronicle reads: “He [Nevukadnetsar] seized the city and captured the king.”

Yehoyakin was carried to Bavel (Babylon) along with 8,000 (2 Kgs 24:16; cf. v 14) officers, artisans, and executives (Yehezkel (Ezekiel) among them) and much booty. In his place Nevukadnetsar appointed Tsidkiyah, Yehoyakin’s uncle, to rule. Tsidkiyah proceeded to organize his government with the less capable and inexperienced help left after the deportation.

Yirmiyah took up his thankless ministry, calling on the Yehudim (Jews) to believe God, obey the laws of Bavel, and reject false hopes in Mitsrayim (Egypt). Tsidkiyah turned a deaf ear to these appeals, listening rather to the unwise advice of his counselors (Jer 37:1-2). During the first year of Tsidkiyah’s rule, Yirmiyah received the vision of the two baskets of figs. The Yehudim carried to Bavel were like good figs, while Tsidkiyah and those who trusted in Mitsrayim were like rotten figs (24:1-8). The reason for this reproachful description was that the Yehudim began plotting rebellion against Bavel along with Edom, Moav (Moab), Amon (Ammon), Tsor (Tyre), and Tsidon (Sidon) from the beginning of the reign of Tsidkiyah (27:1-3), thus breaking their oath of loyalty to Nevukadnetsar and repudiating God’s message through Yirmiyah.

In Mitsrayim the pharaoh began to renew plans to organize dissidents within the Babylonian Empire to revolt. He hired Jewish soldiers to aid him in protecting his southern border. The Jewish soldiers settled on a Nile island called Elephantine, or Yeb (593–410 BC). Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) addressed an oracle to these Yehudim (ch 44). The treaty for Yehudim to help in Mitsrayim evidently also assumed that Mitsrim (Egyptians) would aid Yisrael (Israel). When the Babylonians besieged Yerushalem (Jerusalem) in 589, Par’oh (Pharaoh) Hofra (Hophra) came to the aid of Tsidkiyah. Nevukadnetsar, ruling from Rivlah (Riblah), commanded that the siege against Yerushalem be lifted in order to make a surprise attack on Hofra (37:5). The release gave Yirmiyah an opportunity to journey to Anatot (Anathoth) to secure some family property (v 12). However, Yiriyah (Irijah), captain of the guard, arrested Yirmiyah in the Gate of Benyamin (Benjamin) for defecting to the enemy, and he was beaten and flung into a dungeon. King Tsidkiyah brought him out after many days to obtain a prognostication. With characteristic boldness, Yirmiyah told the king he would shortly become a captive. At the same time, Yirmiyah requested relief from injustice for himself. He gained part of his request but continued as prisoner in the court of the guard.

The Babylonian army chased Par’oh Hofra back to Mitsrayim and returned to crush Yerushalem without further mercy. The siege, which began in 589 BC, was restored with rigor in January of 588, Tsidkiyah’s ninth year (39:1). During this time, the Lord gave Yirmiyah foreknowledge of a visit from a cousin who wished to sell a field near Anatot (32:7-9; cf. 37:12). Yirmiyah bought the field as an object lesson to verify the message of restoration after a captivity of 70 years (29:10).

The armies of Bavel cut off all supplies from Yerushalem and were able to destroy the last two outlying Jewish fortresses of Lakish (Lachish) and Azekah (34:7). Food became scarce. Disease spread. Undisposed-of sewage and impure cistern water caused pestilence. With increased distress came Yirmiyah’s increased appeal for the city to surrender.

Yirmiyah remained in the prison court until the Babylonians breached the city wall in July of 586 BC. The king escaped by night and succeeded in reaching the plains of Yeriho (Jericho) but was captured there and taken to Rivlah. Tsidkiyah’s family and counselors were killed; he himself was blinded and taken in chains to Bavel, where he died soon after (39:6-7).

Back in Yerushalem, Nevuzar-Adan (Nebuzaradan), the Babylonian general, sent most of the Yehudim into captivity. Yirmiyah, however, was granted special consideration; after being released from prison, he was placed under the care of Gedalyah (Gedaliah), son of Ahikam.
After the Fall of Yerushalem

A month after the fall of Yerushalem, the city was burned and the walls broken down. Gedalyah was appointed governor of the remaining agricultural community, with headquarters at Mitspah (Mizpah). Yirmiyah returned to Yerushalem, where, according to tradition, he took up his abode in a grotto near what is now known as Gordon’s Calvary. There he wrote the book of Lamentations.

The Amoni (Ammonite) king Ba’alis (Baalis), plotting rebellion against Bavel, instigated the murder of Gedalyah (40:13). In the reaction that followed, the remaining people followed the leader Yohanan (Johanan) ben Kareah to a camp near Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem), intending to go to Mitsrayim. They asked Yirmiyah, at Yerushalem, to give guidance from the Lord, promising obedience. Yirmiyah’s message required that they remain in Yisrael and not go to Mitsrayim. Disobedience was complete and immediate. Fearing Bavel, they departed from Yehudah (Judah), taking Yirmiyah with them, and entered Mitsrayim (41:16–43:7).

Yirmiyah did not stop his ministry in Mitsrayim. His message at Tahfanhes (Tahpanhes) (43:8-12) assured a victorious conquest of the land by Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar), which took place in 568–567 BC.

Yehudim from all parts of Mitsrayim gathered to discuss their future as exiles. Yirmiyah took the opportunity to denounce their idolatry. Jewish women as well as men argued that they had enjoyed prosperity while serving idols but had suffered since stopping. Yirmiyah condemned their obdurate blindness to reality and gave God’s indictment. For a verifying sign, Yirmiyah predicted that Par’oh Hofra of Mitsrayim would be assassinated (44:30), which happened in 466 BC. No later record of Yirmiyah’s acts exists in the Bible. Tradition says Yirmiyah was stoned to death by the people of the Jewish exile settlement in Tahfanhes.

Though Yirmiyah suffered continued rejection during his life, he has been honored by numerous apocryphal and traditional embellishments to his history. Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) could well have had Yirmiyah in mind when he said, “You build tombs for the prophets your ancestors killed and decorate the graves of the godly people your ancestors destroyed. . . . [You are] the descendants of those who murdered the prophets” (Mt 23:29-31, nlt). See Israel, History of; Jeremiah, Book of; Prophet, Prophetess.
2. Family head in the Transjordan portion of Menasheh (Manasseh) whom Tiglat-Pileser (Tiglath-pileser) took captive (1 Chr 5:23-26; cf. 2 Kgs 15:29).
3. Father of Hamutal, a wife of King Yoshiyah (Josiah) (2 Kgs 23:31; 24:18).
4. Ambidextrous Benyamite (Benjamite) bowman and slinger who joined David at Tsiklag (Ziklag) (1 Chr 12:4).
5, 6. Two Gadi (Gadite) soldiers who joined David’s army (1 Chr 12:10, 13).

7. Postexilic priest who with Nehemyah (Nehemiah) set his seal to the covenant, renewing the people’s promise to obey God’s laws (Neh 10:2). He is mentioned again (12:34) as part of the procession for the dedication of the new wall of Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
8. Priest who returned from exile with Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) (Neh 12:1) and became head of a family of priests (v 12).
9. Father of Ya’azanyah (Jaazaniah), a Recabite who refused to drink wine (Jer 35:3).
