Author

Few doubt that the prophet from Anatot (Anathoth) wrote the book of Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), yet questions persist concerning some parts, particularly chapter 52. The use of the third person cannot be used to discredit Yirmiyah’s authorship, for Yirmiyah used the first and third person, and even the second person, in the same context. For example, 32:6-7 reads: “Yirmiyah said [third person], ‘The word of Yahweh came to me: [first person] . . . your uncle will come to you [second person]’ ” (rsv).

The problem of the passage of time provides the strongest argument against the Jeremian authorship of chapter 52. Yirmiyah was born about 657 BC. Evil-merodoch released Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin) (52:31) about 95 years later. Jeremiah 52:33 summarizes the continuation of events beyond this time. The problem of location also argues against Jeremian authorship, for Yirmiyah took up residence in Mitsrayim (Egypt) (43:6-7) while Yehoyakin dwelt in Bavel (Babylon). Note also that Yirmiyah concludes his writing with chapter 51, making chapter 52 a true editorial appendix. Since chapter 52 parallels 2 Kings 24:18–25:30, it may be that other portions of Yirmiyah that parallel sections of 2 Kings may have been written by someone other than Yirmiyah.

The following table shows such portions and includes harmonic passages in 2 Chronicles. The first column shows historical (chronological) sequence. The last column provides a brief condensation of content.

Baruk (Baruch) served as the secretary for Yirmiyah. The relationship between the two men apparently lasted many years; the prophet gave a word of encouragement as he blessed his helper (45:5). According to the custom of the people, it would have been legitimate for the scribe to write some of the prophet’s messages in his own words. This would not deny inspiration.
Authenticity

That Yirmiyah lived and actually wrote the major part of the book bearing his name is authenticated by numerous references in both biblical and nonbiblical sources (e.g., Dn 9; Ecclus 49; Josephus’s Antiquities 10; Talmud: Baba Bathra). The veracity of the historical sections of Yirmiyah have abundant confirmation in contemporary biblical books and in the secular histories preserved in Bavel, Mitsrayim, and Paras (Persia).

Higher critics sought to discredit the portions of Yirmiyah that were omitted by the Septuagint, or to credit passages to a later writer because of style differences (e.g., chs 30–33) or spelling differences (as found in chs 27–29) or linguistic problems (as in 10:11, written in Aramaic, but this may be a gloss). Another reason for discrediting Yirmiyah’s authorship is that critics dated some prophecies later than indicated in the context. This results from their requiring that predictive writing follow the record of its fulfillment. None of these reasons is sufficient cause for doubting authenticity. The Hebrew text deserves priority over the Septuagint. Aramaic contact with the Yehudim (Jews) became commonplace during this period (cf. Ezr 4–7; Dn 2–7) and therefore explains the presence of Aramaic. Different styles may be expected from the same writer due to differing circumstances and differing purposes. Baruk may have been inspired to write parts of this book and/or edited what Yirmiyah wrote. Prediction preceding fulfillment presents no problem for believers.
The Book of Yirmiyah and the Septuagint

The special problems of the Septuagint translation of Yirmiyah demand attention. The Septuagint translators evidently made an inaccurate translation. About 2,300 Hebrew words are omitted from the Septuagint. After chapter 23, the mistranslation, omissions, and mixed chronological order indicate confusion. However, the Dead Sea Scrolls display texts with both the Hebrew and the Septuagint order, indicating the antiquity of both editions. Both have suffered corruption at the hands of scribes and the ravages of the ages. The Septuagint evidently veers much further from the original, yet it has invaluable clues to help suggest answers to some textual problems. The most evident major shift in the Septuagint consists of the removal of chapters 46–51 of the Hebrew order, and the placement of them in the spot from which 25:13b-14 was removed. These chapters are renumbered 26–31 but are mixed and changed considerably from the order of the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
Background
This is fully discussed in the previous entry. See Jeremiah (Person) #1.
Date

The chronological sequence of the messages of Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) constitutes a major problem that cannot be wholly solved. Nonetheless, the book was written during Yirmiyah’s ministry (c. 627–586 BC).
Origin and Destination

After beginning his ministry in Anatot (Anathoth), Yirmiyah moved to Yerushalem (Jerusalem), where he remained until he was forced to join the disobedient refugees who arrived in Mitsrayim (Egypt) about 584 BC. Until the deportation of Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin) (597 BC), Yirmiyah addressed his messages to the king and the people residing in Yehudah (Judah). Later messages addressed the same group, plus the captives in Bavel (Babylon) (e.g., ch 29). After the departure to Mitsrayim, he addressed Yehudim in that land.
Purpose

Part of God’s commission to Yirmiyah stated the purpose of Yirmiyah’s ministry: “Today I appoint you to stand up against nations and kingdoms. You are to uproot some and tear them down, to destroy and overthrow them. You are to build others up and plant them” (1:10, nlt). The first four parts of the commission required that Yirmiyah, appointed as a “chief governor” over nations, should wreck the existing religious and social structures by his preaching against moral and spiritual sin. Doubtless, the physical destruction caused by the Mitsrim (Egyptians), Assyrians, and Babylonians was the accoutrement for the truth uttered by the prophet. Yirmiyah is consistent in his blasts at moral and religious wickedness, his call to submit to the punishment that God gives through Bavel, and his assurance that such submission will lead to blessing. When Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah) asks advice (38:14), we know what Yirmiyah will say. When the captains of the refugees ask if they should go to Mitsrayim, we already know the answer (42:3). We may also anticipate the obdurate rejection of God’s message on the part of the inquiring people, who apparently want to know God’s will but have no desire to obey it.

Nevertheless, part of Yirmiyah’s purpose focuses on the most distant future when the new covenant will supplant the old (31:31-37), and a transformed people bent on obedience rather than sin will receive God’s promised kingdom.
Teaching
National sin brings national punishment. No truth blazes so clearly as this. Gentiles as well as Yehudim (Jews) stand under the same judgment, for God is not the God of Yisrael (Israel) only.
Individuals are not overlooked in divine judgments on nations. God sets before each the way of life and the way of death (21:8) and appeals to each to choose life (27:13).

Yirmiyah illustrates human depravity by questioning if people can change their skin color or leopards their spots (13:23). The depths of depravity reach beyond man’s ability to measure (17:9-10). People even love falsehood (5:30-31). Yet God promises to transform willing subjects who call on him (33:3) by giving them a “new heart” (24:7; 32:38-41) as the climatic provision of the new covenant (31:33-35). The Messiah, who accomplishes the saving work, is called the Lord our Righteousness, the King, the righteous Branch, the Branch of David (23:5-6; 33:15-16).

A future nation will be made up of individuals who accept this salvation. Passing through the night of tribulation as of travail (30:6-7), the Yehudim will understand the true identity of their Messiah, will believe and receive him with repentant sorrow, will be cleansed (33:8), and will be regathered from all countries (32:37) by the omnipotent God (v 27).
Outline and Content
Though many see no logical order, a careful reading of Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) will reveal a grouping on the basis of content, as suggested by the following outline:
I. Introduction (1)
II. Oracles against the Yehudim (2–25)
III. History—Signs and Sufferings of Yirmiyah before the Siege (26–29)
IV. The Book of Hope written during the Siege (30–33)
V. History—Signs and Sufferings of Yirmiyah after the Siege (34–45)
VI. Oracles against the Nations (46–51)
VII. Conclusion (52)

The prophet opens his ministry with a series of utterances against the sins of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (2:1–3:5), followed by similar messages (through ch 4), concluding with words of judgment (chs 5–6). The message in the temple gate (chs 7–10) leads into the proclamation against covenant breakers (chs 11–13). The lamentation over the drought (ch 14) and subsequent miseries (ch 15) compares with many similar expressions of grief. Yirmiyah did not differ from other prophets in his use of object lessons. The rotted linen waistband (ch 13), the broken jug (ch 19), figs (ch 24), and ox yoke (chs 27–28) may be supplemented by human object lessons (ch 35), and even the prophet himself, whose celibacy (16:1-4), resistance to sympathetic consolation (16:5-7), and withdrawal from feasts (16:8-9) all served to illustrate and confirm his message.

Places where Yirmiyah proclaimed his messages helped bear home his point. He stood in the public gate, where kings came and went, to proclaim that judgment (fire) would come through the gate (17:19, 27; 39:3). Then he went to the potter’s house (ch 18), and then to Hinom (Hinnom) or Topath, which would be called the Slaughter Valley (Valley of Slaughter) (ch 19).

The persecution suffered by Yirmiyah first hinted at (1:8), then predicted (v 19), expresses its venom privately from his home village (11:19-23). The prophet’s kindred join the opposition (12:6). Public opposition brings beatings and the stocks (20:2-3). Yirmiyah prefers to keep silent rather than to speak and suffer (v 9), but he cannot withhold the word that is as fire in his bones. The result: all his familiars reproached, derided, terrorized, and denounced him, then sought his death (vv 7-18). Yirmiyah escaped death at the hands of priests, prophets, and people only because he had a few faithful friends (26:8-24). When his prophecies began to materialize, hatred mounted. He was beaten and put into a dungeon for many days (37:14-17) on a false charge. Temporary relief at the guardhouse (v 21) lasted only a few days. Officials clamored again for his death (38:4) and put him into a cistern, where he sank in the mire (v 6). His rescue (v 10) preserved his life, but his imprisonment at the guardhouse continued (v 28). His writings were cut up and burned (36:23); his words were denied and rejected (43:1-7; 44:16).

The “Book of Hope“ (chs 30–33) does contain some words of judgment (32:28-35), and other sections of the prophecy have a few bright spots (3:11-18; 16:14-16; 23:2-8; 29:10-14), but in a volume otherwise dark, these four chapters bring pleasant relief. The climax of hope, as indicated also in the longest NT quotation from Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) (see Heb 8:8-12), predicts a new covenant (31:31-40). Other prophecies also describe the end of the Mosaic law and sacrament (e.g., 3:16), and the new covenant (32:40; 33:19-26).

Little is known of Yirmiyah’s activity or messages from c. 594–589 BC. Tsidkiyah’s (Zedekiah’s) counselors made clandestine plans for throwing off Bavel’s (Babylon’s) yoke by alliances with neighbor nations. A traitor may have reported the conspiracy to Bavel (perhaps Edom). After Bavel attacked, Tsidkiyah sought a hopeful report from Yirmiyah but did not get it.

The Recabite faithfulness to the Nazarite vow (ch 35) dates to the days of Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) but as an object lesson fits the siege context. Recabites received a human command that they obeyed; Yehudim (Jews) received a divine command that they rejected. Recabites will be blessed (35:18-19); Yehudah (Judah), judged (vv 15-17). The reading of the scroll to Yehoyakim and his scornful rejection of it (ch 36) illustrates the prophetic assertion (35:15) that destruction follows the rejection of God’s message given through the prophets.

The siege comes into focus in chapter 37 with another inquiry from Tsidkiyah (the nonchronological chs 35–36 serve as an illustrative parenthesis). Jeremiah 37:11 moves forward to the time of the lifting of the siege of 589 BC when Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) drove Par’oh (Pharaoh) Hofra’s (Hophra’s) army back to Mitsrayim (Egypt). During the reprieve, Yirmiyah sought to attend a meeting of relatives to settle family matters at or near Anatot (Anathoth). Perhaps the trip involved initiating the purchase that would be made two years later (32:6-15). However, as he was leaving the city, he was arrested for desertion to the Babylonians and jailed in a dungeon cell until Tsidkiyah granted him privileged prisoner status.

The king’s officers had ample cause for the accusation of sedition: Yirmiyah had encouraged desertion (21:9; 38:2). Traitors deserved death, and this was their verdict against Yirmiyah (38:4-5). The violence of the time encouraged the officers to select a cruel method of execution: let Yirmiyah starve and bury himself in the mire at the bottom of an abandoned cistern. A sympathetic Kushi (Ethiopian), Eved-Melek (Ebed-melech), made the rescue. Immediately, the unadulterated prophecies of judgment came forth again from Yirmiyah’s lips, including a message to the king that reflected Yirmiyah’s own recent experience: “[Your friends] have betrayed and misled you. When your feet sank in the mud, they left you to your fate” (38:22, nlt).

Jeremiah 39:1–43:7 records history from the fall of Yerushalem in 586 BC to the flight into Mitsrayim, including the liberation of Yirmiyah (ch 39), appointment and assassination of Gedalyah (Gedaliah) (chs 40–41), a warning from God against going to Mitsrayim (ch 42), and the obdurate disobedience of the people (43:1-7).

The latest writings of Yirmiyah are found in chapter 44. The audience consisted of idolatrous Yehudim (44:4-6) gathered from various parts of Mitsrayim as far as Aswan (Patros (Pathros)). Yirmiyah repeated the appeal of former prophets to reject false gods in favor of Jehovah, but to no avail (44:15-16).

The message to Baruk (Baruch) (ch 45), written about 605 BC, is placed here to round out the main part of the book, which begins with the commission to “break down” and “pluck up” (1:10) and concludes with the same Hebrew words (45:4). If Baruk had ambition to obtain status in the Yehudi (Judean) court like his brother Serayah (Seraiah) (51:59), he was advised that it would be useless because disaster would come, as the preceding chapters indicate.
The oracles against the nations (46–51), introduced by a title superscription (46:1), constitute a distinct stylistic division similar to Isaiah 13–23, Ezekiel 25–32, and Amos 1:3–2:16.
Some of the prophecies against foreign nations in Yirmiyah carry dates that show that they were written at different points during his ministry but were collected together for the book.

The prophecy against Mitsrayim opens with a colorful description of Mitsrayim’s expulsion from Karkemish (Carchemish) (605 BC) after a short occupancy (Jer 46:1-12). The second message (vv 13-26) may picture the attack on Mitsrayim in 601 BC when Nekoh (Neco) stopped Nevukadnetsar at the border; the attack in 589 BC when Hofra lost in his attempt to aid Tsidkiyah; or (most probably) the invasion of Mitsrayim by Nevukadnetsar in 568 BC, when Bavel took advantage of the weakness of Mitsrayim to occupy it. At that time Nevukadnetsar set up his judgment throne as predicted (43:10) and meted out death sentences to all rebels, including those Yehudim who might have been implicated in anti-Babylonian conspiracies. The conclusion of the Mitsrayim oracle repeats part of the Book of Hope (46:27-28, cf. 30:10-11).

Messages against Edom, Arav (Arabia), Phoenician cities, and Amon (Ammon) generally condemn pride, cruelty, and idolatry. The oracle against Eylam (Elam) is unique. No other prophet speaks judgment against this people, whose dwelling east of Bavel meant rare contact with Yehudah. Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) predicted that Eylam would be doomed, then restored. Yehezkel (Ezekiel) counts Eylamites (Elamites) among the inhabitants of Sheol (Ez 32:24).

The final judgment indicates the unbiased attitude of the prophet. His messages placed him in an advantageous position with the Babylonians, who treated him with respect and kindness, in contrast to their cruelty to other Yehudim. But when God spoke against Bavel (Babylon), Yirmiyah uttered God’s words without respect to his own comfort, just as he had spoken against Mitsrayim when silence would have been logical for self-preservation.
Chapter 51 concludes “the words of Yirmiyah.”

Chapter 52 repeats historical facts previously stated prophetically by Yirmiyah, and partially recorded also as history in chapter 39 (cf. 2 Kgs 25 and 2 Chr 36). The editor of Yirmiyah evidently desired to climax the book with a historical confirmation of Yirmiyah’s prophecy, but he included facts beyond those contained elsewhere.
See also Israel, History of; Jeremiah (Person) #1; Prophecy; Prophet, Prophetess.

JERICHO

Ancient city on the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River. The name Yeriho (Jericho) may be connected to the ancient name of the Kena’ani (Canaanite) moon god. The Hebrew words for moon, month, new moon, and Yeriho are very similar. Others associate it with the word for spirit or smell, assuming that the pleasant fragrances of the fruits and spices that grew in this oasis occasioned the name of the place. The OT occasionally calls it “the city of palm trees” (e.g., Dt 34:3; 2 Chr 28:15).

Yeriho was located on the west side of the Yarden River about five miles (8 kilometers) from the southernmost fords and about ten miles (16 kilometers) northwest of the Dead Sea. Being in the broad part of the plain of the Yarden, it lies nearly 1,000 feet (305 meters) below sea level and about 3,500 feet (1,067 meters) below Yerushalem (Jerusalem), which was a mere 17 miles (27 kilometers) away. This simple topographical fact explains the incidental words in Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) parable of the good Shomroni (Samaritan), “down from Yerushalem to Yeriho” (Lk 10:30).
History
Prebiblical Record

Yeriho was a large and thriving city for centuries, even millennia, before the Bible first mentions it in connection with the exodus from Mitsrayim (Egypt). In fact, Yeriho is one of the oldest cities in the world, with remains dating to and before the Neolithic Age 10,000 years ago.

For three reasons primitive people would have chosen this site, first as a settlement and eventually as a key city: (1) It has a copious spring, now called Elisha’s Fountain (cf. 2 Kgs 2:18-22). (2) It has a warm climate in the winter, although “hot” describes it in the summer. (3) It is strategically located at a Yarden ford and at the base of several routes leading westward to the foothills.

The comings and goings of various populations can be reconstructed only sketchily from noninscriptional archaeological data. The civilizations grew more complex over the years, going from a simple food-gathering economy at first to the relatively complex urban society, complete with king, soldiers, and guest houses, that Yehoshua (Joshua) encountered. The first certain identification of its inhabitants occurs in Numbers 13:29: “The Hitim (Hittites), the Yevusim (Jebusites), and the Amorim (Amorites) dwell in the hill country; and the Kena’anim (Canaanites) dwell by the sea, and along the Yarden” (rsv).
In the Old Testament

The Yeriho of the OT is best known as the first city taken by the invading Israelis (Israelites) through the miracle of the falling walls. Having spent some time on the east bank of the Yarden in the plains of Moav (Moab) (Nm 22:1; 26:3, 63), the Israelis targeted it as the first military objective in the Conquest. Yehoshua sent spies to reconnoiter the land and the city. Rahav (Rahab) the harlot took them in and later engineered their escape. For her cooperation, she and her family were spared when Yisrael (Israel) destroyed the city (Jos 2, 6). The fall of the city itself occurred after the Israelis had marched around it in silence, except for the continual blowing of trumpets, once a day for six days and then seven times on the seventh day. Then, as the priests blew the trumpets, the people shouted and the walls collapsed.
Yehoshua laid a curse on anyone who might rebuild Yeriho (Jos 6:26). The curse was fulfilled about 500 years later when Hiel rebuilt the city at the cost of two of his sons (1 Kgs 16:34).

Yeriho (Jericho) was in the territory of Benyamin (Benjamin) but right on the border with the territory of Efrayim (Ephraim) to the north (Jos 16:1, 7; 18:12, 21) and appears in scattered incidents throughout the rest of the OT. In 2 Samuel 10:5 (see also 1 Chr 19:5) David had his humiliated ambassadors wait there until their beards grew back. It served as a kind of headquarters for Elisha and apparently was where a “company of the prophets” lived (2 Kgs 2:5; cf. 1 Sm 10:5). During the time of Ahaz, a return of prisoners took place there (2 Chr 28:15). When Yerushalem fell in 586 BC, the reigning king, Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah), fled to near Yeriho but was caught by the Babylonians, who later put out his eyes at Rivlah (Riblah) in Aram (Syria) (2 Kgs 25:5; Jer 39:5; 52:8). The last OT references to Yeriho are in the census lists of Ezra (Ezr 2:34) and Nehemyah (Nehemiah) (Neh 7:36). Men from Yeriho also helped rebuild the Yerushalem wall (3:2).
In the New Testament

First, it must be understood that the Yeriho of NT times was built by Herodes (Herod) more than a mile to the south of the OT site, at the mouth of the Wadi Qilt. It is possible to sort out the healing of the blind men episodes in the synoptic Gospels by understanding that Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) was passing from the site of ancient Yeriho (Mt 20:29; Mk 10:46) and approaching Herodian Yeriho (Lk 18:35). The modern city of Yeriho includes both these sites. As Yeshua passed through Yeriho (19:1) he met and ate with Zakay (Zacchaeus; Grk. Zakkaios), the wealthy chief tax collector of the new Roman Yeriho. The city also figures in the parable of the Good Shomroni (Samaritan) (10:30-37).
Postbiblical Record

While ancient Yeriho was of small consequence after its destruction under Yehoshua, the Yeriho of Herodes was a city of beauty and importance. But even this city fell into decay with the decline of Roman influence in the Middle East. Most of what we know of the city until modern times comes from the writings of pilgrims to the Holy Land. They usually report seeing certain things of biblical significance, such as the tree that Zakay climbed, but they also report that Yeriho was a squalid, wretched Muslim village. And such it has been until relatively recent times, when it grew in size and importance as a major West Bank city.

JEROBOAM

Name of two kings who reigned in the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel): Yarov’am (Jeroboam) I (930–909 BC), the originator and first monarch of the 10 tribes of Yisrael, and Yarov’am II (793–753 BC), the 14th king of the northern kingdom.

1. Yarov’am I was the son of Nevat (Nebat) from Efrayim’s (Ephraim’s) tribe. He also served King Shelomoh (Solomon) (1 Kgs 11:26) and his efforts had been rewarded by his placement as the supervisor of an Efrati (Ephraimite) work force. Yarov’am, therefore, helped rebuild an important section of the defenses of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (vv 27-28). This efficient and energetic young man did not remain in the employ of Shelomoh for long, however. Yarov’am’s background, his tribe’s pride, and the oppression of Shelomoh had produced a young rebel. Ahiyah (Ahijah), the prophet of Shiloh, met Yarov’am outside Yerushalem one day and did a startling thing—he tore a new garment he was wearing into 12 pieces and gave 10 of them to Yarov’am (1 Kgs 11:29-30). Ahiyah had symbolically shown Yarov’am that God would give him 10 tribes and would leave the Davidic line intact (vv 31-39). Shelomoh’s idolatry had brought this judgment upon the Davidic line (v 33). Although precise details of a revolt are not given (v 7), Yarov’am fled to Mitsrayim (Egypt) in order to save his life (v 40).

After Shelomoh’s death, Yarov’am returned to Palestine and approached Rehav’am (Rehoboam), Shelomoh’s son, with a request that his program of oppression cease (1 Kgs 12:1-4). Rehav’am asked for three days to consult with his advisers before answering (vv 5-11). The counsel of the older advisers was toward clemency, but younger hotheads prevailed with their counsel of increased taxation and forced labor (vv 12-14).

The Israelis (Israelites) responded by rejecting Rehav’am. Yarov’am was quickly elected king of the northern tribes (1 Kgs 12:20), and an uneasy cease-fire temporarily stabilized relationships between the two kingdoms at their division (930 BC).

Being ambitious and skillful, Yarov’am built two capital cities, one at Shekem (Shechem) (cf. Gn 12:6-8; Jos 8:30-35), in the territory west of the Yarden (Jordan), and one at Penuel (cf. Gn 32:30; Jgs 8:17), east of the Yarden (1 Kgs 12:25). He reinstituted the cult of the golden calves, substituting an ancient religion for the worship of Jehovah. He changed the centers of worship, the object of worship, the priesthood, and the time of worship. The new centers became Beyt-El (Bethel) and Dan (v 29); Beyt-El was a place of patriarchal worship (Gn 28:10-22; 31:13; 35:1-7), and Dan was the site of a renegade Levitical worship established for the tribe of Dan in the days of the judges (Jgs 18).

The object of worship became the idol calf (1 Kgs 12:28). The worship was based upon Aharon’s (Aaron’s) participation in the first instance of this idolatry in Yisrael. Aharon had presented the golden calf at Sinay (Sinai) as a visible representation of the invisible Yahweh who had brought Yisrael out of Mitsrayim (Ex 32:4-5). This compromise religion would yet have an appeal to Yahweh worshipers. Aharon’s prior establishment of this worship added to the appeal for those who were reluctant to separate from Levitical methodology. The Levites in Dan would also add to the authentication of the calf worship.

Doubtless, the Mitsri (Egyptian) sojourn of Yarov’am contributed to this turn of events. The Mitsrim’s (Egyptians’) worship of Amon-Re, the sun god, included his representation as a bull. The bull in Mitsri worship was intended to visibly represent an invisible deity. This concept could have easily been transferred by the Israelis to their worship of the invisible Yahweh.

Yarov’am’s idolatry would result in the ultimate destruction of his line (1 Kgs 13:33-34). An immediate result was the death of his son Aviyah (Abijah) (14:1-18). Yarov’am’s plan to deceive the prophet Ahiyah failed and became the means of pronouncing judgment upon the house of Yarov’am and the northern kingdom (vv 7-16). One manifestation of the gradual decline of Yisrael was the defeat Yarov’am suffered at the hand of Aviyah of Yehudah (Judah) (2 Chr 13:1-20).

Yarov’am I died after reigning 22 years over Yisrael (1 Kgs 14:19-20). His remaining son, Nadav (Nadab), ruled for only two years before he was assassinated by Baesha (Baasha) of the tribe of Yisakar (Issachar) (1 Kgs 14:20; 15:25-31). The whole household of Yarov’am was then killed by Baesha, fulfilling the prophecy of Ahiyah concerning the end of the dynasty of Yarov’am. Yet even Baesha walked in the footsteps of Yarov’am’s apostasy (1 Kgs 15:34).

2. Yarov’am II, the son of Yoash (Joash) (or Yehoash (Jehoash), 798–782 BC), reigned over Yisrael longer than any other northern king even though he followed the evil example of his ancestral namesake, Yarov’am I (2 Kgs 14:23-24). His reign of 41 years included an 11-year co-regency with his father. Evidently, Yoash had taken steps to ensure the stability of his kingdom before meeting Amatsyah (Amaziah) of Yehudah in battle (2 Kgs 14:8-14; 2 Chr 25:5-24).

Yarov’am II ruled in the city of Shomron (Samaria) (2 Kgs 14:23). The archaeological evidence at Shomron indicates a reconstruction program in the royal palace during the prosperous reigns of Yoash and Yarov’am II. In 1910 excavators found over 60 inscribed potsherds that were invoices or labels for oil and wine sent to the royal stores for use in the king’s service. The limited number of place-names (27) on the potsherds indicates that the shipments of these commodities were not a nationwide levy of taxes but were probably all from properties belonging to the royal house. These illustrate the extensive holdings and opulence of the royal house in Yisrael during the reign of Yarov’am II.

Large numbers of carved decorative plaques and panels of ivory were also found in the ruins of Shomron, a reminder of the wealth of the northern kingdom in its latter days. The influence of the pagan societies of Aram (Syria), Ashur (Assyria), and Mitsrayim can be seen by the various figures of deities on the ivories.

The prophet Yonah (Jonah), son of Amitay (Amittai), had prophesied the acquisition of power by Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II (2 Kgs 14:25). Although Yarov’am’s reign was late in the history of the northern kingdom, God still desired to exhibit his long-suffering and faithful covenant-keeping love, offering Yisrael (Israel) repentance (vv 26-28).

The northern kingdom reached its greatest extension since the time of Shelomoh (Solomon) as the result of God’s care for Yisrael during Yarov’am’s reign. The boundaries stretched from Hamat (Hamath) on the Orontes River in the north to the Gulf of Aqaba, with its cities of Eylot (Elath) and Etsyon-Gever (Ezion-geber), in the south. Prosperity did not suffice to deliver Yisrael from internal and external problems, however. The extensive corruption in government and the degenerate spiritual state of the people propelled Yisrael into the tumultuous days that would end in the utter destruction of the northern kingdom. Yarov’am’s own life must have been in danger from conspirators. Amatsyah, a priest at Beyt-El, even accused the prophet Amos of conspiring to assassinate Yarov’am (Am 7:8-17). Amos had actually prophesied the captivity of Yisrael and the fall of Yarov’am’s dynasty. The word of God had become a threat to Yarov’am because of the hardness of the hearts of all in Yisrael, including the king.

Economic depression, moral deterioration, political weakness, and governmental corruption served to hasten the fall of Yisrael. The rich landowners, including Yarov’am II, had oppressed the less wealthy citizens and had forced small landowners to migrate from their farms to the cities.

Within six months of the death of Yarov’am II, the prophecy concerning the end of the dynasty of Yehu (Jehu) (Yarov’am was the fourth king of that line) was fulfilled (2 Kgs 14:29; 15:8-12; cf. 10:12-31). As the son of Yarov’am I, Nadav, was assassinated, so the son of Yarov’am II, Zekaryah (Zechariah), was assassinated. Thirty-one years after the death of Yarov’am II, the prophecies concerning the captivity of Yisrael were fulfilled (722 BC; 2 Kgs 17:5-41).
See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Israel, History of.
JEROHAM

1. Levite of the family of Kohat (Kohath), father of Elkanah and a forefather of the prophet Shmuel (Samuel) and Heyman (Heman) the singer. Heyman was a musician in the sanctuary during David’s reign (1 Sm 1:1; 1 Chr 6:27, 34).
2. Benyamite (Benjamite) whose sons lived in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and were leaders among their people (1 Chr 8:27). He is perhaps identical with #3 below.
3. Benyamite and Yivneyah’s (Ibneiah’s) father. Yivneyah, head of his family, returned to Yerushalem from exile in Bavel (Babylon) (1 Chr 9:8).
4. Descendant of Pashhur and the father of Adayah (Adaiah) the priest. Adayah returned to Yerushalem after the exile (1 Chr 9:12; Neh 11:12).
5. Benyamite from Gedor whose two sons, Yoelah (Joelah) and Zevadyah (Zebadiah), came to David’s support at Tsiklag (Ziklag) (1 Chr 12:7).
6. Father of Azarel, the chief official of the Danim (Danites) during David’s reign (1 Chr 27:22).

7. Father of Azaryah (Azariah), one of the commanders who was instrumental in removing Queen Atalyah (Athaliah) from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) throne to make way for Yoash (Joash) (Yehoash (Jehoash)), the rightful claimant (2 Chr 23:1).
JERUBBAAL
Name given to Gid’on (Gideon) after he destroyed an altar to Ba’al (Baal) (Jgs 6:32). The name means “let Ba’al contend against him.” See Gideon.
JERUBBESHETH*
An alternate name for Gid’on (Gideon) (2 Sm 11:21) See Gideon.
JERUEL
Wilderness lying southeast of Tekoa near Eyn-Gedi (En-gedi), just above and west of the cliff of Tsits (Ziz) (2 Chr 20:16). Some identify it with el-Hasasah.
JERUSALEM
Historic city sacred to Christians, Yehudim (Jews), and Muslims; the chief city of ancient Palestine and of the modern state of Yisrael (Israel).

Meaning of the Name
Mitsri (Egyptian) Meaning
The earliest mention of the name occurs in the Mitsri Execration Texts of the 19th and 18th centuries BC in the form probably transliterated Urusalimum.
Semitic Meaning

In the 14th century BC the name appears in the Abdi-Hepa correspondence from Tell el-Amarna, written Urusalim. Later it is found in the inscription of the Assyrian monarch Sanheriv (Sennacherib), written Ursalimmu. The two transparently Semitic elements, uru (city) and salim (a divine name), have produced the hyphenated composite meaning “the city of [the god] Saleim (Salim).” Hyphenating geographic names to incorporate divine elements was a common practice in the ancient Near Eastern world, and the deity Saleim, or Shalem (Akkadian, Shulmanu; cf. Shelomoh (Solomon)), was a member of the Amori (Amorite) pantheon (cf. Ez 16:3). Since the oldest textual evidence—Mitsri, West Semitic, and Akkadian—supports only urusalim, and since the OT itself attests that Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was not originally a Hebrew city, it is probable that the Semitic etymological origin of this name produced the meaning “the city of [the god] Saleim.”
Hebrew/Aramaic Meaning

In the Hebrew OT, Yerushalem is written yerushalayim, and in the Aramaic portions the name is rendered yerushalem. Containing the elements yarah (“to found,” cf. Jb 38:6) and shalem (a divine name), it yields the meaning “the foundation of [the god] Shalem,” the sh of the Hebrew/Aramaic to be taken as the phonemic equivalent of the Akkadian s.
Greek Meaning

In the NT, Yerushalem translates the two Greek words Ierousalem and Hierosoluma. The former is simply the Greek transliteration of the OT Aramaic form; the latter reflects the word hieros (holy), representing a Hellenized paronomasia, corresponding neither with the Semitic root of the name nor with the city’s historical reality.
Geographical Situation

Yerushalem is situated 31º 46’ 45” north latitude and 35º 13’ 25” east longitude. The city rises to just over 2,500 feet (762 meters) above sea level and rests some 14 miles (22.5 kilometers) west of the northern end of the Dead Sea and approximately 33 miles (53 kilometers) east of the Mediterranean coast.

A Mediterranean climate pervades Yerushalem. From October to May, the city experiences its rainy season, with an annual accumulation of about 25 inches (63.5 centimeters). Throughout January and February the rains are often driven by winds, and the mercury drops to near freezing (cf. Ezr 10:9); the coldest weather coincides with the days of heaviest rainfall. Snow falls two years out of three. There is no rain between May and September, and a high percentage of solar radiation produces oppressive heat.

Like Romai (Rome), Yerushalem is a city set on hills. A cluster of five hills comprise the denuded quadrilateral landmass roughly one mile (1.6 kilometers) long and one-half mile (.8 kilometer) wide, bordered on all sides, except the north, by deep ravines. Stationed astride the crest of Palestine’s central plateau and located at the crossroad of the watershed route connecting Hevron (Hebron), Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem), Shekem (Shechem) (Nablus), and points north with the longitudinal route from the Yarden (Jordan) Valley and the several arteries to the Mediterranean, Yerushalem is commercially central to the country. The lateral highway through the Yehudi (Judean) mountains and eastward could not pass south of Yerushalem, being blocked by the Dead Sea and its sheer cliffs. Because it lacked significant water supply, the city’s strategic commercial location was probably the deciding criterion for its original occupation.

Water, a lifeline of civilization, has always been in meager supply at Yerushalem. The only natural source of permanent water was the spring at Gihon, today sometimes called the Virgin’s Fountain, located in the Kidron Valley immediately east of the ancient fortress conquered by David. Tunnels were burrowed to provide access to the Gihon when Yerushalem was besieged. Later, the Siloam Tunnel was cut through nearly 1,800 feet (548.6 meters) of limestone, allowing the waters of the Gihon to pass through the hill of Tsiyon (Zion) to the pool of Siloam.

Farther south, where the Kidron and Hinom (Hinnom) Valleys converge, there was another spring, called Eyn-Rogel (En-rogel) in the Bible (modern Bir Eyyub). Owing to the lowering of the water table, this source of water ceased to percolate and was subsequently converted into a well.

These two sources were clearly insufficient to sustain a sizable population, and both were too deep in the Kidron to be employed for irrigation. Hence, a vast network of cisterns, reservoirs, and water conduits for supplemental supply has been devised since ancient times.
History
The Pre-Israelite Period

Paleolithic and Mesolithic flint implements of an Acheulian type found in the plain of the Refaim (Rephaim) constitute the earliest evidence of the existence of human beings in the area of Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Near the beginning of the fourth millennium BC, the southeastern hill was first occupied by a sedentary group, a fact evinced from the artifactual remains recovered from three graves and the pottery type discovered on bedrock. By 1800 BC, the crest of the southeastern hill was walled in rudimentary form.

From the Bible one learns that Avraham (Abraham) paid tithes to Malki-Tsedek (Melchizedek), king of Shalem (Salem) (Gn 14:17-20). Again (ch 22) the great patriarch visited an area later incorporated into Yerushalem, Mt Moriyah (Moriah), the site where Yitshak (Isaac) was nearly sacrificed. Second Chronicles 3:1 identifies Mt Moriyah as the temple hill. In the 15th century BC or thereabouts the Hurrians (possibly the biblical Horim (Horites)) penetrated into Palestine. About the same time at Yerushalem, extensive building activities were initiated and improved fortification methods were introduced. Accordingly, most writers attribute these projects at Yerushalem to the Hurrian infiltration.
Conquest and Settlement Period

Upon learning of Giveon’s (Gibeon’s) placation of Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) army (Jos 9), Adoni-Tsedek (Adoni-zedek), king of Yerushalem, formed a coalition with the kings of Hevron, Yarmut (Jarmuth), Lakish (Lachish), and Eglon and attacked Giveon. In response, Yehoshua marshaled his forces and defeated the coalition, killing all five monarchs at Makedah (Makkedah) (Jos 10:16-27). It appears that the tribe of Yehudah (Judah) temporarily took control of Yerushalem and burned it in the wake of this victory (Jgs 1:8). However, the Yevusim (Jebusites) reoccupied the site (Jos 15:63; 1 Chr 11:4-5). Apparently, the Yevusim more or less maintained control of Yerushalem until the time of David.

The city appears again as a boundary separating the tribal inheritances of Yehudah and Benyamin (Benjamin), becoming the southern border of the latter’s domain. The identification of the “shoulder of the Yevusi (Jebusite)” (rsv Jos 15:8; 18:16) with Yerushalem is usually explained as a reference to the southwestern hill, probably held also by the Yevusim at this time.
David’s Yerushalem

Following the Pelishti (Philistine) victory atop Mt Gilboa, where Sha’ul (Saul) and Yonatan (Jonathan) were killed in battle (1 Sm 31), David reigned over the tribe of Yehudah from Hevron (Hebron), while a surviving son of Sha’ul, Ish-Boshet (Ishbosheth), ruled over the northern tribes from Mahanayim (Mahanaim). During the two-year struggle that ensued, the house of David grew stronger while the forces of Ish-Boshet shrunk considerably (2 Sm 3:1). This struggle culminated in the death and decapitation of Ish-Boshet and the dispersion of his forces. David became the undisputed monarch of all the tribes of Yisrael (Israel).

But the new monarch recognized that a consolidated national capital acceptable to both the north and the south would have to be created. Yerushalem had remained neutral in the conflict, being the site of a Yevusi enclave. It also represented a location that was militarily desirable, and by being commercially central to the fledgling nation, it was ideally suited.

In the course of David’s 33-year reign at Yerushalem he made the city into the center of an empire that stretched from Mitsrayim (Egypt) to the Perat (Euphrates) River. He engaged in considerable building and expansion of the city. He fortified the Kena’ani (Canaanite) walls and prepared an extension of the city, possibly along the east slope of Tsiyon (Zion).

David also constructed a royal residence, receiving the technology and many materials from Hiram, king of Tsor (Tyre) (2 Sm 5:11). Nehemiah 12:37 suggests that this palace also may have been near the east side of the southeastern hill. It was from a window of this house that Mikal (Michal) saw David dancing in an undignified manner—according to her perception (2 Sm 6:16-23). From the roof of this palace David gazed upon Bat-Sheva (Bathsheba) as she bathed (11:2-5), and from this residence he plotted the murder of her husband, Uriyah (Uriah) (vv 14-25).

By bringing the ark of the covenant to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (2 Sm 6:1-15)—implying that Yahweh would reside there—David displayed his most profound leadership. For in this perceptive act he merged for the first time in Yisrael’s history its political and religious capitals. Yerushalem took on the unique character of a holy city and a royal city. As a result, the city would be known as the “city of David” (5:7) as well as the “city of God” (Ps 46:4). Adult male Yehudim (Jews) would make their pilgrimages to Yerushalem to take part in the feasts and offerings. It only remained for David to make this arrangement permanent, to enshrine Yahweh at Yerushalem forever by building him a temple. David aspired to do so (2 Sm 7), but God responded that such an undertaking was to be reserved for a son of the king.
The First Temple Period

A growing national realization of the extent and impact of the Davidic empire was employed by Shelomoh (Solomon) to full advantage. Himself an innovative and dynamic administrator, Shelomoh turned Yerushalem into a cosmopolitan center. The revenues of caravans from Mitsrayim to Bavel (Babylonia) as well as the Phoenician trade with Eylot (Elath), the Red Sea, and Ofir (Ophir) passed through his royal capital. Shelomoh’s own naval fleet traveled as far as Tarshish, most likely located on an island along the western coast of Spania (Spain). These expeditions returned every three years with such exotic commodities as apes, peacocks, silver, iron, tin, ivory, and gold. The capital swelled with residents and visitors, and the monarch’s fame became proverbial (1 Kgs 10).

Shelomoh was the great OT builder of Yerushalem. His most significant building enterprise was undoubtedly the first temple. Erected on the summit of the temple hill, this edifice required seven years to construct, from April/May 966 (1 Kgs 6:1) to October/November 959 (v 38). Hiram again provided both the technology and the cedar beams.

One may find in 1 Kings 10:27 a succinct encapsulation of the economic wealth lavished upon Yerushalem by Shelomoh: silver became as abundant as stone, and cedar was as common as sycamore. It is estimated that the annual revenues that coursed into Yerushalem were as high as $17 million. Ironically, it was the fiscal factor that became the burden of Shelomoh’s monarchy. Overextending himself financially, his economic and political programs soon required the levying of heavy taxes (1 Kgs 4:7-19) and the drafting of Israelis (Israelites) into forced labor (1 Kgs 5:13-18; cf. 9:20-23). These were the primary factors that prompted the schism in Yisrael’s political structure after the death of Shelomoh and resulted in a divided monarchy by 930 BC.

When the Babylonian army laid final siege to Yerushalem (588 BC), capturing it after many months, the city was completely decimated. The temple and Shelomoh’s palace were destroyed with fire; the city walls were demolished. The temple treasures were completely plundered, and the citizens were deported in large numbers.
The Second Temple Period

Yerushalem’s doom and 70-year captivity had been spelled out by Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) (Jer 25:11; 29:10; cf. 2 Chr 36:21; Dn 9:2). In 538 BC, after the fall of Bavel, Koresh (Cyrus), king of Paras (Persia), issued his famous proclamation (2 Chr 36:22-23; Ezr 1:1-4; cf. Is 44:28; 45:1). Thereupon, a humble group of Yehudim returned to Yerushalem with Sheshebatsar (Sheshbazzar), a prince of Yehudah (Judah) (Ezr 1:8-11) and Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) (2:2). In 515 BC, the doors of the second temple were opened officially, and the Passover feast was again observed from Yerushalem (6:15-18).

Ezra came to Yerushalem in the seventh year of Artahshashta (Artaxerxes) (Ezr 7:7). Assuming this is a reference to Artahshashta I, the date of Ezra’s return would have been 458 BC. Again, it was only a meager remnant who felt the compelling urge to make that difficult journey (cf. Josephus’s Antiquities 11.1.3).

Moved by reports of troubled conditions (Neh 1:3-4), Nehemyah (Nehemiah), in the 20th year of Artahshashta (445 BC), was able to leave his post as cup-bearer to the king and to go to Yerushalem. If the concern of the earlier returnees focused upon the temple, Nehemyah’s was upon the city walls. His is the most comprehensive description of Yerushalem’s postexilic city walls and topography (Neh 2:11-16). Spurred on by his energetic enthusiasm, the people completed the task of rebuilding the walls in 52 days (6:15).
The Roman Period

In 40 BC, with the aid of the Parthia (Parthians), Antigonus attacked and seized Yerushalem (Jerusalem), forcing Herodes (Herod) to escape by night. He journeyed to Romai (Rome), where the Senate appointed him as “king of the Yehudim (Jews)” (cf. Mt 2:1). Armed with this new authority, Herodes marshaled two Roman legions, and in 37 BC, he succeeded in forever expelling the Parthia. So began the long and infamous rule of Herodes, who reigned at Yerushalem for 33 years (37–4 BC).

It cannot be denied that Yerushalem enjoyed prosperous and peaceful years during his reign. Herodes transformed the external aspect of Yerushalem. He transferred the seat of government to the southwestern hill. Here he erected a lavish palace, an arena for athletic contests, a theater, and a vast aqueduct network.

Other building projects concerned the temple hill. Herodes transformed the old Maccabean fortress into a much larger structure and named it Antonia, in honor of Markos (Mark) Antony. In the temple area proper he enlarged the esplanade on both the north and south sides, giving it a rectangular shape. Herodes’s reconstruction of the temple was undertaken in 20 BC, and it was not completed until around AD 64, just six years prior to its destruction by Titos (Titus) (cf. Jn 2:20).

JERUSALEM, New

Phrase appearing only twice in the Bible, once near the beginning and once near the end of the book of Revelation (Rv 3:12; 21:2). In the first of the great visions of that book, the risen Christ speaks to his people in the midst of their conflict in this world. Among his promises to those who conquer is that they will one day be citizens of the new Yerushalem (Jerusalem). The last of the book’s visions shows the fulfillment of this promise. There we see not only the victorious people of God but also the city that is to be their home in a new world.
This does not, of course, answer the question “What is the new Yerushalem?” A description of what it is like would be relatively simple. An explanation of what it is would be more complicated.
Description of the City

An angel takes Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) to a mountaintop to show him the new Yerushalem. In the account that follows (Rv 21:10–22:5), the first thing Yohan notes is the light, like a great jewel-like lamp, that lights the city (“the glory of God,” 21:11). Then he describes its walls and gates (21:12-14). The 12 gates bear the names of the tribes of Yisrael (Israel), and the wall between each gate and the next forms a single “foundation,” or block, bearing the name of one of the 12 apostles of Christ. Next, the measurements of the city are given (vv 15-17). It is 1,400 miles (2,220 kilometers) each way—not only in breadth and in length but also in height—and its wall is 216 feet (65.8 meters) thick (or high?). By working out these equivalents in miles and feet, however, we miss what Yohan would probably have thought much more important. According to the biblical units of measurement, the city is 12,000 stadia broad and its wall is 144 cubits thick. These numbers are symbolic; as multiples of 12, they signify perfection, as do other occurrences of 12 in Revelation (e.g., 7:4-8).

After this, Yohan describes the materials of which the new Yerushalem is built (21:18-21). The wall is of jasper; its foundation layers are encrusted with other precious stones; its gates are pearls; and the streets and buildings within are made of “transparent gold.” As for the city itself, Yohan notes a series of things that it does not have (vv 22-27)—no temple, no sun or moon, no night, no closing of its gates, and no evil. Finally, there are the three wonderful things that it does have (22:1-5)—the river of the water of life, the tree of life, and the throne and presence of God himself.
Such is the new Yerushalem as Yohan describes it. But he wants us not so much to picture what the city looks like as to understand what it means.
Background of the City

OT history presents the city of David, old Yerushalem, as the place where God’s rule over his people and his presence among them was centered. In that Yerushalem stood both the temple, where the priests served, and the throne of the kings who governed as God’s deputies. It was the metropolis, or “mother city,” of Yisrael, the people of God. But the whole Bible is about God’s redeeming a people for himself, out of all nations, in all ages—a greater Yisrael of which OT Yisrael is only the vanguard. So it is natural that the last revelation the Bible gives should be a vision of that greater people—home at last in the true mother city, a new and greater Yerushalem.

The OT prophets witnessed the decline of old Yerushalem. They watched with grief and anger as it disappointed the hope that it would live up to its high destiny. As it became infected with sin and folly, and as its kings and priests increasingly betrayed their calling, two of these prophets in particular began to look forward to a Yerushalem that one day would be what it was meant to be. Yehezkel (Ezekiel) (chs 40–48) foresaw the city and its temple reconstructed in detail; Yeshayah (Isaiah) (chs 52, 60–66) described this latter-day Yerushalem in even more glowing terms. The vision of both prophets tie in closely with the vision Yohan records in Revelation 21–22.

In the period between the OT and NT, Jewish writers became yet more disillusioned with the way things were going, and they encouraged their readers not so much with hopes of the renewal of the earthly Yerushalem as with imaginative descriptions of the heavenly one. This, they reckoned, existed already; at the end of the age it would come down from God out of heaven, the metropolis of his people, populous and beautiful, the place of his temple and throne. In fact, what was imagined by these apocalyptic writers is in many respects very like what would in due course actually be seen by Yohan.

Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) develops all these lines of thought in quite a remarkable way. It is not simply that he foretells the final destruction of Yerushalem and its temple (Mk 13; Lk 19:41-44). If that were all, it would leave a great question unanswered. For old Yerushalem existed for a purpose, as we have seen; and if it is to be destroyed, how can that purpose then be fulfilled? Where will God’s people then find his throne and his temple?

Yeshua’s answer is that, since the Incarnation, God’s rule and God’s presence are to be found in him (Mt 28:18; Jn 14:9). He himself is the “new Yerushalem (Jerusalem)”—an entirely new kind of Yerushalem. This is borne out by the word for “new” that Yohan uses in Revelation. There are two distinct Greek words translated in English Bibles as “new.” Sometime after the destruction of Yerushalem in AD 70, the emperor Hadrian built a “new” Yerushalem; that was the kind of “new” that simply meant the latest in a series of cities on the same site. But Yohan’s vision is of a Yerushalem that is “new” in the sense of being fresh, clean, and different. The NT speaks in the same way of the new covenant and the new commandment (Jn 13:34; Heb 8:8), the new creation and the new man (2 Cor 5:17; Eph 2:15). Yohan’s vision brings out the same truth by telling of seven things that will exist “no more” in the new heaven and earth: no more sea, death, sorrow, crying, pain, curse, or night (Rv 21:1, 4; 22:3-5). In these respects all will be new and different.

There are five passages elsewhere in the NT that help to fill in the background to Revelation 21. In Galatians 4:26 Paulos (Paul) speaks of “Yerushalem above,” the mother city of all who receive salvation by faith, as opposed to the old Yerushalem, where those belong who seek to please God by trying to obey the law (v 25). In Ephesians 5:25-32 he speaks of the bride of Christ, by which he means the church; in Yohan’s vision the “bride” is the “city” (Rv 21:9-10). In Philippians 3:20 we are told that the heavenly city is not simply the future home of believers but also the place of their present “citizenship.” Hebrews 12:22 makes the same point: those who believe have arrived already at the “heavenly Yerushalem.” In other words, this Yerushalem is the home of all God’s believing people, Yehudi (Jew) and Gentile, from OT and NT times, and it seems not only to be future but also to exist already, in some sense, in the present. What, then, are we to make of Yohan’s vision?
Meaning of the City

Some of those who expect a future Millennium (1,000-year earthly reign of Christ, between his second coming and final defeat of Satan) believe that the new Yerushalem belongs to the Millennium, because of certain indications that they think suit that period better than the eternal state that will follow it (Rv 21:24-26; 22:2). They visualize it as a literal, material city. It will presumably, then, be in the shape of a cube, or perhaps a pyramid, and some even picture it hovering like an immense spaceship above the surface of the earth.

Most millennarians, however, and also many who do not believe in a millennium in the sense just mentioned, think that Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) is describing the city as it will be in eternity. They, too, may take it literally, or they think that giving the literal details in these chapters—the city’s measurements, materials, and so on—is the only way in which Yohan could describe something that is in fact indescribable (though nonetheless real).

In line with the message of the entire book of Revelation, many take the new Yerushalem to be the ideal city of God, which belongs not only to the future but also to the present. It exists here and now because it is a spiritual truth, not a material one. It is always “coming down . . . out of heaven” precisely because it comes to men “from God” (21:2). The fact remains, of course, that everything Yohan records in the last two chapters of Revelation belongs to a world that will only appear after the first heaven and the first earth have passed away—a world that is (to us, at any rate) still future.

Taking into account all these Scriptures, we may come closest to understanding the new Yerushalem if we see it as the community of Christ and his people, which will appear in its perfection only when this age has come to an end. Yet, in another sense, Christians belong to it already, and it gives them both an ideal to strive for in this world and a hope to anticipate in the next.
See also Bride of Christ; Church; Jerusalem.
JERUSALEM COUNCIL*

Meeting described in Acts 15:6-29, held about AD 50. Acts records that the conference was held to deal with the question of the requirement for gentile salvation raised by Yehudim (Jews) first in Antiokeia (Antioch) (14:26–15:1) and later in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (15:3-5). The matter was subjected to lengthy consideration by the apostles and the elders (v 6), with Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) (vv 7-11), Paulos (Paul) and Barnabas (vv 12, 22-26), and Ya’akov (James) the brother of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) (vv 13-21), who seems to have been the moderator.

The major points agreed upon by the council were the following: (1) God makes no distinction between believers, Jewish or Gentile (15:9); (2) salvation is by grace through faith (vv 9-11); (3) God confirmed his acceptance of Gentiles through signs and wonders (vv 8, 12); (4) inclusion of the Gentiles among his people was part of the divine intention revealed in the OT (vv 15-18; quoting Am 9:11-12). The assembly also issued a list (sometimes called “the decree”) instructing gentile Christians to abstain from (1) idolatry, (2) fornication, (3) eating animals that had been strangled, and (4) consuming blood. (The last two items pertained to dietary matters that greatly separated Yehudim from Gentiles.) The decision was circulated by letter to churches in Antiokeia, Aram (Syria), and Kilikia (Cilicia) (Acts 15:23; cf. 16:4).

The account, when viewed within its place in the book of Acts as a whole, forms the culmination of the struggle by the early church to understand itself. The Youdaismos (Judaism) from which Christianity arose was a legalistic religion wherein people sought to earn God’s favor by observing ceremonies and keeping laws. It also held to an exclusive nationalistic outlook that regarded Yisrael (Israel) alone as “the people of God” and that required non-Jews desiring to be identified with God to submit to circumcision and the Mosaic law as well as offer prescribed sacrifices. The earliest Christians in Yerushalem seem to have held at least some of these views even after recognizing Yeshua as the Messiah.

Acts portrays a series of events through which the fallacy of the Jewish legalistic and exclusivistic attitudes were exposed. Stefanos (Stephen) questioned the narrow religious view that restricted God’s presence, activity, and concern to Yerushalem (ch 7). Filippos (Philip) led Shomronim (Samaritans) and an Kushi (Ethiopian) official, representatives of groups with only loose traditional connections to Youdaismos, to faith in Yeshua (ch 8). At the direct command of God, Kefa proclaimed Yeshua as Messiah and Lord to Kornelios (Cornelius), a good God-fearing but uncircumcised Gentile (ch 10). Through this incident Kefa came to recognize that God does not discriminate between peoples (10:34-35). The undeniable coming of the Holy Spirit upon Kornelios and his household (v 44) provided surprising proof of God’s acceptance of the Gentiles, which could not be doubted even by members of the scrupulously Jewish, pro-circumcision group who witnessed the event (vv 45-48) or to whom it was later reported (11:1-18). The conversion of Kornelios became a precedent later cited by Kefa at the council (15:7-11).

God’s acceptance of Kornelios might have been regarded as an exceptional case by strict Jewish Christians. This was made impossible by the conversion of Greeks at Antiokeia (11:20, nlt mg), the establishment of a racially and culturally mixed church in that city (as implied by the diverse backgrounds of the leaders mentioned in Acts 13:1), and the large number of Gentiles converted during Paulos’s missionary journey into south-central Asia Minor (chs 13–14).

Acts records that at this juncture Jewish Christians from Yerushalem came to Antiokeia and precipitated the crisis that made necessary the convening of the council. Their insistence that gentile believers be circumcised and submit to the Mosaic law was tantamount to requiring them to become Yehudim nationally, socially, and religiously in order to become Christians. The early church was thus faced with the necessity of clarifying its relation to Youdaismos (was it a part of or separate from it?) and the nature of the salvation it proclaimed (nationalistic and legalistic or by grace through faith?).

The Yerushalem Council established the truth that salvation is a free gift to be received by faith; it rejected human effort as a means of or contributor to salvation. By implication it also dissociated Christianity from any attempt to restrict it to a particular racial, national, cultural, or social group. The council affirmed Christians to be free from the obligation to earn salvation through ceremonies or law-keeping. At the same time it recognized the practical necessity of responsible and appropriate conduct, which takes into account the moral nature of God and the sensitivities and concerns of other Christians.
See also Acts of the Apostles, Book of the; Galatians, Letter to the; Judaizers; Paul, The Apostle.
JERUSHA, JERUSHAH*
Tsadok’s (Zadok’s) daughter, wife of King Uziyah (Uzziah) of Yehudah (Judah) and mother of King Yotam (Jotham) (2 Kgs 15:33; 2 Chr 27:1, alternately spelled “Yerushah (Jerushah)”).
JESHAIAH
1. Hananyah’s (Hananiah’s) son; the father of Refayah (Rephaiah) and a descendant of David through Zerubavel’s (Zerubbabel’s) line, who lived in postexilic Palestine (1 Chr 3:21).
2. Yedutun’s (Jeduthun’s) son and the leader of the eighth of 24 divisions of musicians trained for service in the sanctuary during David’s reign (1 Chr 25:3, 15).
3. Rehavyah’s (Rehabiah’s) son and one of the Levites in charge of the temple treasury during David’s reign (1 Chr 26:25).
4. Son of Atalyah (Athaliah) from the house of Eylam (Elam), who returned with Ezra to Yehudah (Judah) following the Babylonian captivity (Ezr 8:7).
5. Levite of the family of Merari, who returned with Ezra to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) after the exile (Ezr 8:19).
6. Benyamite (Benjamite), Itiel’s (Ithiel’s) father, and an ancestor of Salu (Sallu). Salu resettled in Yerushalem during the postexilic era (Neh 11:7).
JESHANAH

Border city in the hill country of Efrayim (Ephraim) that King Aviyah (Abijah) of Yehudah (Judah) (913–910 BC) seized from King Yarov’am (Jeroboam) I (930–909 BC) and the northern kingdom during a civil war (2 Chr 13:19). The Greek and Syriac reading of “Yeshanah (Jeshanah)” as one of the towns between which Shmuel (Samuel) erected the Even-Ha’ezer (Ebenezer) stone may be preferred to the Hebrew “Shen” in 1 Samuel 7:12. Its location is perhaps near Burj el-Isaneh, four miles (6.4 kilometers) north of Beyt-El (Bethel).
JESHARELAH*
A variant for Asarelah (Asharelah) or Asarelah, the name of a Levite musician, in 1 Chronicles 25:14 (kjv; niv “Jesarelah”). See Asharelah.
JESHEBEAB
Levite family leader assigned to temple duty during David’s reign (1 Chr 24:13).
JESHER
Kalev’s (Caleb’s) son from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 2:18).
JESHIMON

1. Desolate wilderness at the end of the Dead Sea, not far from Pisgah and Pe’or (Peor) (Nm 21:20; 23:28). In both passages the nlt renders it “wasteland” in the text but has “Yeshimon (Jeshimon)” in the margin, allowing it to be translated as a specific area. The rsv uses “desert.”
2. Wilderness to the north of the hill of Hakilah and of Maeon (Maon) (1 Sm 23:19, 24; 26:1-3); this location was probably just a few miles south of Hevron (Hebron).
JESHISHAI
Descendant of Gad in the days of Yotam (Jotham), king of Yehudah (Judah) (1 Chr 5:14).
JESHOHAIAH

One of the 13 Shim’oni (Simeonite) princes in the days of Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) who participated in the invasion of the valley of Gedor; they killed the inhabitants of the territory and took the land for the pasture of their sheep (1 Chr 4:36).
JESHUA (Person)

1. Levite and head of the ninth of 24 divisions of priests formed during David’s reign (1 Chr 24:11). He was perhaps the forefather of 973 descendants who returned with Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) to Yehudah (Judah) following the exile (Ezr 2:36; Neh 7:39).
2. One of the Levites assisting Kore in the distribution of the offerings among his fellow priests living in the priestly cities of Yehudah during the days of King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) (2 Chr 31:15).

3. Son of Yotsadak (Jozadak) (alternately “Yehotsadak (Jehozadak)”) the high priest. Yotsadak was deported by Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) to Bavel (Babylon) (1 Chr 6:14-15). Yeshua (Jeshua), Yotsadak’s successor as high priest, returned with Zerubavel to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) after the exile (Ezr 2:2; Neh 7:7; 12:1). Upon arrival, he led his fellow priests in making the altar of God (Ezr 3:2; 5:2) and eventually headed up a construction program to rebuild the temple (3:8). Confirmed as God’s leader by Hagay (Haggai) and Zekaryah (Zechariah) (Hg 1:1-14; 2:2, 4; Zec 3:1-9; 6:11), Yeshua (alternately “Yehoshua (Joshua)” in these passages) resolutely resisted attempts by adversaries to infiltrate his people and hinder the work on the temple (Ezr 4:3). Yoyakim (Joiakim) was Yeshua’s son and successor as high priest, serving in the days of Nehemyah (Nehemiah) and Ezra (Neh 12:12, 26).
4. Descendant of Pahat-Moav (Pahath-moab) and the forefather of a family of Yehudim (Jews) who returned with Zerubavel to Yehudah following the Babylonian captivity (Ezr 2:6; Neh 7:11).

5. Father of a family of Levites who returned to Yerushalem with Zerubavel (Ezr 2:40; Neh 7:43; 12:8). He and his sons were responsible for overseeing the workmen building the temple (Ezr 3:9; this Yeshua may be identical with #3 above).

6. Levite and Yozavad’s (Jozabad’s) father. Yozavad assisted Meremot (Meremoth), Eleazar, and Noadyah (Noadiah) with taking inventory of the temple’s precious metals and vessels during the days of Ezra (Ezr 8:33).
7. Ezer’s father. Ezer was ruler of Mitspah (Mizpah), who repaired a section of the Yerushalem wall during the days of Nehemyah (Neh 3:19).

8. Azanyah’s (Azaniah’s) son and a leader of the Levites in the days of Ezra and Nehemyah. Yeshua assisted Ezra with teaching the people the law (Neh 8:7) and later set his seal on Ezra’s covenant (10:9).
9. Alternate spelling of Yehoshua, the son of Nun, in Nehemiah 8:17. See Joshua (Person) #1.
JESHUA (Place)

Town in the Negev listed before Moladah among the towns where Yehudim (Judeans) returned after exile (Neh 11:26; cf. v 20). It may be identical with the Shema mentioned next to Moladah in Joshua 15:26. The name is perhaps preserved in Tell es-Sa’weh, northeast of Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba).
JESHUAH*
KJV spelling of Yeshua (Jeshua), a priest during David’s time, in 1 Chronicles 24:11. See Jeshua (Person) #1.
JESHURUN*

Poetical name for Yisrael (Israel), possibly derived from the Hebrew root meaning “upright,” but according to many scholars a diminutive of Yisrael. The name Yeshurun (Jeshurun) is mentioned in Deuteronomy 32:15 and 33:5, 26 (see nlt mg). In the Septuagint, the word is not translated as a proper name but as an adjective, “beloved.” In Isaiah 44:2 Ya’akov (Jacob) is described as “Yisrael, my chosen one” (with mg note saying “Yeshurun,” see nlt), thus linking the name with the idea of election. In Deuteronomy 33:5 Yisrael is reminded that “Yahweh became king in Yeshurun” (rsv), and in verse 26 it is told that there is none like God. If we follow the Septuagint, there is a link with the term “beloved” used of Christ (Mt 3:17; Mk 1:11; Eph 1:6) and of the church (Col 3:12; 1 Thes 1:4; 2 Thes 2:13; Jude 1:1).
JESIAH*
1. KJV rendering of Yishiyah (Isshiah), one of David’s ambidextrous archers, in 1 Chronicles 12:6. See Isshiah #2.
2. KJV rendering of Yishiyah, Uziel’s (Uzziel’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 23:20. See Isshiah #3.
JESIMIEL

One of the 13 Shim’oni (Simeonite) princes who participated in the invasion of the valley of Gedor in King Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) day, killing the inhabitants and taking the land for the pasture of their sheep (1 Chr 4:36).
JESSE (Person)

Son of Oved (Obed) and grandson of Ruth and Boaz (Ru 4:17, 22). Yishay (Jesse) was a shepherd from Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem). He had eight sons, of whom David was the youngest. He had at least two daughters, Tseruyah (Zeruiah) and Avigayil (Abigail), who became mothers of famous warriors.

When Shmuel (Samuel) went to Yishay’s home to search for and anoint a king, Yishay did not at first feel it worthwhile to call David for examination (1 Sm 16:11). Later he sent David to play the lyre for Sha’ul (Saul) (vv 19-21). After David became a fugitive from Sha’ul, Yishay and others of the family came to David in the cave of Adulam (Adullam). David then brought his father and mother to Mitspah (Mizpah) in Moav (Moab) (22:3). Nothing further is heard of Yishay.

After Sha’ul broke with David, he commonly spoke of David derisively as a “son of Yishay” to underscore his humble origins (1 Sm 20:31; 22:7). This same emphasis on Yishay’s modest station in life is found in such messianic references as Isaiah 11:1 and 10, which speak of the “shoot from the stump of Yishay” and “the root of Yishay” (rsv).
See also David; Jesse, Root of.
JESSE*, Root of

Figure of speech used by Yeshayah (Isaiah) (Is 11:10) to express the hope of a messianic king from the line of David. The “root” of a family is its progenitor. Yishay (Jesse), David’s father, is listed as an ancestor of the Messiah (Is 11:1, 10; Mt 1:5-6; Lk 3:32; Acts 13:22-23). Yeshayah pictures God’s judgment upon Ashur (Assyria) as the cutting down of a forest (Is 10:33-34); Yehudah (Judah) likewise will be felled and the proud tree of David’s sovereignty hewn down, but a remnant will remain, described by Yeshayah as a shoot from a stump (6:13). The messianic shoot will come forth from the stump of Yishay as a branch from his roots. The Spirit of the Lord will rest upon this one who stands as an ensign to the people, so that the nations will seek him in the glory of his dwelling place (Is 11:1-10; see Is 53:2; Jer 23:5; 33:15; Ez 17:22-23; Zec 3:8; 6:12).

The apostle Paulos (Paul), quoting Yeshayah’s prophecy, identified Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) as “the root of Yishay” in whom the Gentiles hope (Rom 15:12). Christ is not only “a shoot from the stump of Yishay” (Is 11:1) but is himself the “root of Yishay” (Is 11:10; Rom 15:12; see Rv 5:5; 22:16, “root of David”). This means that Yeshua not only came from Yishay’s line but that Yishay (and David) came from Yeshua. In other words, the image points to Yeshua’s divinity. While Yeshua was the son of David, Yeshua was also David’s “Lord.” This is the point Yeshua made in his debate with the religious leaders of his day who recognized only that the Messiah was a human descendant of David. Matthew 22:42-45 reads: “ ‘What do you think about the Messiah? Whose son is he?’ They replied, ‘He is the son of David.’ Yeshua responded, ‘Then why does David, speaking under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, call him Lord? For David said, “Yahweh said to my Lord, sit in honor at my right hand until I humble your enemies beneath your feet.” Since David called him Lord, how can he be his son at the same time?’ ”
See also Christology; David; Genealogy of Jesus Christ; Jesse (Person); Jesus Christ, Teachings of.
JESUI*, JESUITE*
KJV forms of Yishvi (Ishvi) and Yishvi, one of Asher’s descendants and his family, in Numbers 26:44. See Ishvi #1.
JESURUN*
KJV spelling of Yeshurun (Jeshurun), a poetical name for Yisrael (Israel), in Isaiah 44:2. See Jeshurun.
JESUS
1. Name meaning “savior” or “Jehovah [Yahweh] is salvation” given to the Messiah. See Jesus Christ.
2. KJV translation of Yehoshua (Joshua), son of Nun, in Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8. See Joshua (Person) #1.
3. Jewish Christian, surnamed Yustos (Justus), who sent his greetings to the believers at Kolossai (Colosse) in the salutation of Paulos’s (Paul’s) Letter to the Colossians (Col 4:11).
JESUS CHRIST
Messiah, Savior, and founder of the Christian church.

In providing a biography of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ it must be borne in mind that each of the Gospels has its own distinctive purpose. Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios), for instance, presents Yeshua as the messianic King, whereas the emphasis in Markos (Mark) is more on Yeshua as the servant of all. Lukas (Luke) tends to present Yeshua in a softer light, showing particularly his amazing compassion to the less fortunate, whereas Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) plunges the reader into a deeper and more spiritual understanding of Yeshua. These different aims caused the four Evangelists to select and arrange the events of Yeshua’s life differently, resulting in a fourfold portrait of the same man. It was undoubtedly for this reason that the Christian church preserved four Gospels instead of only one.

The following sections present the main events in what may be regarded as the chief stages of the life of Yeshua. These stages show a definite progression from Christ’s incarnation to his cross. The amount of space devoted to each stage in each of the Gospels is dictated by theological rather than biographical interest. The whole presentation of Christ’s life centers on the cross and the subsequent triumphant resurrection and is more an account of God’s message to humanity than a plain historic account of the life of Yeshua.
