Author

The question of the authorship of the book of Iyov (Job) is a difficult one. The difficulty is compounded not only by the lack of ascription of authorship to any individual but also by the structure of the book which, according to some scholars, is a composite consisting of several literary works.

Some scholars who think the book is a composite work base their views on alleged incongruities existing among the various sections. The prologue (chs 1–2) and the epilogue (42:7-17), for example, are seen as separate from the body of the book because they seem to present Iyov as a man of perfect moral character. The dialogues, however, picture a somewhat more human Iyov whose utterances about God are at times brash and shocking.

It is true that Iyov is depicted as a man of perfect moral character in the prologue. But it should be noted that while he refuses his wife’s suggestion to curse God, an account recorded in the prologue (2:9-10), he does not curse God in the dialogues either. The very point of the book seems to be that even one of the highest moral character must struggle with the ways of God in this world. Only after the series of misfortunes recorded in chapters 1 and 2, and the period of inner struggle that no doubt transpired during the seven days and seven nights before he began to speak (2:11-13), did Iyov find those deep inner questions that the book deals with. Iyov’s high moral character is quite evident in the dialogues, for throughout, even though he cannot comprehend God, he speaks the truth before him.

Other portions alleged to be additions to the book are the speeches of Elihu (32–37), the discourse of God (38–41), and the discourse on wisdom in chapter 28. Some scholars think the author of the final version borrowed these existing works to provide a literary structure for his own work.

The main structure of the book, consisting of prologue, dialogues, and an epilogue, need not necessarily be regarded as the result of a complex process of editing. The Code of Hammurabi, for example, has a similar structure, as does an ancient Mitsri (Egyptian) work called A Dispute over Suicide.

With regard to the problem of authorship, it seems best to acknowledge that the author is anonymous. His theology is certainly Yahwistic; thus, he was probably a Hebrew. His literary skills were remarkable, for he has produced one of the finest works known through the ages.
Date

Since the authorship of the book is in question, so is the date of the book. Most modern scholars place the book in the postexilic period, around the fifth century BC. However, some place it toward the end of the exile. Others put it in the Solomonic era, while still others place it in the period of the patriarchs.

The internal evidence points to a very early setting for the book. There are no Levitical institutions cited. Iyov sacrifices for his family as in the period before the priesthood (1:5). The wealth of Iyov, given in terms of livestock, seems to reflect the patriarchal milieu (v 3).

The language of the book may also point to an early date. Certain linguistic elements indicate more archaic forms of Hebrew, as preserved in the epic material from Ugarit. It may be that Iyov himself lived in the second millennium BC. If the book—or part of it—was written then, it may represent the first written material to find its way into the biblical canon. The book may have come into its final form in the Solomonic era, when so much of the Hebrew Wisdom Literature was produced.
Background

The book of Iyov (Job) belongs to the body of OT materials known as the Wisdom Literature. This literature deals with the basic issues of human life. The Israelis (Israelites) were not the only ancient people to produce Wisdom Literature. This type of material came out of pagan cultures as well, and often represents efforts to explain the course of human events within the structure of pagan religion.

Several ancient works similar to the OT book of Iyov are known from ancient cultures. A Sumerian book exists that does not compare with the biblical book, either in literary scope or depth of feeling. It depicts the plight of a young man whose sorrow was turned to joy as a result of extended pleading to his personal deity. According to Sumerian thought, the gods were responsible for evil as well as good. Only placation of some kind could prevent the evil they might do. There is no attempt to philosophize or expound the problem of the presence of evil in the world.

A Babylonian book, commonly titled I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom, is philosophically similar to the Sumerian Iyov. In the work the writer describes his suffering in vivid terminology. No one can help him. He wonders whether the ritual obligations of his pagan religion really are pleasing to a god. An emissary of the god Merodak (Marduk) appears to him in a dream and relieves his suffering. The work ends with a section of praise to Merodak in which occurs the affirmation that the offerings he gave the gods served to gladden the hearts of the gods.

Another work, “A Dialogue about Human Misery,” is also similar to the biblical book of Iyov. It struggles with the fact that worship of the deities seems to make no difference in the quality of one’s life. A figure in this work reminds the sufferer that the ways of the gods are difficult to understand, and man is naturally perverse. The sufferer appeals to the gods, but the dialogue ends at that point with no resolution to the problem.

These literary works are not comparable to the OT book of Iyov theologically or philosophically. They offer only a fatalistic outlook on life and understand life to be governed by the capricious will of the gods. However, these documents, which date variously between the second and first millennia BC, may provide us with the literary ground from which the book of Iyov sprang. That is, the book of Iyov may present the inspired answer to the deep questions that were being considered at this time in history. Thus, this type of literature may argue for an early date for the book of Iyov.
Purpose and Theological Teaching

The question of the central purpose of the book of Iyov has been a serious one in biblical scholarship for ages. It is difficult to assert that the purpose of the book is to present the solution to the problem of evil, for at the very point where an answer is expected, God asks questions instead of giving answers.

Some have suggested that the central purpose is to answer the question “Why do the righteous suffer?” It is true that the book has much to do with this question, but it too presents various problems. When one comes to the end of the book, he or she has only the words of the comforters and the statements of Elihu relating to that question—not a great deal at all. Then one may wonder why we were given the long dialogues with their record of Iyov’s internal struggles. When God speaks from the whirlwind, we find no concern to explain why the righteous suffer. Iyov is simply led to accept his place in the universe.

It seems best to adopt another approach to the book. In attempting to find the central theme of any literary work, one should look to the prologue and the epilogue. In the prologue one can see what the author intends to do, and in the epilogue the reader will find the author’s understanding of what the author actually has done.

In the prologue of Iyov, the author deftly establishes an atmosphere of suspense. We are told of Iyov’s perfect moral character. Then Satan taunts, “Take away everything he has, and he will surely curse you to your face!” (1:11, nlt). We wonder whether Iyov will curse God and thus deny his faith, but then we hear his great affirmation of trust: “Yahweh gave me everything I had, and Yahweh has taken it away. Praise the name of Yahweh!” (v 21).

The writer then sets up another suspenseful situation when Satan proposes to afflict Iyov. To this trial is added the discouraging words of Iyov’s wife: “Curse God and die.” Again we wonder whether this trial will destroy Iyov’s faith. The suspense is broken when we read that “in all this, Iyov said nothing wrong” (2:10).

The writer then introduces Iyov’s (Job’s) friends into the narrative. We are told that they remained silent for seven days. We wonder what is going on in Iyov’s mind. Is he still the man of staunch faith, or is his trust being eroded as the disease eats at his flesh? When Iyov speaks and curses the day of his birth, the suspense becomes intense. The writer has raised a question in our minds: Will Iyov’s faith remain secure?

At times we think it will. Iyov makes several great affirmations of faith. He states that God will vindicate him. One of the greatest affirmations of the book occurs in 19:25-27 (nlt): “But as for me, I know that my Redeemer lives, and that he will stand upon the earth at last. And after my body has decayed, yet in my body I will see God! I will see him for myself. Yes, I will see him with my own eyes. I am overwhelmed at the thought!” At other times Iyov expresses deep doubts about God’s orderly control of the universe. The suspense continues. Throughout the dialogues we trace the pattern of Iyov’s struggle. It is an emotional struggle in which Iyov speaks from the depths of despair and the heights of triumphant faith.

In the epilogue the suspense is resolved. Iyov’s trials have not destroyed or even eroded his faith. He emerges triumphant, with a humble faith. He can finally say to God, “I know that you can do anything, and no one can stop you. You ask, ‘Who is this that questions my wisdom with such ignorance?’ It is I. And I was talking about things I did not understand, things far too wonderful for me” (42:2-3, nlt).

The purpose of the writer is clear. At the outset he has raised the question “Will Iyov’s faith endure in spite of trial?” The dialogues have heightened the suspense, and the epilogue resolves it. Iyov has remained faithful to God in the midst of his suffering. We learn that Iyov’s faith is genuine.

The book of Iyov, therefore, is a treatise on faith and the role that suffering plays in faith. The book of Iyov teaches that the truly righteous person will remain faithful to God in spite of the seeming delay of God’s justice. He may not be able to comprehend all that God does in history, but his faith in God’s good plan and wise providence will remain secure. This aspect of faith is one facet of the total spectrum of faith in the Bible. It does not allow for works but is totally dependent on God.

The same relationship between faith and suffering may be found in the NT as well. In James 1:12 trials and faithfulness are woven together in the word “Blessed is the man who endures trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him” (rsv; see also 1 Pt 1:3-7). According to these passages, trials provide the test of faith and thus reveal whether one’s faith is true or false. Faith that is not true will not stand the test of suffering (Mt 13:20-21). The book of Iyov connects faith and trials; it portrays the nature of a genuine faith, a faith unbroken by suffering.

There are other principles in this rich book. It teaches that sin brings punishment. There is truth in the words of the comforters that is corroborated by Scripture. Yet this is but a small part of the role of suffering in life. The book also teaches that suffering has a didactic function, for it is chastening from the Almighty. In the section in which God speaks from the whirlwind, we learn that suffering is part of the structure of things and that we must submit to the wisdom of the Creator. In this section God reveals himself personally. Iyov could say, “I had heard about you before, but now I have seen you with my own eyes” (42:5, nlt). When we experience trials, we need a God who is near much more than a philosophical treatise on the problem of evil. Another emphasis is the role of suffering in producing true righteousness. While Iyov was depicted as a righteous man at the beginning of the book, his righteousness lacked what suffering could give it. At the end of the book, Iyov is a more humble man, one who sees his role in the universe and who has submitted to the wisdom of God.
Content
The Prologue (1:1–2:13)
This section of the book describes the events that led to the suffering of Iyov. He is pictured at the outset as a man of wealth with a family for whom he cared deeply.

In a dramatic scene set in heaven, Satan appears and is asked by the Lord, “Have you noticed my servant Iyov? He is the finest man in all the earth—a man of complete integrity. He fears God and will have nothing to do with evil” (1:8, nlt). Satan’s reply is “But take away everything he has, and he will surely curse you to your face!” (v 11). There follows the first of Iyov’s great calamities, the loss of his family and his possessions.

Another encounter between the Lord and Satan leads to the physical suffering of Iyov (Job). It is this loathsome disease that provides the context for the dialogues that follow. In all of this the writer is careful to tell us that Iyov did not sin. He has resisted his wife’s plea to curse God. He has resisted the temptation to forsake God because of the loss of his children. But suddenly the placid picture ends with dialogues as we listen to Iyov’s complaints. We wonder, has Iyov given up his faith in God?
Three of Iyov’s friends have come to comfort him. They sit silent in his presence for seven days, reluctant to speak. After the period of silence they begin their dialogues with Iyov.
The Dialogues (3:1–31:40)
The First Cycle (3:1–14:22)
Iyov’s complaint, recorded in chapter 3, questions the wisdom of God in allowing him to be born. He wonders why life was given to one whose lot in life is to suffer.

Elifaz (Eliphaz) is the first of Iyov’s friends to speak. A polite man on the surface, he is heartless underneath. His answer is that Iyov must have sinned—why else would he be suffering so (4:7-11)? Elifaz clearly believes that Iyov’s questioning represents a negative attitude toward God. He appeals to Iyov to trust in the Lord (4:8) and give up his vexation toward God, since his anger will lead only to ruin (5:2). He sees a positive element in suffering, for he affirms that it is chastening from the Almighty (v 17).

Iyov responds by pointing out that his vexation is warranted in view of the terrible suffering he is enduring (6:1-7). He also complains that Elifaz is in the wrong in not showing him kindness, likening him to a wadi in the desert that offers no water in the hot, dry season (vv 14-23).

The next comforter, Bildad, is even more heartless than Elifaz. He, too, repeats the accusation that Iyov has sinned. His pitiless attitude is evident in his reference to Iyov’s children, blaming their deaths on probable sin in their lives (8:4).

Bildad, like Elifaz, appeals to Iyov to turn to God (8:5), assuring him that God will surely respond (v 6). He pictures Iyov’s misfortunes as the result of turning from God (vv 11-19) but assures him that God will not reject a blameless man (v 20).

Iyov’s response to Bildad begins with a poignant question: “How can a person be declared innocent in the eyes of God?” (9:2, nlt). This question is followed by an eloquent statement in which Iyov pictures the magnitude of God’s power as seen in the universe (vv 3-12). Iyov stands before the mighty God completely helpless to withstand his power. He protests that he cannot contend with such a God, nor protest his innocence before him, for he is too powerful to oppose.

Iyov also complains that he cannot gain a fair hearing from God because God believes him guilty. The fact that God has punished him with his affliction proves that he does not regard him as innocent (9:14-24). Iyov continues his response and again questions God’s wisdom in bringing him into existence (10:18-22).

The next to speak is Tsofar (Zophar). He also accuses Iyov (Job) of sin (11:4-6). In an insulting statement he says that God “knows those who are false, and he takes note of all their sins. An empty-headed person won’t become wise any more than a wild donkey can bear human offspring” (vv 11-12, nlt).
Iyov’s anger is kindled by Tsofar’s insulting accusations (12:2-3), and he calls on God to withdraw his hand from him and demands that God speak (13:20-28).
The Second Cycle (15:1–21:34)

The second cycle of discourses continues in the same pattern as the first. Elifaz, Bildad, and Tsofar continue their accusations, attributing Iyov’s misfortune to sin in his life. But as the narrative continues, the speakers begin to become more involved in their own assertions, and they no longer answer each other’s arguments as directly as they did in the first series of dialogues.
The Third Cycle (22:1–31:40)

In the third series of dialogues only Elifaz (Eliphaz) and Bildad speak. The accusations of sin in Iyov become even more pointed and cruel. Elifaz says, “It [your suffering] is because of your wickedness! Your guilt has no limit!” (22:5, nlt). This third dialogue is unusual in that Iyov speaks more than he does in the others. While Bildad’s argument extends for only six verses, Iyov’s reply goes on for six chapters (chs 26–31).

Chapter 31 is an important one. In it Iyov protests his innocence. It is a chapter in which Iyov’s sincerity cannot be doubted. He affirms that he has been morally pure (vv 1-4), he has not been deceitful (vv 5-8), he has not been guilty of adultery (vv 9-12), he has concern for others (vv 13-23), he has not trusted in wealth (vv 24-28). He concludes with a general affirmation of his innocence (vv 29-40).

A pattern begins to develop. Iyov gradually moves away from his friends in the discussion. They become more insistent on sin as the cause of his misfortunes, and Iyov more firmly asserts his innocence. The writer of the book deftly weaves the account so that the reader can find little that is unorthodox in the statements of the friends. Yet while we may agree with their words, we cannot approve their attitudes. It is true that sin brings punishment, but the friends emphasize only that. The next friend, Elihu, will point out another function of suffering.

We hear the ring of truth in Iyov’s protestations of innocence. But if we believe Iyov and also believe the comforters, we have the same dilemma as Iyov. We do not know where the truth lies. We do not know why Iyov is suffering.
The Speech of Elihu (32:1–37:24)

Elihu is a young man who listens to Iyov and to his fellow comforters with growing impatience (32:3). He is overly sensitive about his youth (vv 6-22), but when he speaks, he reveals an understanding of suffering that is more mature than that of his companions.

Elihu emphasizes the fact that God speaks in many ways and that suffering is chastening (33:19), which reveals the goodness of God (vv 29-33). While this thought was found in Elifaz’s first speech (5:17), it is given greater prominence by Elihu, who emphasizes a dimension of suffering that reveals the love of God. But still one feels that the whole answer has not been given. Another dimension follows in the words of God.
The Voice from the Whirlwind and Iyov’s (Job’s) Response (38:1–42:6)

God speaks in this section. He poses one question after another to Iyov, all having to do with some aspect of the Creation. God asks, “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” Then, in a note of sarcasm, he adds, “Tell me, if you know so much” (38:4, nlt).

God refers to the seas and asks Iyov who made the ocean basins (38:8-11). He pictures the rising dawn and asks Iyov, “Have you ever commanded the morning to appear and caused the dawn to rise in the east?” (v 12, nlt). Further questions relate to light (vv 19-21), snow (vv 22-24), rain (vv 25-30), the constellations (vv 31-33), storms (vv 34-38), and animals (38:39–39:30). Iyov is made to realize the vastness of God’s power as revealed in the Creation. Iyov must have felt rather small and insignificant as he contemplated God’s might.

But the questions are meant to accomplish more than to make Iyov feel small. They are meant to make him feel ashamed of his presumption as well. The sarcasm in this section is particularly biting, and one can imagine Iyov sinking deeper into the ash heap with each question. In the section dealing with light (38:19-21, nlt), the questions “Where does the light come from, and where does the darkness go? Can you take it to its home? Do you know how to get there?” are followed by “But of course you know all this! For you were born before it was all created, and you are so very experienced!” And in the section dealing with the constellations God asks Iyov, “Can you hold back the movements of the stars? Are you able to restrain the Pleiades or Orion?” (v 31).

Iyov has been somewhat brash in his statements to God in the dialogues. He has demanded that God speak to him (13:22), and has accused God of injustice (19:6-7; 24:1; 27:2). Now, as he is reminded of the power of the Almighty, Iyov begins to recognize his proper place in the universe.

The crucial questions in this long series are those in 40:15–41:34. Here, in an unusual sequence, God draws Iyov’s attention to behemoth (40:15) and leviathan (41:1). While some scholars see these as mythical figures, it is most probable that these, like the others cited throughout this section, are literary depictions of ordinary animals known for their great size and strength. It is suggested by many scholars that behemoth is the hippopotamus and leviathan the crocodile. The contexts in which these animals are described seem to support this. These references to two powerful animals end the section in which the voice of God speaks from the whirlwind. It is a section filled with suspense. At the end of it, the reader finds that Iyov has learned his lesson (42:1-3).

There is an important reason for these questions that came to Iyov with such insistent force. Iyov has been led to see that he does not control the universe—God does. Iyov is forced to face the power of God and learn that he is only part of this vast structure that reflects God’s almighty power. By demanding that God speak to him, Iyov was attempting to control God. By implying that God was unjust, he was making a judgment on God, thus making himself equal, if not superior, to God. God demands that Iyov face the power displayed in the universe and repeat his petulant words. Iyov wanted a God he could control; God demands submission. Iyov wanted a world run his way; God created a world to be run his way. Iyov had manufactured an illusory God, one who should obey his own whims. By recognizing God’s sovereign control in this world, he is led to see that suffering has a purpose. Iyov may not recognize that purpose, but it is part of the creation of the Almighty. It is no wonder that Iyov begins to enter into a settled peace and acknowledge God’s sovereignty (42:5-6).

This section of questions is followed by a poignant response from Iyov. He confesses God’s might (42:2). He admits that he did not fully understand things too wonderful for him (v 3), and he repents in dust and ashes (v 6).
The Epilogue (42:7-17)

The final part of the book begins with a denunciation of Iyov’s comforters. They are condemned because they did not speak that which was right (42:7). This seemed most unusual, since their words have seemed quite orthodox. Yet, in the final analysis, they did not say what was right because their answer to the problem of suffering was only a partial answer, and because it was partial, it was dangerous. It caricatured God as an austere being who used suffering only to punish sin. It did not allow room for the loving hand of God in suffering, as did Elihu’s answer to the problem.

While Iyov said some things about God that were harsh, he was not berated. In fact, the text says that Iyov spoke of God that which was right (42:8). This evidently refers to Iyov’s concluding words in 42:1-6, where, purified by suffering, he humbly yielded himself to God’s sovereign will.
See also Job (Person) #2; Wisdom; Wisdom Literature.
JOBAB
1. Yaketan’s (Joktan’s) son in Ever’s (Eber’s) line (Gn 10:29; 1 Chr 1:23).
2. Early Edomi (Edomite) king. He was the son of Zerah of Batserah (Bozrah) (Gn 36:33-34; 1 Chr 1:44-45).

3. King of Madon who, along with other Kena’ani (Canaanite) kings, joined Yavin (Jabin) of Hatsor (Hazor) in a northern confederacy to stop the Israelis (Israelites) from taking over the northern section of Kena’an (Canaan). He was killed in battle at the waters of Merom (Jos 11:1; 12:19).
4. Shaharayim’s (Shaharaim’s) son by his wife Hodesh, a member of Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe (1 Chr 8:9).
5. Elpa’al’s (Elpaal’s) son from Benyamin’s tribe (1 Chr 8:18).
JOCHEBED
Amram’s wife and the mother of Mosheh (Moses), Aharon (Aaron), and Miryam (Miriam) (Ex 6:20; Nm 26:59).
JODA
Yohanan’s (Joanan’s) son, the father of Yosek (Josech), and a forefather of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ living in Palestine during the postexilic era (Lk 3:26). See Genealogy of Jesus Christ.
JOED

Descendant of Benyamin (Benjamin) living in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) during the days of Nehemyah (Nehemiah) (Neh 11:7). His name, meaning “Yahweh is witness,” does not appear in a parallel list in 1 Chronicles 9:7.
JOEL (Person)
1. Levite from the family of Kohat (Kohath). He was Azaryah’s (Azariah’s) son and an ancestor of Elkanah, the father of Shmuel (Samuel) the prophet (1 Sm 1:1; 1 Chr 6:36).

2. Oldest son of Shmuel the prophet. He and his brother Aviyah (Abijah) so corrupted the office of judge that the elders increased their demands for a king (1 Sm 8:2-5). He was the father of Heyman (Heman) the singer (1 Chr 6:33; 15:17). His name has been mistakenly translated “Vashini (Vashni)” in the kjv in 1 Chronicles 6:28.
3. Prince from one of the Shim’oni (Simeonite) families that emigrated to the valley of Gedor (1 Chr 4:35).
4. Member of Re’uven’s (Reuben’s) tribe (1 Chr 5:4, 8).
5. Chief of Gad’s tribe residing in Bashan (1 Chr 5:12).
6. Third of Yizrahyah’s (Izrahiah’s) four named sons and a chief of Yisakar’s (Issachar’s) tribe in David’s time (1 Chr 7:3).
7. Natan’s (Nathan’s) brother and one of David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:38). He is alternately called Yigal (Igal) the son of Natan in 2 Samuel 23:36. See Igal #2.

8. Levite from the family of Gereshon (Gershon) who participated in the royal procession that brought the ark of God to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) during David’s reign (1 Chr 15:7-11). He may have administered the treasuries of the temple in Yerushalem (1 Chr 26:22).
9. Pedayah’s (Pedaiah’s) son, who acted as tribal chieftain over the west half of Menasheh’s (Manasseh’s) tribe during David’s reign (1 Chr 27:20)
10. Levite from the family of Kohat who assisted in King Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) reform of the temple in Yerushalem (2 Chr 29:12).
11. Nevo’s (Nebo’s) son, who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic period (Ezr 10:43).
12. Zicri’s son and the supervisor of 128 Benjaminites who moved to postexilic Yerushalem (Neh 11:9).
13. Prophet who wrote the second book of the Minor Prophets. Little is known about him except that he was Petuel’s (Pethuel’s) son (Jl 1:1; Acts 2:16). See Joel, Book of.
JOEL, Book of
Old Testament book; second of the Minor Prophets.

Author

In the first verse the contents of the book of Yoel (Joel) are described as the “message” of the Lord that “came to Yoel, the son of Petuel (Pethuel).” We are told nothing more in Scripture about Yoel or Petuel. The name Yoel was common; there are 13 different Joels in the OT. From what is said in the book, it would seem that Yoel was not a priest but was closely associated with the priests of the temple, and in all probability a man of Yerushalem (Jerusalem). More than that we cannot say.
Date

Many different views of the date of Yoel have been taken by those who have studied this book carefully; thus it is difficult to be dogmatic. The book may be dated to a time after the return to Yerushalem of the Jewish exiles who had been in Bavel (Babylon)—more precisely, to a time after Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah’s) work of rebuilding the walls of Yerushalem (c. 400 BC). Reasons given in support of this are as follows:

1. Joel 3:2 says that the people of Yehudah (Judah) and Yerushalem had been scattered among the nations and their land divided up, but they have been brought back, and their city once again has its walls (2:9).

2. When a call is issued to prayer and fasting, the priests and elders are to take the lead (1:13; 2:16-17). There is no mention of a king at any point in the book. There were kings until the time of the exile, but not for 400 years after it.

3. The preexilic prophets—Amos, Hoshea (Hosea), Yeshayah (Isaiah), Mikah (Micah), and Yirmiyah (Jeremiah)—were often critical of the people for offering sacrifices while they departed from the ways of the Lord in their daily lives. Postexilic prophets like Hagay (Haggai) and Malaki (Malachi) offer encouragement and deep concern for the offering of sacrifices. In the preexilic prophets there was constant rebuke of the people for their worship of idols; this was not a problem with the people after the exile. In both these concerns Yoel seems to fit better the postexilic than the preexilic scene.

4. There is no reference to the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel) in this book. Much is said of Yehudah and Yerushalem; when “Yisrael” is spoken of, the reference seems to be to the same people (2:27; 3:16). We would expect to find a different way of speaking before the fall of the northern kingdom to the Assyrians in 722 BC.

5. The other kingdoms referred to are Edom, Tsor (Tyre) and Tsidon (Sidon), the Pelishtim (Philistines), and the Greeks. There is no mention of Aram (Syria), Ashur (Assyria), and Bavel, the inveterate enemies from whom the people suffered so much in preexilic days. Those mentioned were certainly significant to the people in postexilic times, and only then are the Greeks of importance on the Palestinian scene.

Some scholars think there is no great strength in these arguments and that everything in the book can be made to fit a much earlier date. It has sometimes been argued that the book is deliberately placed in the Hebrew Scriptures alongside the two eighth-century BC prophets Hoshea and Amos. But the order of the books in the prophetic canon does not determine their date. The postexilic Ovadyah (Obadiah) stands between the eighth-century BC prophets Amos and Mikah, and in fact in the Greek OT Yoel was placed in a different position from its place in the Hebrew Bible. Most likely Yoel and Amos stand together, as Amos 1:2 has the same words found at the close of the book of Yoel (Jl 3:16). Some of those who favor a preexilic date for the book place it in the ninth century, in the early period of the reign of Yoash (Joash) when the king was too young to actually function as ruler of the land. Others place it sometime shortly before the death of Yoshiyah (Josiah) in 609 BC because of the reference to the enemy coming from the north (as in Yirmiyah) and because of the appeal to the people (like Yirmiyah’s appeal) to return to the Lord with all their hearts (2:12).
Content

A plague of locusts more devastating than any that past generations had experienced had come on the land (vv 2-4). Drinkers were summoned to see the grapevines devastated and the fig trees stripped (vv 5-7). People were called to mourn at the sight of fields laid waste—especially the priests, as they would no longer be able to bring cereal and drink offerings to the Lord (vv 8-10). Farmers must grieve over the ruin of their harvest, in anguish at the loss of the fruits of the land (vv 11-12).

Because of what had happened, the people were called to prayer and fasting; the priests were to come before the Lord in sackcloth, grieving that no offerings could be brought (v 13). Elders and people alike must come to the temple to pray (v 14). Such a time of crisis, with the crops lost and the sheep and cattle having no pasture, was to be seen as foreshadowing the great coming Day of the Lord, for which everyone should be prepared (vv 15-18). The prophet himself could only cry out to God when he saw the devastation of the land (vv 19-20).

In this section the prophet speaks of a time when God’s judgment threatens the whole land. It is a time for the alarm to be sounded, when a great and powerful “people” come up on the land, a more threatening foe than any known before. Further, it is a warning of the coming “Day of the Lord,” “a day of darkness and gloom” (vv 1-2). The land is devastated as by fire; what was like the Garden of Eden becomes a wilderness (v 3). This invasion is like that of cavalry and the sound of the insurgents like “the rumbling of chariots.” Everyone is in anguish at their advance. They march like warriors, burst through the weapons, scale the walls of the city, and come into the houses like thieves (vv 4-9).

Some have taken this description to be a picture of armies of nations who are the foes of Yisrael (Israel), used by the Lord in judgment on his own people. But in that they are described as horses in battle, their noise like “the rumbling of chariots,” their advance “like a mighty army moving into battle,” it seems that the locust plague is still in mind. Yet the dark cloud of the locusts in the sky and their terrible effect on the land foreshadows the great day when the Lord will speak and act in judgment on all peoples. Then heaven and earth will tremble; sun, moon, and stars will be darkened (vv 10-11).

The prophet repeatedly calls the people to the Lord in humility and penitence so that his mercy and grace may be found. Then it will be possible “to offer grain and wine to Yahweh your God as before” (v 14, nlt). A fast is to be appointed, a solemn assembly of young and old called. Even the newlyweds are to come. The priests must lead the people in prayer to God to spare his people (vv 14-17).

According to this passage, it seems that the people did turn to God as the prophet required; in response, the Lord had compassion on them and assured them of renewing their grain, wine, and oil, and removing their reproach (vv 18-19). The “armies from the north” would retreat, and God would restore the pastures of the land, its fruit trees, and its vines (vv 20-22). The people would rejoice, and with the blessing of the early and late rains the land would again be abundantly productive. The losses from the locust plague would be made good (vv 23-25). People would eat food in plenty and praise God. They would know that the one great living God was among them, and they would not be put to shame anymore (vv 26-27).

The prophet also saw that the blessing experienced in this renewal after the plague of locusts foreshadowed greater blessings to come, just as the judgment experienced brought the warning of the great and terrible Day of the Lord to come. God would do greater things for his people in the future; in particular, he would pour out his Spirit on men and women, young and old, slave and free (vv 28-29). There would be awe-inspiring signs in heaven and on earth (vv 30-31). All who called on the name of the Lord would know his salvation (v 32).

The meaning of the Day of the Lord for Yisrael as a nation and its significance for all nations must be realized. God’s people would find restoration by turning to him; those who had scattered them, taken their land, and sold them as slaves would come under his judgment (vv 1-3). Tsor (Tyre) and Tsidon (Sidon) and the Pelishtim (Philistines) especially would have to give account for what they had done, taking the Lord’s silver and gold, removing his people from their land, and selling them as slaves to the Greeks. The sons and daughters of these slave traders would in turn be sold as slaves (vv 4-8). So the nations must be prepared for war—to melt their plowshares into swords and to beat pruning hooks into spears—but not for a battle between human armies. Those who have fought against the living God must reckon with him as a mighty warrior (vv 9-11). This mighty warrior is coming to execute judgment. The scene changes from a battleground to a court of justice; great crowds will stand before the Lord “in the valley of decision” on the Day of the Lord, which is a day of dread darkness for those who have made themselves enemies of the Almighty (vv 12-15).

After men have spoken and done their worst, God will speak and act. He will show himself to be his people’s “refuge and strength” (v 16). Their city will then be kept from invasion by strangers (v 17). Their land will be wonderfully productive (v 18). Because of what Mitsrayim (Egypt) and Edom have done in violence to Yehudah (Judah), they will be desolate (v 19). Yisrael will be avenged and restored, and to all it will be clear that the Lord’s home is in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) with his people (vv 20-21).

This account of the contents of the book is based on the view that Yoel (Joel) experienced a plague of locusts in his day and that he saw this as a warning of a greater judgment of God to come. At the same time, he also spoke of a greater restoration and blessing when the people turned back to God with prayer and fasting. Others see the enemies throughout the book as human foes, at least in chapter 2. Some think of the whole book as prophetic of battles to come, and in particular of a final battle of the Lord against those who have made themselves his enemies. Some think of two prophets, or two parts of the book written at different times. But the view of the book taken above seems exposed to the fewest difficulties and makes good sense and meaning of the whole.
Message

What can be said finally of the abiding significance of the message of Yoel? His, like that of most of the OT prophets, was a message of mercy and judgment. Such a catastrophe as a plague of locusts was a warning of God’s judgment of all men and nations, within history and ultimately at the great Day of the Lord at the consummation of history, when all will be gathered before him. The message of Yoel, with its challenge to repentance arising from the events of his time, can be set alongside the words of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) himself when he was asked about those who had suffered in the catastrophic events of his time. When asked whether they were worse sinners than others, he answered in the negative, but with the warning, “Unless you repent, you will all of you come to the same end” (Lk 13:5, neb). The word of God through Yoel called people to turn back to him to find his mercy; then to the assurance of mercy was added the hope of the greater things that God in his goodness would do. He would pour out his Spirit freely on all. These words of promise (Jl 2:28) were made more significant than any others in the book of Yoel by their quotation in the NT in Kefa’s (Peter’s; Grk. Petros’) sermon on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21). They stand true for the Christian church ever since that beginning of their fulfilment, and with them stands Yoel’s great assurance that God makes his home in the midst of his people and that those who turn to him will never be ashamed.
See also Israel, History of; Prophecy; Prophet, Prophetess.
JOELAH
Warrior who joined David at Tsiklag (Ziklag) in his struggle against King Sha’ul (Saul). Yoelah (Joelah) was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers (1 Chr 12:7).
JOEZER

Warrior who joined David at Tsiklag (Ziklag) in his struggle against King Sha’ul (Saul). He was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers (1 Chr 12:6). He was called a Korhi (Korahite), which probably refers to his place of origin.
JOGBEHAH

City in Gilead (Transjordan) built and fortified by Gad’s tribe (Nm 32:35). During the period of the judges, Gid’on (Gideon), in his pursuit of the Midyanites (Midianites), circled to the east of Yagebehah (Jogbehah) in order to attack the unsuspecting camp of Midyan (Midian) at Karkor (Jgs 8:11). This ancient city is now identified with Khirbet el-Ajbeihat, seven miles (11.3 kilometers) northwest of Amman.
JOGLI
Father of Buki (Bukki), a Dani (Danite) leader who helped oversee the distribution of the Promised Land west of the Yarden (Jordan) River (Nm 34:22).
JOHA
1. Benyamite (Benjamite) and one of Beriah’s nine sons (1 Chr 8:16).
2. Titsi (Tizite), the brother of Yedieael (Jediael) and one of David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:45).
JOHANAN

Name meaning “Yahweh has been gracious.” It occurs also in the alternate form of Yehohanan (Jehohanan). The name Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) is derived from these names. Several men of this name appear in the OT.

1. Son of Kareah (2 Kgs 25:23). Yohanan (Johanan) was a Jewish leader, a contemporary of Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), and supportive of Gedalyah (Gedaliah), the governor of Yehudah (Judah) after the fall of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Jer 40:8, 13). He forewarned Gedalyah of Yishmael’s (Ishmael’s) plan to assassinate him (vv 13-16). When the warning was ignored and Yohanan was refused permission to execute the would-be assassin, Gedalyah was murdered. Yohanan took vengeance against Yishmael and rescued those who had been captured (41:14-18), but he was unable to pursue Yishmael. In fear of a Babylonian reprisal, he made plans to seek asylum in Mitsrayim (Egypt). Yirmiyah, whom he consulted, gave God’s word against this move (42:1-22), but Yohanan was unwilling to take counsel (43:2-3). He led the Yehudim (Judeans), including Yirmiyah and Baruk (Baruch), to Mitsrayim (vv 5-7).
2. Eldest son of Yoshiyah (Josiah), king of Yehudah (1 Chr 3:15). Possibly he died young, for he did not succeed his father on the throne, even though he was the firstborn.
3. Son of Elyehoeynay (Elioenai) (1 Chr 3:24), a descendant of Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin), one of the last kings of Yehudah.
4. Grandson of Ahima’ats (Ahimaaz). He was the father of Azaryah (Azariah), who served as high priest in the temple of Shelomoh (Solomon) (1 Chr 6:9-10).

5. Warrior from Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe. He joined David’s special forces of 30 men at Tsiklag (Ziklag) (1 Chr 12:4). The special forces could shoot arrows and sling stones with either hand (v 2).

6. Gadi (Gadite) who joined David in the wilderness (1 Chr 12:8-12). He was also specially trained for war, in that he could handle both shield and spear, could endure hardship, and was quick on his feet.

7. Efrati (Ephraimite) whose son was a leader in the northern Kingdom during the regime of Pekah and protested against the enslavement of 200,000 Yehudim (2 Chr 28:12; nlt “Yehohanan”), who were subsequently freed.

8. Son of Hakatan (Hakkatan) (“the younger” or “the smaller”). The designation may be read as “Yohanan the younger.” He was head of a family who claimed their descent from Azgad (Ezr 8:12). He joined Ezra with 110 men in traveling from Bavel (Babylonia) to Yehudah.

9. Priest under Yoyakim (Joiakim). He was one of the priests during whose ministry the Levites and priests formally registered (Neh 12:22). He is alternately called Yehohanan in Ezra 10:6 and Yonatan (Jonathan) in Neh 12:11. See Jehohanan #4.
10. KJV spelling of Yehohanan, Toviyah’s (Tobiah’s) son, in Nehemiah 6:18. See Jehohanan #6.
JOHANAN BEN ZAKKAI*

Leading Jewish sage at the end of the second temple period. His place of birth is not known; he went to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to study, and after 18 years there spent some time in Galil (Galilee). Later, he returned to Yerushalem and taught “in the shadow of the temple.” He encouraged the Farisaios (Pharisees) among the priesthood rather than the Saddoukaios (Sadducees). During the siege of Yerushalem, he managed to leave, in a coffin according to one version. He was a prisoner of Vespasian, probably in AD 68, who gave him permission to settle in Yavneh (Jamnia). There he began quietly to lay the groundwork for the survival of Youdaismos (Judaism) without its temple.
See also Judaism; Pharisees.
JOHN (Person)

1. Father of Shim’on (Simon) Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) and Andreas (Andrew) (Jn 1:40-42; 21:15-17). According to Matthew 16:17, Kefa’s father was named Jona (Yonah (Jonas), Yonah). Either Jona was an alternate form of the name Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) or, more probably, two independent traditions existed regarding his name.

2. Member of the high priestly family who, along with Hanan (Annas; Grk. Hannas), Kayafa (Caiaphas; Grk. Kaiafas), and Alexandros (Alexander), questioned Kefa and Yohan after the two apostles had healed a lame man (Acts 4:6).

3. According to the early church bishop Papias, a member of the larger group of Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) disciples outside the Twelve (cf. Lk 10:1). Known as “Yohan the elder” (the presbyter), he is often credited with the authorship of 2 and 3 Yohan (2 Jn 1:1; 3 Jn 1:1), although the term “elder” there more likely refers to Yohan the apostle.
4. The apostle. See John, The Apostle.
5. The Baptist. See John the Baptist.
6. An early disciple known as Yohan Markos (Mark), author of the second Gospel. See Mark, John.
JOHN, The Apostle
The apostle known as “the disciple whom Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) loved”; author of the fourth Gospel, three epistles, and probably Revelation.

The apostle Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) has a high reputation among Christian people, and his influence has been felt throughout the centuries. Despite this, he is a surprisingly shadowy figure. When he appears in the pages of the NT, it is almost always in company with Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) or Ya’akov (James), and if there is speaking to be done, it is usually his companion Kefa who does it; thus, there is not a great deal on which to base a biography.

Yohan’s father’s name was Zavday (Zebedee), and Yohan had a brother called Ya’akov (Mt 4:21). Among the women at the cross, Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios) names Maria (Mary) Magdala (Magdalene), Maria the mother of Ya’akov and Yosef (Joseph), and “the mother of Zavday’s children” (27:56). Markos (Mark) names the two Marys and adds Salome (Mk 15:40). This indicates that Salome may be the name of Yohan’s mother. If Matay and Markos are naming the same women as does Yohan, then Salome was Yeshua’ “mother’s sister” (Jn 19:25). This would make Yohan a cousin of Yeshua. We cannot be certain of this, for there were many women there (Mt 27:55) and there is no way of being sure that Matay, Markos, and Yohan all name the same three. Many accept the identification, but we can scarcely say more.

Yohan was among those whom Yeshua called by the Sea of Galil (Galilee) (Mt 4:21-22; Mk 1:19-20). This makes him one of the first disciples. It is also possible that he was the unnamed companion of Andreas (Andrew) when that apostle first followed Yeshua (Jn 1:35-37). Yohan was important in the little group around Yeshua since he was one of three who were especially close to the Master. These disciples were selected to be with Yeshua on many great occasions. Yohan, along with his brother Ya’akov and Kefa, was present at the Transfiguration (Mt 17:1-2; Mk 9:2; Lk 9:28-29). Yeshua also took just these three into the house of Yair (Jairus) when he brought that man’s daughter back to life (Mk 5:37; Lk 8:51). Before Yeshua’s arrest, it was this trio that he took to pray with him in the Garden of Gethsaimanai (Gethsemane) (Mt 26:37; Mk 14:33). Though the three were admonished for sleeping instead of watching in prayer, we must not overlook the fact that in that time of great difficulty, when Yeshua faced the prospect of death on a cross, it was to these three that he looked for support.

There are other occasions when Yohan is mentioned in the Gospels. Lukas (Luke) tells us of Yohan’s surprise when the miraculous catch of fish took place (Lk 5:9-10). This is especially noteworthy since Yohan was a fisherman. Toward the close of Yeshua’s ministry, we find Yohan coming to Yeshua with Kefa, Ya’akov, and Andreas to ask when the end would come and what would be the sign when all things come to their climax (Mk 13:3-4). And on the last evening, Yeshua sent Kefa and Yohan to prepare the Passover meal (Lk 22:8).

Passages like these show that Yohan was highly esteemed among the apostles and that he stood especially close to Yeshua. But there are indications that at first Yohan was far from appreciating what Yeshua stood for. When Markos gives his list of the Twelve, he tells us that Yeshua gave to Ya’akov and Yohan the name “Thunder Brothers (Boanerges),” which means “sons of thunder” (Mk 3:17). Some in the early church understood this name as a compliment, thinking it meant that Ya’akov’s and Yohan’s witness to Yeshua would be as strong as thunder. But most see it as pointing to their tempestuousness of character. We see this, for example, when Yohan encounters a man who was casting out demons in Yeshua’s name. Yohan instructs him not to, “for he isn’t one of our group” (Mk 9:38; Lk 9:49).

Markos also tells us of an occasion when the sons of Zavday asked Yeshua for the two chief places in his kingdom, one to be on his right and the other on his left (Mk 10:35-40). Matay adds the point that the words were spoken by the men’s mother, but he leaves us no doubt that Ya’akov and Yohan were in on it (Mt 20:20-22). Yeshua proceeded to ask them whether they could drink the cup he would drink and be baptized with the baptism he would receive. (Clearly, these are metaphors for the suffering Yeshua would in due course undergo.) Ya’akov and Yohan affirmed that they could, and Yeshua assured them that they would indeed do this. However, he gave them no assurance about their places in the Father’s kingdom. (But it is plain that Ya’akov and Yohan would suffer for Christ.) At that time they also failed to understand the loving spirit that moved their Master and was required of them as well.

Another incident that shows the same tempestuous spirit is one involving Shomroni (Samaritan) villagers who refused to receive the little band as they traveled. When Ya’akov and Yohan heard of it, they asked Yeshua whether he wanted them to call down fire from heaven to consume the villagers (Lk 9:54). They were clearly at variance with Yeshua, and indeed he rebuked them. But we should not miss the zeal they displayed for their Lord, nor their conviction that if they did call down fire it would come. They were sure that God would not fail to answer the prayer of those who asked for vengeance on the opponents of Yeshua. There is zeal here and faith, though also a spirit of lovelessness.

The synoptic Gospels thus show us Yohan as a zealous and loyal follower of Yeshua. He is not depicted as gentle and considerate. At this time, he knew little of the love that should characterize a follower of Yeshua, but he did have faith and a passionate conviction that God would prosper Yeshua and those who served him.

Yohan is not mentioned by name in the fourth Gospel, but there are passages that speak about “the disciple whom Yeshua loved” (Jn 13:23; 19:26; 20:2; 21:7, 20). We are not told who this was, but the evidence seems to indicate that it was the apostle Yohan. For example, there is an account of a fishing trip in chapter 21, with a listing of those who went fishing. It includes Kefa, who must be ruled out as “the disciple whom Yeshua loved” because he is often mentioned along with the beloved disciple. Toma (Thomas) and Netanel (Nathanael) were there, but there seems to be no reason for seeing either as a likely candidate. Two unnamed men and the sons of Zavday make up the remainder of the party. Ya’akov is excluded as being the author because of his early death—around AD 44 (Acts 12:2). This leaves us with Yohan or one of the unnamed men. Yohan is favored by the fact that the beloved disciple is linked with Kefa on a number of occasions (Jn 13:23-24; 20:2; 21:7). We know from the other Gospels that Kefa and Yohan (together with Ya’akov) were especially close (see also Acts 3; 8:14; Gal 2:9). Of course, one of the unnamed disciples may have been the beloved disciple, but we have no reason to assume this. Further, such a supposition faces the problem of the omission of the name of Yohan the apostle throughout the entire fourth Gospel. If Yohan wrote this book, we can understand his not mentioning himself. But if it was written by someone else, why would that person omit all mention of a man as prominent in the apostolic band as the other Gospels show Yohan to have been? In addition, if Yohan is the author, it would explain why Yohan the immerser is called simply “Yohan.”

It is argued that “the disciple whom Yeshua loved” is not the kind of title a man would naturally use of himself, but it must be said also that it is not the kind of title a man would naturally use of someone else, either. And it may be that Yohan uses it in a modest fashion—partly because he did not want to draw attention to himself by using his name, and partly because he wanted to emphasize the truth that it was the fact that Yeshua loved him that made him what he was.

If this identification may be accepted, we learn more about the apostle. We should not, of course, read the words “the disciple whom Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) loved” as though they meant that Yeshua did not love the other disciples. He loved them all. But as applied to Yohan, they mean that he was indeed beloved, probably also that he recognized that he owed all he had and all he was to that love. That he was specially close to Yeshua is indicated by the fact that he leaned on Yeshua’s breast at the Last Supper (Jn 13:23). It also tells us something of his relationship to the Master that he was at the cross when Christ was crucified and that it was to him that Yeshua gave the charge to look after his mother (19:26-27). One would have expected that Yeshua would have selected one of his family for this responsibility. But his brothers did not believe in him, whereas both Yohan and Maria did. This event certainly shows that a close relationship existed between Yeshua and the disciple he loved.

On the first Easter morning, Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) raced with Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) to the tomb when Maria Magdala told them it was empty. He won the race but stood outside the tomb until Kefa came. Kefa, the leader of men, went right in, and Yohan followed. We read that he “saw and believed” (Jn 20:8). Then in chapter 21 we read of the beloved disciple fishing with the others. Significantly, it was he who recognized that it was Yeshua who stood on the shore and told them where to cast the net (21:7).

There is not much to add to this picture when we turn to Acts. At the beginning, Yohan’s name occurs in a list of the Twelve (Acts 1:13); and later, when we are told of Ya’akov’s (James’) death, it is noted that he was Yohan’s brother (12:2). In every other reference to Yohan, he is in the company of Kefa. These two were the instruments God used in bringing healing to a lame man (ch 3). At that time, they were going to the temple at the hour of prayer. This says something about their habits of devotion. Prayer at the ninth hour apparently refers to the Jewish service of prayer that was held at the same time as the evening offering (i.e., at about three o’clock in the afternoon). Evidently, Kefa and Yohan were continuing the devotional habits of pious Yehudim (Jews) with an interest in the temple and all its doings. On another occasion, these two were arrested and jailed on account of their preaching about Yeshua’s resurrection (4:1-3). They were brought before the council, where Kefa spoke for them. The council saw that these two men were “uneducated, common men” (v 13). This means that they had never had the normal rabbinic education. By the standards of the council, they were uneducated. The council forbade them to speak about Yeshua, but the apostles’ reply displays Yohan’s typical boldness: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge; for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard” (vv 19-20, rsv).

Yohan was associated with Kefa again when the gospel was first preached in Shomron (Samaria). Filippos (Philip) was the evangelist to the Shomronim (Samaritans), but the apostles in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) decided to send Kefa and Yohan to Shomron when they heard how the people had accepted the gospel message. “As soon as they arrived, they began praying for these new Christians to receive the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8:15, tlb), a revealing illustration of apostolic priorities. In due course, they laid their hands on the new believers and they received the Holy Spirit (8:17). Yohan is not specifically mentioned, but he no doubt was included in “the apostles” who were arrested and jailed because of the jealousy of prominent Yehudim (5:17-18). But that imprisonment did not last long, for an angel released them at night, so that they resumed their preaching in the early morning (v 21). Yohan is mentioned by name in Galatians 2:9, where he is joined with Kefa and Ya’akov and the three are called “the pillars of the church.”

This appears to be the extent of the NT’s record of the apostle Yohan. Clearly he was an important figure in the little band of early Christians. On almost every occasion when he comes before us in the record, he is in the company of someone else and normally the speaking is done by his companion, not by Yohan. But we may justly conclude that he stood very close to Yeshua. Perhaps he had entered into the mind of Yeshua more than any of the others. The best evidence of this is the Gospel of Yohan. Clearly the man who wrote this had great spiritual insight. Yohan may have been more the thinker than a man of action and leader of men.

We have seen that there is good reason to think that the fourth Gospel was written by the apostle Yohan. The epistles of Yohan probably came from him also (though, as they stand, they are anonymous). All the Johannine writings probably emanated from the province of Asia. The heretics alluded to in 1 Yohan resemble the Cerinthians (followers of the heretic Cerinthus), who were in Asia Minor at the end of the first century, and tradition connects the author of 1 Yohan with Efesos (Ephesus). It is certain that the same person wrote all three letters, and reasonably certain that this author also wrote the Gospel of Yohan; the Gospel and the letters certainly represent the same mind at work in different situations.

An author named Yohan wrote the book of Revelation (Rv 1:1), though it is not clear whether this is the apostle or another Yohan. Tradition has identified the Yohan of Revelation (see Rv 1:1, 9; 22:8) with Yohan the apostle, the author of the Gospel of Yohan and the three letters of Yohan. This view was held by Justin Martyr as early as 140. The main objection to this view is that the original Greek is unlike that of the other Johannine writings, showing scant respect for the rules of the language. Some have suggested that a different Yohan wrote Revelation, others that Yohan’s disciples wrote the Gospel and letters and that Yohan himself wrote Revelation. But it is still plausible that the apostle Yohan (or one of his close disciples) wrote the Gospel and the letters.

Assuming Yohan the apostle wrote Revelation, he was exiled to Patmos (Rv 1:9). But the date of this is uncertain. Some probably unreliable evidence from the late fifth century suggests that Yohan was martyred at about the same time as his brother Ya’akov (c. 44; see also Acts 12:2). Yeshua’s prophecy in Mk 10:39 need not imply that both met with a simultaneous and violent end. Much stronger is the tradition reflected by Polycrates, bishop of Efesos (c. 190), that Yohan died a natural death in Efesos, and by Irenaeus (c. 175–195) that Yohan lingered on in Efesos until the time of the emperor Trajan (ruled c. 97–117).

The fourth Gospel.
