Author

The book of Yonah has been traditionally ascribed to Yonah the son of Amitay (Amittai), a prophet of great influence, who ministered during the reign of Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II of Yisrael (Israel) (2 Kgs 14:25).

The content of the book describes Yonah as an intensely patriotic person, but his misguided patriotism caused him to rebel at the possibility of Yisrael’s former enemies receiving forgiveness from God. One of the most important lessons of the book emerges when God rebukes Yonah’s exclusivistic attitude (Jon 4:6-11).

Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) used two of the experiences of Yonah as signs to his generation. The three days and nights spent by Yonah in the great fish served as an analogy of Yeshua’s death and resurrection (Mt 12:38-41). Also, the positive response of the Nineuitais (Ninevites) to Yonah’s preaching was used by Yeshua as a condemnation of the failure of many in his generation to believe in him (Lk 11:32).
Authenticity

The unusual elements in the book of Yonah (Jonah) have led to widely varying views of its nature. Not only has the account of Yonah being swallowed by the fish led some to think the book to be of a fabulous nature, but the account of the repentance of the people of Nineveh (Jon 3:5) also has been regarded as highly unlikely.

The historicity of the book has been championed by outstanding biblical scholars. The basic approach of these scholars has been to counter the arguments of those who deny its historicity and to point to what is regarded as positive evidence for the historicity of the book in Yeshua’s allusions to the prophecy and in early Jewish tradition.

Opponents of the authenticity of Yonah point to the following difficulties: (1) The use of the expression “king of Nineveh” (3:6) appears to be an inaccuracy because Nineveh was the capital of Ashur (Assyria). A contemporary would have referred to the king as the king of Ashur. (2) The use of the past tense to describe the city of Nineveh (v 3) seems to point to a much later date than the traditional view of the authorship of the book would permit. (3) The size of the city of Nineveh is described in greatly exaggerated terms (v 3). (4) The mass repentance of the Nineuitais lacks historical support. (5) It is unlikely that a human being could exist within a fish for an extended period of time.

With regard to the use of “king of Nineveh,” it should be noted that similar expressions may be found in the OT. Ahav (Ahab), the king of Yisrael, is called “king of Shomron (Samaria)” (1 Kgs 21:1), and Ben-Hadad (Ben-hadad), the king of Aram (Syria), is designated “king of Damesek (Damascus)” (2 Chr 24:23). The designation “king of Nineveh” is therefore not anomalous.
The use of the past tense to describe the city of Nineveh may be regarded as nothing more than a simple narrative past tense describing the size of the city at the time that Yonah prophesied there.

The description of the size of the city (“three days’ journey”) may be an indication of the length of time that it would take one to go through the suburbs included in the administrative district of Nineveh.

The repentance of the Nineuitais is not to be understood as a mass conversion to Yahweh, the God of Yisrael. The book of Yonah describes their response as repentance in view of the impending destruction threatened by Yonah (Jon 3:4). While secular history does not record such an event, there is evidence that such a response was possible. In less than a decade (765–759 BC) the city of Nineveh had experienced a total eclipse of the sun and two serious plagues. One can understand how the citizens of Nineveh may have been prepared for the preaching of this prophet who came to them in such an unusual way.

It should also be noted that one of the kings of Ashur, Adad-nirari III, limited his worship to the god Nevo (Nebo). If the prophetic ministry of Yonah was active during the time of his reign (810–783 BC), it is possible that the Jewish monotheism represented by Yonah may have found a more favorable climate than one would normally expect in a pagan society.
The participation of the animals in the national penitence that followed Yonah’s preaching (3:7-8) is not unknown from history. The historian Herodotus records a similar event in the Persian Empire.

The event that creates the greatest difficulty, however, is the experience of Yonah in the fish. It has often been pointed out that the gullets of most whales are not large enough to admit an object the size of a man. But the book does not say that it was a whale that swallowed Yonah, but simply a great fish (1:17). Even so, it is possible for a sperm whale to swallow an object as large as a man.

Numerous examples of individuals being swallowed by whales have been cited in the past. While many of these accounts may be disregarded as fancy, it would be wrong to uncritically reject all of them. (An interesting account of one of these experiences may be found in the Princeton Theological Review 25, 1927, p. 636.) The experience of Yonah in the great fish need not be regarded as an absolute impossibility. The activities of God in history have often been accompanied by unusual or miraculous events.

The difficulties of the book of Yonah (Jonah) have led many to regard the book as a prophetic parable rather than a record of historical fact. The most common interpretation is that the book is an expression of the universal concerns of God. As such, it inveighs against the exclusive nationalism of the Yehudim (Jews). This narrow-minded attitude, some suggest, fits best into the postexilic period, when the hatred of Yisrael (Israel) for its former captors was still very bitter.

There are several difficulties with this view. While there are a number of parables in the OT, none is as extensive as the book of Yonah. Also, since the major elements of a parable symbolize persons, objects, or concepts that contribute to the main teaching of the parable, the proponents of this view are hard pressed to show how the account of Yonah’s experience in the fish contributes to the central lesson of the parable.

Another approach to the book is to regard it as an extended allegory. An allegory is a literary form, the basic elements of which are intended to symbolize or explain aspects of real life to which they are analogous. The intended meaning is usually evident or explained by the author. In the OT, allegories are short literary forms used to lend force to a pronouncement. The book of Yonah does not seem to fit this category. It is a narrative account with no evident meaning given to the various persons, objects, and events cited.

There seems to be no convincing reason for rejecting the historicity of the book of Yonah on the basis of the arguments generally given. Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) referred to the account of Yonah in a way that seems to imply his acceptance of its validity.
Date

If Yonah was the son of Amitay (Amittai) cited in 2 Kings 14:25, the prophecy would have to be dated in the reign of Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II of Yisrael (793–753 BC). Yonah would then be one of the great eighth-century prophets who ministered during the Silver Age of Yisrael.
Those who understand the book to have been written by an author other than Yonah place the writing at various times, from the period following the fall of Nineveh to well into the postexilic period.
Background

Archaeological excavations at the site of ancient Nineveh have yielded many artifacts and literary works indicating that it was a cultural center for a great part of its history. In the Middle Assyrian period, the city of Nineveh was greatly enlarged and became an administrative center. Some of the most powerful Assyrian kings ruled from Nineveh.

The city of Kelah (Calah), to the south of Nineveh, had an area much smaller than Nineveh but housed almost 70,000 persons. The description of the vast population of Nineveh in the prophecy of Yonah seems to fit with this.
Purpose

The purpose of the book of Yonah (Jonah) is to teach that God’s grace was not limited to the Hebrew people. This lesson is taught in the dramatic climax of the book. Yonah, filled with self-pity, laments the loss of the plant that gave him shade. God shows Yonah’s concern for the plant in stark contrast to his own concern for the thousands of people of Nineveh.

The book clearly sets forth the fact that God’s mercy was not the sole possession of the Hebrew people of Yonah’s time but was available to all through repentance. Even Yisrael’s (Israel’s) enemies could experience God’s mercy.
Content

The book of Yonah begins with a command from the Lord to the prophet directing him to preach to the people of Nineveh. Yonah was reluctant to go to Nineveh because he knew that the Nineuitais (Ninevites) would repent. He would therefore find himself in the dubious position of proclaiming God’s mercy to the hated Assyrians. Therefore, he fled from Yafo (Joppa) by ship in a futile attempt to flee from the presence of God. He boarded a ship bound for Tarshish, a Phoenician colony in southern Spania (Spain). It was as far west as Yonah could flee within the scope of the ancient Mediterranean world (1:1-3).

God would not allow his servant to disobey without chastisement, however (1:4-16). God’s love demanded Yonah’s discipline. The program of discipline commenced with a divinely originated storm (v 4). In the midst of the terrifying rage of this storm, the sailors busied themselves with supplications to their individual pagan deities and with casting excess cargo overboard (v 5). Through all the commotion Yonah was asleep in the hold of the ship.
The sailors were as yet unaware that Yonah was the real problem. The captain of the ship aroused Yonah and told him to pray to his god for deliverance from the tempest (v 6).

Receiving no response to their supplications, the sailors proceeded to cast lots in an attempt to determine who on board was the cause of the wrath of the god who had brought the storm upon them (1:7); the lot indicated that Yonah was to blame. The sailors then wanted to know what god was responsible for the storm and why. Yonah’s testimony was simple and to the point: he was a Hebrew who worshiped the Lord who created both land and sea (v 9).

The sailors asked Yonah what they should do to him since the storm was increasing in its fury (1:11). The captain had previously told Yonah to pray or perish. Now Yonah revealed that praying would not accomplish what his perishing could (v 12). He asked them to throw him into the sea.

Before yielding to Yonah’s request, the sailors struggled to save the ship (1:13). Failing in their attempt, they cast him into the sea (v 15). Imagine the impression made on these sailors when the storm ceased as soon as Yonah’s body was in the sea. Their experience caused the ship’s crew to fear the Lord, and they offered a sacrifice and made vows to him (v 16).

But God was not through with Yonah, for he prepared a great fish to swallow him (1:17). Yonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and nights (cf. Mt 12:38-41). From within the fish Yonah prayed to God (Jon 2:1), and thanked him for hearing his prayer and saving him from death in the sea (vv 7-8). Yonah’s deliverance brought him to the point of renewed devotion to God (v 9). It is significant that his prayer reflected a deep personal acquaintance with the Psalms (cf. Pss 3:8; 5:7; 18:4-19; 30:2-3; 31:6, 22; 39:9; 42:6-7; 59:17; 69:1-2; 120:1; 142:3; 144:2).

The ultimate answer to Yonah’s (Jonah’s) prayers came when God provided him with the opportunity of obeying his commission and keeping his vows. The sea creature spit Yonah out upon the shore (Jon 2:10).

The writer now turns his attention to God’s dealing with the city of Nineveh (chs 3–4). Yonah repented of his disobedience and manifested that repentance by going to Nineveh to declare God’s message (3:1-3). Upon his arrival in Nineveh, he proceeded to proclaim God’s message. The inhabitants of the city were told they had 40 days (v 4), but they evidently responded immediately.
The people and their king repented in sackcloth and with fasting (3:5-6). Having repented privately, the king made a public proclamation to reinforce the response to God’s message (vv 7-9).

God’s acceptance of Nineveh’s repentance (3:10) caused Yonah’s grudging attitude to return and he complained (4:1-3). His recently uttered psalm of prayerful praise to God (2:1-9) now turned to bitter grumbling. Yonah prayed again to God (4:2), revealing his reason for refusing to obey the first commission. He had personal knowledge of God’s loving and forgiving nature, and he resented that love and forgiveness being extended to the enemies of his country. In foolish abandon, Yonah asked to die rather than to see God’s work among the Nineuitais (Ninevites) (v 3).

God’s compassion had been manifested to Nineveh, but he was also to show compassion again to Yonah by illustration and instruction (4:4-11). God’s quiet question, “Is it right for you to be angry about this?” must have probed Yonah’s innermost being (v 4). But the prophet preferred to put in a temporary shelter on the east side of Nineveh (v 5) waiting to see if anything would happen.

God added a plant (something with large leaves) to the number of nature’s objects that he used in his dealings with Yonah (4:6). This provision for Yonah’s comfort brought him joy. But the plant was destroyed by a worm sent by God (v 7). Then God sent the hot sirocco wind to dry out the air, increase the heat, and add to Yonah’s misery (v 8). Again, Yonah begged to die.

For the second time God questioned Yonah, “Is it right for you to be angry because the plant died?” (4:9, nlt). The point of the illustration was being driven home to the insensitive prophet. Yonah, however, responded with more bitterness (v 9). Yonah was greatly agitated because the loss of the plant affected him personally, even though he had nothing to do with its creation (v 10). The Lord Yahweh had created man. The Lord was concerned for the welfare of the Nineuitais. Did not the great Creator have the right to be agitated over the destruction of Nineveh with its 120,000 children and all its animals (v 11)? As Yonah had desired the preservation of the plant, so God had desired even more exceedingly the preservation of Nineveh.
See also Jonah (Person); Prophecy; Prophet, Prophetess.

JONATHAN

1. Levite from Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) in Yehudah (Judah), a descendant of Gereshom (Gershom), son of Mosheh (Moses) (cf. 1 Chr 23:14-15); he was a priest first to Mikah (Micah) in Efrayim (Ephraim) and later to Dan’s tribe during the period of the judges (Jgs 17:7-10; 18:30).

2. Benyamite (Benjamite), the firstborn son of Sha’ul (Saul) and the father of Meriv-Ba’al (Meribbaal) (1 Sm 14:49; 1 Chr 8:33-34). Yonatan (Jonathan) was a valiant warrior (1 Sm 13:2-4; 14:1-15; 2 Sm 1:22) and a devoted friend to David (1 Sm 18:1-5; 19:1-7). He was eventually killed, along with his brothers, by the Pelishtim (Philistines) at Mt Gilboa (1 Sm 31:2; 1 Chr 10:2).
3. Son of the high priest Evyatar (Abiathar) and one of David’s loyal servants (2 Sm 15:27, 36; 17:17, 20; 1 Kgs 1:42-43).
4. Shimei’s son and the nephew of David (2 Sm 21:21; 1 Chr 20:7).
5. Son of Shageh (Shagee) the Harari (Hararite) and one of David’s mighty warriors (2 Sm 23:33; 1 Chr 11:34).
6. Judahite, Yada’s (Jada’s) son, the brother of Yeter (Jether), and the father of Pelet (Peleth) and Zaza (1 Chr 2:32-33).
7. Son of Uziyah (Uzziah) and one of David’s treasurers (1 Chr 27:25).
8. David’s relative who served as counselor and scribe in the royal household (1 Chr 27:32).
9. Eved’s (Ebed’s) father. Eved returned with Ezra to Yehudah following the Babylonian captivity (Ezr 8:6).

10. Asahel’s son, who, with Yahzeyah (Jahzeiah), opposed Ezra’s suggestion that the sons of Yisrael (Israel) should divorce the foreign woman they had married since returning to Palestine from exile (Ezr 10:15).

11. Levite, the son of Yoyada (Joiada), the father of Yadua (Jaddua), and a descendant of Yeshua (Jeshua), the high priest (Neh 12:11). He is perhaps the same man as Yehohanan (Jehohanan) (or Yohanan (Johanan)), Elyashiv’s (Eliashib’s) grandson, in Ezra 10:6 (cf. Neh 12:23, nlt). See Jehohanan #4.
12. Priest and the head of Maluk’s (Malluch’s) house during the days of Yoyakim (Joiakim) the high priest (Neh 12:14).
13. Priest, father of Zekaryah (Zechariah), and a descendant of Asaf (Asaph) (Neh 12:35).
14. Secretary in whose house Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) was at one point imprisoned during the reign of King Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah) of Yehudah (Judah) (Jer 37:15, 20; 38:26).
15. Kareah’s son who sought protection under Gedalyah (Gedaliah) (Jer 40:8).

16. Youngest son of Matityah (Mattathias) and brother of Yehudah Maccabeus. When Yehudah Maccabeus was killed in battle with Bakides (Bacchides) (1 Macc 9:18), his brother Yonatan (Jonathan) became his successor (vv 28-31). Yonatan continued the struggle against Aram (Syria) for three years with a small band of guerrillas. But the Aramim (Syrians) were busy with an internal struggle for political power, and so, in 157 BC, made peace with him. The political machinations in Aram worked to Yonatan’s advantage, and five years later he became high priest in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and administrator of Judea (10:1-11). Under his management, Jewish territory and power increased. This occurred partly because Yonatan was able to play the Arami (Syrian) political rivals against one another. One of these was Trufon (Tryphon), a pretender to the Arami throne who saw that his influence was threatened by Yonatan’s power. So in 143 BC he decided to overthrow the Jewish leader. Yonatan was taken prisoner by Trufon through treachery and eventually killed, leaving his brother Shim’on (Simon) to lead the Yehudim (Jews) (1 Macc 12–13).

JOPPA

City about 35 miles (56.3 kilometers) northwest of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) that served as Yerushalem’s seaport. Yafo (Joppa) was built on a rocky hill about 116 feet (35.4 meters) high, with a cape projecting beyond the coastline into the sea, and was the only natural harbor on the Mediterranean coast between Mitsrayim (Egypt) and the OT town of Ako (Acco). Some 300 to 400 feet (91.4 to 121.9 meters) offshore a series of reefs formed a breakwater so that entrance into the harbor was gained from the north. It is possible that the harbor was larger and better protected in biblical times than it is today. The biblical city was well supplied with water, and the land surrounding it was quite fertile.

Yafo first appears in ancient records in the Mitsri (Egyptian) list of Palestinian cities captured by Thutmose III (1490–1432 BC). During the Amarna period, it was ruled by a local prince in alliance with Yerushalem. One source from this period describes its beautiful gardens and the craftsmanship of its workers in metal, leather, and wood. When Palestine was divided among the 12 tribes, Yafo was assigned to Dan (Jos 19:46; kjv “Japho”). It was soon taken by the Pelishtim (Philistines), who made it one of their seaports. David’s conquest of the Pelishtim restored Yafo to Yisrael (Israel), and during Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) reign, it became a major port serving Yerushalem. Cedar logs were floated from Levanon (Lebanon) to Yafo and then transported to Yerushalem for use in building the temple (2 Chr 2:16).

Yafo was the seaport to which Yonah (Jonah) fled in an attempt to avoid preaching to Nineveh (Jon 1:3); there, hoping to escape his responsibility, he boarded a ship bound for Tarshish. When Tiglat-Pileser (Tiglath-pileser) III invaded Peleshet (Philistia) in 743 BC, Yafo probably was one of the Pelishti (Philistine) cities that fell to him. Sanheriv (Sennacherib), in his campaign of 701 BC, lists Yafo as one of the cities he occupied. Subsequent to that, little is known of it until the time of Ezra, when once again cedar logs from Levanon were floated to Yafo and taken to Yerushalem for the rebuilding of the temple (Ezr 3:7). During the fourth century BC, Eshmunazar of Tsidon (Sidon) controlled the city. When Tsidon revolted against Paras (Persia) and was destroyed by Artahshashta (Artaxerxes) III, Yafo apparently became a free city. Alexandros (Alexander) the Great changed its name from Japho (its OT name) to Yafo and established a mint there, making it a city of some importance in the Greek Empire. Following Alexandros’s death, his successors fought over the city several times. It was ruled by Mitsrayim from 301 BC until 197 BC, when Antiokos (Antiochus) III made it a part of the Seleucid kingdom.

During the Maccabean period, Yafo had varied experiences. When Antiokos IV Epifanes (Epiphanes) moved toward Yerushalem in 168 BC to enforce his program of Hellenization, he landed his troops at Yafo. In 164 BC, because of the success of Yehudah (Judas; Grk. Yudas) Maccabeus against the Seleucids, non-Jewish citizens drowned about 200 Yehudim (Jews). Yehudah retaliated by burning the harbor installations and the boats anchored there but was unable to conquer the city itself (2 Macc 12:3-9). In 147 BC Yonatan (Jonathan) and Shim’on (Simon) defeated Appollonius Taos, the Arami (Syrian) general, and occupied Yafo for Alexandros I Epifanes, a contender for the Arami throne (1 Macc 10:74-86). Through a series of political moves in the next few years Shim’on was able to fortify the city, expel the Greek inhabitants, and firmly establish Yafo as a Jewish city. During Pompey’s Roman occupation, Yafo was declared a free city; it was returned to the Yehudim by Yulios (Julius) Kaisar (Caesar) (47 BC); and it was captured by Herodes (Herod) the Great in 37 BC. Hated by the residents of Yafo, Herodes built a new port at Kaisareia (Caesarea), about 40 miles (64.4 kilometers) north of Yafo. By the time of Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) birth, Yafo was under the rule of Kaisareia in the province of Aram (Syria) (Josephus’s Antiquities 17.13.2-4).

A Christian congregation appeared quite early in Yafo. Among the disciples living there were Dorkas (Dorcas), whom Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) raised from death (Acts 9:36-41), and Shim’on the tanner (v 43). From Yafo, Kefa was called to Kaisareia to present the gospel to the Roman centurion Kornelios (Cornelius) (10:1-48).

Yafo was a primary center of revolt against the Romans. It was destroyed by Vespasian in AD 68 and replaced with a Roman army camp. It was later rebuilt, and is known today as Jaffa, a suburb of Tel Aviv.

JORDAN RIVER

River lying in the bottom of a great canyon called the Yarden (Jordan) Rift, an elongated depression stretching from lower southwest Asia Minor (Aram (Syria)) to the Gulf of Aqaba. The rift was once filled by the Lisan Lake, but significant geologic activity caused it to recede, and the result was the formation of three separate aqueous bodies: the Huleh Lake, the Sea of Galil (Galilee), and the Dead Sea. To this day each of these are fed by the Yarden River, the stream whose name in Hebrew means “the descender.”
Sources

Originating at the northern end of the Huleh Basin, the river comprises four separate streams: Nahr Bereighith, Nahr Hasbani, Nahr el-Liddani, and Nahr Baniyas. In the northwest corner of the Huleh Valley the Bereighith emerges within the area of Merj Ayoun, flowing from a spring located on a modest knoll west of Mt Hermon. Slightly to the east is the Hasbani, a stream that descends from a spring 1,700 feet (518.2 meters) above sea level and follows a course of about 24 miles (38.6 kilometers). These two smaller streams merge less than a mile above their confluence with the el-Liddani and the Baniyas. The el-Liddani, lying between the Nahr Hasbani and the Nahr Baniyas, is located near Tel el-Qadi (the biblical city of Dan). The most powerful stream of the four; it is fed by ‘Ayin (Ain) Leddan, a spring that is nestled among thick underbrush and is fed by the melting snows off Mt Hermon. Flowing quickly and briefly, the el-Liddani rushes to meet the Nahr Baniyas, the last of the four streams. In the northeast corner of the Huleh Valley, at the NT site of Kaisareia-Filippi (Caesarea Philippi), the Baniyas originates from a cave approximately 1,100 feet (335 meters) above sea level and follows a steep descent to its confluence with the others. These four streams, making up the Yarden River, then flow together along a southerly course of 10 miles (16 kilometers) before entering Huleh Lake.
Course and Character of the River

The course of the Yarden follows a north-south route through the Great Rift, descending gradually from the Huleh Lake (7 feet, or 2 meters, above sea level) to the Dead Sea (1,274 feet, or 388 meters, below sea level). From the Huleh Lake the river follows a 20-mile (32.2-kilometer) course, passing through the basaltic lip that forms the southern dam of the Huleh Basin (Rosh Pinnah Sill) and descends quickly to the Sea of Galil (685 feet, or 209 meters, below sea level). To the south lies the Dead Sea at a distance of approximately 65 miles (105 kilometers). The river that connects these two seas, however, travels a circuitous route of 200 miles (322 kilometers), following a snakelike riverbed cut through the Ghor, the canyon floor.

The Yarden has many tributaries, not all of which are perennial. If there is no consistent water source, such as a spring at the head of the riverbed, then these V-shaped watercourses remain dry until a seasonal deluge. When the rain comes, these dry, narrow courses are filled with fast-paced streams that flow off the sides of the canyon into the Yarden River. North of the Sea of Galil four major systems feed the fluvial system in the Huleh Basin: Nahr Dishon and Nahr Hatsor (Hazor) on the west, and Nahr Shuah and Nahr Gilbon on the east. Between the Sea of Galil and the Dead Sea are the following major tributary systems: on the east—Yarmuq, ‘Aravi (Arab), Tayibeh, Ziqlab, Jurm, Yabis, Kufrinjia, Rajib, Zarqa, Nimrin, Abu Gharuba; on the west—Fejjas, Bireh, Jalub, Malih, Far’ah, Aujah, el-Qelt.

The character of the Ghor varies from north to south as the canyon floor drops farther below sea level. Just south of the Sea of Galil arable fields may be cultivated without irrigation, which permits occupation and settlement. South of this and farther below sea level, beyond the narrowest constriction of the canyon at Ghor el-Wahadina, the terrain and climate change. Since the floor now consistently approaches 1,000 feet (305 meters) below sea level, the climatic conditions approximate that of the desert. In this dry and desolate region, the river and its immediate environs now assume a more prominent role, becoming a lifeline to the flora and the fauna that hug its banks. Its course and character are more easily discerned as it has become a veritable stream in the desert. The dense foliage on the banks of the Yarden is still today a wildlife haunt as it was in antiquity, the low-lying shrubs and the tamarisk alike providing thick ground cover. This lower section of the canyon, called the Zor, is 150 feet (45.7 meters) below the Ghor and separated by the qattara (a sedimentary deposit of grayish-white marls and clays that form precipitous and barren slopes) from the canyon floor above. Generally inaccessible and extremely dangerous, the Zor and qattara form a natural barrier between Cis-Jordan (west) and Transjordan (east). Thus, trade, settlement, and travel were necessarily affected by the various topographical features that characterize this area.
Biblical Events

The OT Israelis (Israelites) passed across the Yarden upon entry into the Promised Land (Jos 3:14-17). The fords of the Yarden were the sites of conflict in the war of Yiftah (Jephthah) and the Giladim (Gileadites) against the Efrayimim (Ephraimites) (Jgs 12:1-6). The prophet Eliyah (Elijah) sought refuge from Ahav (Ahab) king of Yisrael (Israel) by the brook of Kerith east of the Yarden (1 Kgs 17:1-5). Eliyah was translated up to heaven in a whirlwind after having crossed the Yarden with Elisha on dry ground (2 Kgs 2:6-12). Na’aman (Naaman), the Arami (Syrian) general, bathed in the Yarden at the command of Elisha and his leprosy was healed (5:8-14). Elisha made the ax head float here (2 Kgs 6:1-7). In the NT, Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) was baptized by Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) the immerser in the Yarden (Mt 3:13-17). Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) confessed that Yeshua was the “Christ, the Son of the living God” at Kaisareia-Filippi—located on one of the sources of the Yarden, Nahr Baniyas (16:13-20). Yeshua healed two blind men at Yeriho (Jericho), which is near the Yarden (20:29-34) and visited with Zakay (Zacchaeus; Grk. Zakkaios) in that same city (Lk 19:1-10).

JOSEPH

1. Ya’akov’s (Jacob’s) 11th son and the firstborn son of Rahel (Rachel). Rahel named the boy Yosef (Joseph), meaning “may he add,” expressing her desire that God would give her another son (Gn 30:24).

Nothing more is said about Yosef until, at the age of 17, he is seen tending his father’s flocks with his brothers (Gn 37:2). Yosef was the favorite of his father, since he was the son of his old age (v 3) and the firstborn son of his favorite wife. Because of this, his brothers hated Yosef. This envy was magnified when Ya’akov gave Yosef a ground-length, long-sleeved, multicolored robe (vv 3-4). (This type of garment is illustrated by the paintings in the Asiatic tombs of Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan and of the nobles at Gurneh, near Luxor.) The animosity of his brothers increased still more when Yosef revealed to them his dreams of dominion over them (vv 5-11). Subsequently, when Yosef was sent to check on his brothers and the flocks near Shekem (Shechem), his brothers sold him to a caravan of traders going down to Mitsrayim (Egypt) (vv 25-28). His brothers then took his robe, dipped it in goat’s blood, and brought it to Ya’akov, who concluded that Yosef had been killed by wild animals (vv 31-33); Ya’akov was overwhelmed with grief (vv 34-35).

In Mitsrayim, Yosef was sold to Potifar (Potiphar), an Mitsri (Egyptian) officer of the guard (Gn 37:36; 39:1), who eventually put Yosef in charge of his entire household. However, trouble arose from Potifar’s wife, who was attracted to the young Hebrew and tried to seduce him (39:6-10). He steadfastly resisted her advances, protesting that to comply with her wishes would be a disservice to his master and a sin against God (v 9). One day she seized his garment, but he left the garment behind and fled. Potifar’s wife accused Yosef of attempted rape; her report was believed, and Yosef was incarcerated in the king’s prison (v 20), where Par’oh’s (Pharaoh’s) butler and baker were also confined. While in prison, Yosef, with the Lord’s help, interpreted these men’s troublesome dreams. As Yosef had foretold, the baker was executed and the butler was restored to royal favor (ch 40).

Two years later Par’oh had two dreams that his magicians and wise men could not interpret. The butler, remembering Yosef, had him summoned from prison. God revealed to Yosef that the dreams foretold seven years of abundance, followed by seven years of famine (Gn 41:25-36). Par’oh, impressed with Yosef’s interpretation, made him ruler of Mitsrayim, second only to himself (vv 39-44). Yosef was given a new name, Tsofnat-Pa’neah (Zaphenath-paneah), and a wife, Esenat (Asenath), the daughter of Poti-Fera (Potiphera) (v 45).

Yosef was 30 years old when he became ruler of Mitsrayim. During the seven years of prosperity, he gathered the good supplies for the seven years of famine to come (Gn 41:53-56). When the famine eventually became severe in Palestine, Ya’akov sent all his sons, except Benyamin (Benjamin), his youngest son, to Mitsrayim to purchase grain. Appearing before Yosef in Mitsrayim, they did not recognize him. But he knew them and remembered his dreams of years before (42:8-9). After listening to the report of their family, he accused them of being spies (vv 9-14) and insisted that they leave one of their brothers as hostage and return with Benyamin to verify the truthfulness of their report (vv 19-20). Thus Shim’on (Simeon) was bound and left in Mitsrayim (v 24).

After the famine worsened in Palestine, Ya’akov asked his sons to go back to Mitsrayim to buy more grain (Gn 43:1-2); reluctantly agreeing to the conditions that the Mitsri administrator had placed on them, Ya’akov allowed Benyamin to go with them (vv 11-13). When they arrived in Mitsrayim, they were taken to Yosef’s house, where Shim’on was restored to them (v 23) and a meal was prepared for them (v 33). Yosef at last disclosed his identity and declared that God had sent him before them to preserve their lives (45:4-8). Arrangements were then made to send for Ya’akov; wagons were provided, along with provisions for the journey (v 21). When Ya’akov came to Goshen in the Nile Delta, Yosef went out to meet him, and another great reunion took place (46:28-29). He also presented his father and brothers to Par’oh, who let them live in the land of Goshen (47:6).

Upon learning that his father was ill, Yosef took his two sons, Menasheh (Manasseh) and Efrayim (Ephraim), to him for his blessing. He presented the sons so that the older would be at Ya’akov’s right hand and the younger at his left in order that Menasheh would receive the blessing of the firstborn. Ya’akov, however, crossed his hands and with his right hand on Efrayim gave him the greater blessing (Gn 48:14-20). He also gave to Yosef the land that he had taken from the Amorim (Amorites) (v 22). At Ya’akov’s death, Yosef made the funeral arrangements; and after the customary funerary practices were carried out, a great funeral procession went to Kena’an (Canaan), where Ya’akov was buried by his sons in the cave of Makpelah (Machpelah) near Hevron (Hebron) (50:1-12).

When Yosef was 110 years old, he called his brothers and told them that he was about to die. He made them take an oath that when they returned to Kena’an they would take his bones with them. So he died, was embalmed, and was placed in a coffin in Mitsrayim (Gn 50:26). Many years later, during the exodus, Mosheh (Moses) took the bones of Yosef with him from Mitsrayim (Ex 13:19). Yosef’s remains were eventually interred at Shekem in the parcel of land that Ya’akov had bought from Hamor, the father of Shekem (Gn 33:18-20; Jos 24:32). See Israel, History of; Patriarchs, Period of the.
2. Yigal’s (Igal’s) father from Yisakar’s (Issachar’s) tribe. Yigal was one of the 12 spies sent by Mosheh to search out the land of Kena’an (Nm 13:7).
3. Asaf’s (Asaph’s) second son and the leader of the first course of priests serving in the sanctuary during David’s reign (1 Chr 25:2, 9).
4. One of Binuy’s (Binnui’s) descendants who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era (Ezr 10:42).

6. Descendant of David (Mt 1:16; Lk 3:23) and the husband of Maria (Mary), the mother of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus). Yosef (Joseph) was betrothed to Maria, a young woman of the city of Nazaret (Nazareth). Maria had learned from the angel Gavriel (Gabriel) that she was to bear the Son of God, whom she was to name Yeshua (Lk 1:31) and that this conception was to be a work of the Holy Spirit (v 35). Yosef was not aware of this, so when he learned that Maria was pregnant, he decided to divorce her quietly, for he was a just man and did not want to humiliate her publicly (Mt 1:19). An angel subsequently appeared to him in a dream to tell him what was happening (Mt 1:21; cf. Is 7:14). The text of Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios) makes it clear that there was no sexual union between Yosef and Maria until after Yeshua was born (Mt 1:18, 25; see also Lk 1:34-37).

When Kaisar (Caesar) Augustus issued a decree that everyone had to register in his native city for purposes of taxation, Yosef and Maria returned to Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem), where Yeshua was subsequently born (Lk 2:1-6). Later, Yosef and Maria took the infant Yeshua to the temple to present him to the Lord (vv 22, 33). After the visit of the wise men, an angel appeared to Yosef in a dream and instructed him to take Yeshua and Maria to Mitsrayim (Egypt) to protect the child from King Herodes (Herod) (Mt 2:13). Upon the death of Herodes, an angel similarly advised him to return to Yisrael (Israel), so the family went to live in Nazaret. The last recorded event that involves Yosef is the incident of Yeshua at the temple at age 12 (Lk 2:41-51). Yosef is not mentioned by name, but Maria told Yeshua that she and his father had been looking for him anxiously.

Yeshua was identified by people around Nazaret as “Yosef’s son” (Lk 4:22; Jn 1:45; 6:42). It is only through references identifying Yeshua that we learn of Yosef’s trade. Twice Yeshua is referred to as “the carpenter’s son” (Mt 13:55; Mk 6:3). Yosef was not a carpenter in our sense of the word, for houses were built mostly of stone and earth. He was a woodworker or artificer in wood, and probably most of his work was with furniture and agricultural implements.

During the ministry of Yeshua, it was his mother and his brothers who came to look for him (Mt 12:46-50; Mk 3:31-35), so it is assumed that by this time Yosef was dead. Yosef was most likely the father of Ya’akov (James), Yosef, Shim’on (Simon), Yehudah (Judas; Grk. Yudas), and unnamed sisters (Mt 13:55; Mk 6:3).
See also Brothers of Jesus; Genealogy of Jesus Christ.

In a nearby garden was Yosef’s own new rock-cut tomb in which no one had ever been buried. Here they placed Yeshua and sealed the tomb with a large stone.

JOSEPHUS*, Flavius
Jewish military officer and historian (AD 37–c. 100).

Josephus was born into an aristocratic priestly family in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Through his mother he was related to the Hasmoneans. In his youth he was noted for his memory and ease in learning. As a teenager he attached himself to a member of an ascetic sect. Then he became a Farisaios (Pharisee).

In AD 64 Josephus was a member of an official party sent to Romai (Rome) to secure the release of some priests. The empire’s capital made an indelible impression on him. After his return to Yerushalem, the first Jewish revolt erupted (AD 66). The Sanhedrin (the Jewish governing council) appointed Josephus commander of Galil (Galilee). He organized the province well but incurred the opposition of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) of Gischala, Galil’s former leader. Conflict between the two men’s forces continued until the arrival of the Roman general Vespasian in the spring of 67.

Josephus and the Galilim (Galileans) entrenched themselves at Jotapata. After a siege of six weeks, the Roman army captured and destroyed the city, but Josephus and 40 soldiers escaped to a cave. Josephus, whose life was assured by the Romans through a friend’s intervention, persuaded his fellow soldiers to kill each other rather than be captured. When only he and one other remained alive, he surrendered to the Romans.

When Josephus appeared before Vespasian and prophesied that Vespasian would become emperor, his life was spared. Nonetheless, Josephus was held prisoner. Vespasian was proclaimed emperor in the year 69 and Josephus was set free. He then adopted Vespasian’s family name, Flavius. In 70, when Vespasian’s son Titos (Titus) marched on Yerushalem, Josephus accompanied him. Several times Josephus tried unsuccessfully to persuade the Yehudim (Jews) to surrender.

After Titos’s destruction of Yerushalem, Josephus went to Romai, where Vespasian favored him with Roman citizenship and a pension. Free to write, Josephus produced a number of books of considerable historical value. In The Jewish War (AD 77–78) Josephus described the Roman-Jewish conflict from the time of Antiokos (Antiochus) Ephiphanes to slightly beyond the fall of Yerushalem. Perhaps Josephus’s greatest work was Antiquities of the Yehudim (c. 94). A 20-volume work designed to glorify the Yehudim and eliminate gentile hostility, it traces Jewish history from the Creation to the outbreak of war with Romai in 66. His autobiography, Life, was primarily a vindication of his activities as governor of Galil. Josephus wrote Against Apion to counteract claims of anti-Semites; in this work he used logical arguments as well as derision.

As a historian, Josephus sometimes distorted facts in favor of his patrons. However, he was witness to many of the events about which he wrote. His works illumine the period in which the church came into existence, especially concerning the religion, politics, geography, and prominent persons of the early Christian era. Of particular interest to Christians are his references to Yohan the immerser, Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), and Ya’akov (James) the Just (Yeshua’s brother).
