JOSHUA (Person)

1. Son of Nun, Mosheh’s (Moses’) assistant and successor, and the military leader whom God chose to lead the Israelis (Israelites) in the conquest of Kena’an (Canaan) (Nm 13:16, kjv “Jehoshua”; also spelled “Jehoshuah” in 1 Chr 7:27 and “Yeshua (Jeshua)” in Neh 8:17).

Early in the exodus, Yehoshua (Joshua) was sent by Mosheh to fight against the Amalekim (Amalekites) (Ex 17:8-15). Yehoshua defeated Amalek, and Mosheh wrote of the event and built an altar that he called “Yahweh Is My Banner” (v 15).

When Mosheh sent 12 men from Kadesh-Barnea (Kadesh-barnea) to spy out the land of Kena’an, Yehoshua represented the tribe of Efrayim (Ephraim) (Nm 13:8). At that time Yehoshua was called Hoshea, but Mosheh changed his name to Yehoshua (vv 8, 16). Yehoshua and Kalev (Caleb) were the only two spies to bring back an affirmative report concerning an Israeli (Israelite) invasion of the land (14:6-9). Consequently, of all the adult Israeli males to leave Mitsrayim (Egypt) in the exodus, only these two crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River and entered the Promised Land (v 30).

When the Lord announced to Mosheh his impending death, Mosheh asked about his successor, and the Lord appointed Yehoshua to that position (Nm 27:12-23). After the death of Mosheh on Mt Nevo (Nebo), Yehoshua’s leadership was confirmed (34:17), and the Lord told Yehoshua to go over the Yarden and take the land (Jos 1:1-2).

From the Transjordan, Yehoshua sent two men across the river to reconnoiter Yeriho (Jericho) (ch 2). In Yeriho they were concealed by Rahav (Rahab) and later safely made their way back to Yehoshua to report that the people of the land were fainthearted because of the Israelis (vv 23-24).

When Yisrael (Israel) had crossed the river, the Lord instructed Yehoshua to set up a circle of 12 stones at Gilgal to commemorate this passage (Jos 4:1-7). The Lord then commanded all of the males who had been born during the exodus to be circumcised (5:2-9).

While camped at Gilgal, near Yeriho, Yehoshua was confronted by a man with a drawn sword. When Yehoshua challenged the man, he learned that it was the Lord, who told him to remove his shoes, for the ground was holy (Jos 5:13-15). The Lord gave Yehoshua directions for the destruction of Yeriho; these were followed explicitly and the city fell (ch 6). The attack on Ay (Ai) ended in temporary defeat, until the matter of Akan’s (Achan’s) sin was discovered and judged (7:10-26). Then Ay was taken and destroyed.
Yehoshua built an altar on Mt Eyval (Ebal) (Jos 8:30-32), and the blessings and curses were read, as commanded by God through Mosheh (Jos 8:33-35; cf. Dt 27–28).

Because the Israelis failed to ask direction from the Lord (Jos 9:14), Yehoshua was tricked into making a covenant of peace with the Hivim (Hivites) of Giveon (Gibeon). Yehoshua then reduced them to doing menial tasks in Yisrael (vv 21-27).

The kings of the various Kena’ani (Canaanite) cities allied themselves against the Israeli threat (Jos 9:1-2) and a league of five Amori (Amorite) cities (Yerushalem (Jerusalem), Hevron (Hebron), Yarmut (Jarmuth), Lakish (Lachish), and Eglon) attacked Giveon (10:1-5). The Givonim (Gibeonites) appealed to Yehoshua for help; he responded quickly against this Amori confederation and routed the Amori forces. It was on this occasion that Yehoshua commanded the sun and the moon to stand still so that Yisrael could have more time to defeat these adversaries (vv 12-14). This victory was followed by a series of successful attacks on enemy towns (vv 28-43).

A northern alliance headed by Yavin (Jabin), king of Hatsor (Hazor), was the next opposition (Jos 11:1-5). The Lord assured Yehoshua of success, and the city of Hatsor was taken and destroyed by fire (vv 6-15). Joshua 11:23 summarizes the conquest of the land, and chapter 12 enumerates the kings who were conquered.

Yehoshua was now old, and the Lord told him that much land remained to be possessed. These territories are listed, but the Lord directed Yehoshua to proceed with the division of the land among the nine and a half tribes (Jos 13:7; cf. 13:8–18:28). Yehoshua himself was given the city he asked for, Timnat-Serah (Timnath-serah), in the hill country of Efrayim, which he rebuilt and settled (19:49-50).

The Lord told Yehoshua (Joshua) to appoint cities of refuge to which a person guilty of manslaughter could flee to escape the avenger of blood (Jos 20). Then the Levites came to Eleazar the priest and Yehoshua to request that they be given their cities, as the Lord had commanded through Mosheh (Moses) (21:1-42).

In his advanced years Yehoshua summoned all Yisrael and solemnly charged them to continue in faithfulness to the Lord (Jos 23). Finally, he called all Yisrael to Shekem (Shechem), where he gave them his farewell message. He summed up the Lord’s dealings with them from the time of Avraham (Abraham) and again challenged them to serve the Lord, putting before them the well-known choice and decision: “Choose today whom you will serve. . . . As for me and my family, we will serve Yahweh” (24:15, nlt).

Yehoshua died at the age of 110 years and was buried in the land of his inheritance at Timnat-Serah (Jos 24:29-30; the parallel account in Jgs 2:8-9 reads “Timnat-Heres (Timnath-heres),” nlt mg). Yisrael served the Lord during all the days of Yehoshua and the elders who outlived him (Jos 24:31; Jgs 2:7).
See also Conquest and Allotment of the Land; Israel, History of; Joshua, Book of.

2. Inhabitant of Beyt-Shemesh (Beth-shemesh). It was his grainfield into which the cart carrying the ark sent by the Pelishtim (Philistines) came. It stopped by a large stone which was then used to commemorate this event (1 Sm 6:14, 18).
3. Governor of Yerushalem during King Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) reign (2 Kgs 23:8).

4. Yotsadak’s (Jozadak’s) son and high priest during the days of Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) in postexilic Yerushalem (Hg 1:1-14; 2:2-4; Zec 3:1-9; 6:11; nlt “Yeshua (Jeshua)”). Yehoshua is alternately called Yeshua in Ezra and Nehemyah (Nehemiah). See Jeshua (Person) #3.
5. Eliezer’s son and an ancestor of Yeshua Christ (Lk 3:29). See Genealogy of Jesus Christ.
JOSHUA, Book of

First of the historical books in the English Bible and the first of the Former Prophets (including Judges, the books of Shmuel (Samuel), and the books of Kings) in the Hebrew Bible. It begins with the Lord’s commission of Yehoshua (Joshua) (Jos 1:1-9) and concludes with the burial of Yehoshua, Eleazar, and the bones of Yosef (Joseph) (24:29-33). The purpose of the book is to show how Yehoshua continued in the footsteps of Mosheh (Moses), how the Lord gave the land to Yisrael (Israel), and how Yisrael might prosper in the land.
Preview
• Author and Date
• Problems of Interpretation
• Purpose
• Content
Author and Date

According to the Talmud, Yehoshua wrote the book. This ancient tradition is possibly based on the brief statement that Yehoshua “recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God” (24:26, nlt). However, this applies only to the renewal of the covenant (ch 24). The issue of authorship is tied up with the dating of the book. Since the book has no unambiguous markers on date and authorship, neither critics nor conservative scholars have been able to come to any agreement on these issues. According to a conservative analysis of Yehoshua, the book was written between 1375 BC and 1045 BC (premonarchic). The argument is based on the references to the migration of Dan (19:47; cf. Jgs 18:27-31), to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) as a Yevusi (Jebusite) city (Jos 15:8, 63; 18:16, 28), to Tsidon (Sidon) rather than Tsor (Tyre) as the prominent Phoenician city (11:8; 13:4-6; 19:28), and also on the eyewitness style (5:1, 6—in the MT). But critical scholars have raised issues that they considered could best be resolved by positing a seventh-century BC or even an exilic date.
Problems of Interpretation
Holy War

The morality of the Conquest may be explained by the concept of holy war. The holy war motif would explain why Yisrael (Israel) was to destroy the indigenous population (Dt 7:16; 20:16-18; Jos 6:21; 8:24-26; 10:10, 28-30, 35-42; 11:11). The justification may lie in the concept that Yisrael was God’s instrument of judgment on the Kena’ani (Canaanite) nations. This argument is related to the mention of the wickedness of the Kena’anim (Canaanites) (Gn 15:16; Dt 7:2-5, 25-26; 12:30-31; Jos 23:7; Jgs 2:11). However, the canonical narrative of the progression of the Conquest puts the responsibility on the Kena’anim. They marched and fought against Yisrael (Nm 21:21-35; Jos 7:4-5; 8:5, 16-17; 9:1-2; 10:1-6; 11:1-5; 24:11). Therefore, it could be argued that in the process of war a sincere invitation to make peace was given to the kings (cf. Nm 21:21-22; Dt 20:10-11) but was refused. Instead, the kings took the initiative in battle. The responsibility for the destruction of the native population thus lay with the leadership. Yet all this was evidence of God’s working in human affairs, which the Bible simply states, “For it was Yahweh himself who hardened their hearts to wage war against Yisrael, so that he might destroy them totally, exterminating them without mercy, as Yahweh had commanded Mosheh (Moses)” (Jos 11:20, niv). Even as Par’oh (Pharaoh), whose heart the Lord hardened, was responsible for the plagues in Mitsrayim (Egypt), so the Kena’ani rulers were responsible for the extermination of their populations. The biblical account of the Conquest affirms the mystery of human responsibility and divine sovereignty without explaining it.
Nature of the Conquest

Various explanations of the nature of the Conquest have been given. The traditional view of a blitzkrieg type of conquest, which resulted in a complete occupation of the whole land (cf. Jos 10:40; 11:1-3, 16-19), does not fit within the whole picture of the book. The book presents a realistic description of the areas that still had to be conquered (13:1-7) and of the military strength of the indigenous population (cf. 13:13; 15:63; 16:10; 17:12-18; 19:47). Moreover, Yehoshua (Joshua) promised that the Lord would continue to help Yisrael to occupy the land, as its population and needs developed (23:5). The occupation of Kena’an (Canaan) was in two stages: conquest and gradual occupation (cf. Ex 23:29-30; Dt 7:22).
Purpose

The role of the final (canonical) form of the book is to present Yehoshua’s obedience to the law of Mosheh. Victory and defeat are illustrations of obedience and disobedience. Of course, there is tension in this because the descriptions of the Conquest are complete and yet incomplete. The tension is a dynamic device to show that the Conquest and enjoyment of the land depend wholly on obedience. The period of Yehoshua is viewed as a paradigm of obedient Yisrael. Thus, a holistic reading of the book presents an appeal to covenant loyalty directed to future generations.
Content
Conquest of the Land, 1:1–12:24
The Lord’s Commission of Yehoshua, 1:1-9

With the death of Mosheh (Jos 1:1), the Lord himself confirms Mosheh’s ordination of Yehoshua (Dt 34:9). He charges him with leadership in the conquest of Kena’an (Jos 1:2-3), defines the geographical boundaries of the land (v 4), encourages him with his continued presence (vv 5, 9), and expects him to devoutly follow in “the law of Mosheh” (i.e., the law given in Dt; cf. Dt 31:9, 24-26; Jos 23:6), so that he may succeed in his mission (1:7-8). The original mission, as well as the ministry of Mosheh, find their continuity in Yehoshua.
Crossing the Yarden (Jordan), 1:10–5:12

The first stage calls for the preparation of Yisrael. As their leader, Yehoshua must demonstrate to the people that he follows in the footsteps of Mosheh. He does this by reminding the Transjordan tribes to demonstrate loyalty to the command of Mosheh by joining with the other tribes in the conquest of Kena’an (1:13-15; cf. Nm 32:20-27). They submitted to Yehoshua’s authority as to Mosheh’ (Jos 1:16-18). He demonstrates his military leadership in sending the two spies to Yeriho (Jericho) (ch 2). His authority is accepted by priests (3:6; 4:10) and people (3:5-9) as they cross the Yarden. The crossing of the Yarden marks the public recognition of Yehoshua as a leader like Mosheh (4:14).

The account of the crossing marks an important transition from the era of the exodus/wilderness to the era of the Conquest. On the one hand, the story of Rahav (Rahab) illustrates how the Kena’anim (Canaanites) had heard about the Lord’s mighty acts (2:10-11) and reacted with great fear (cf. Ex 15:15; 23:27-28; Dt 2:25; 7:23; 11:25; 32:30). Rahav’s expression of faith in Yisrael’s (Israel’s) God (2:11) anticipates the inclusion of the Gentiles in the covenant community as promised to the patriarchs (Gn 12:3). By faith Rahav was included in the covenant and was richly rewarded by the inclusion of her name in the lineage of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) (Mt 1:5).

The Israelis (Israelites) crossed the Yarden with the knowledge that the fear of God had come on the Kena’anim (Jos 2:24). However, they were also instructed to show their reverence for the Lord by keeping a safe distance between themselves and the ark of the covenant (3:4) and by consecrating themselves (v 5). The “living God” was among them and required holiness and reverence from his people (v 10). He, in turn, would demonstrate his loyalty in the marvelous passage through the Yarden River (v 13) and in the conquest of the land (3:10). After the tribes had crossed the river (4:1), each leader of the 12 tribes took up a stone out of the dried-up riverbed and set up a memorial at Gilgal (vv 1-9, 20). Thus, Yisrael was to remember that the stones, taken from the place where the priests who carried the ark had stood, were reminders of the majestic presence of God. Future generations who were to hear this report (vv 21-24) were hereby encouraged because the fear of God would fall on all the peoples of the land (v 24).

The consecration before the conquest of Yeriho is also symbolized by the act of circumcision (5:1-9) and by the celebration of the Passover (vv 10-12). The events are not necessarily chronologically related but were selected as examples of Yisrael’s responsiveness to Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) ministry. Mosheh’s (Moses’) appeal to the new generation had its effect (cf. Dt 4:4-14; 6:1-5). The new generation served the Lord as long as Yehoshua and the elders were alive (Jos 24:31). Physical circumcision, neglected during the wilderness journey (5:5) due to unbelief, was a sign of spiritual responsiveness. The responsive nation received the external sign of the covenant with the anticipation that the Lord of the covenant would bless his people in giving them victory and the fruit of the land. Their reproach was rolled away (v 9). The covenant continuity is also brought out in the brief mention of the Passover celebration. The newness is their eating the fruit of the land. With the taste of the food of Kena’an (Canaan), the manna stopped. The desert experience was over. A new era was ushered in with their presence in the Promised Land (vv 11-12).
Conquest of Yeriho, 5:13–6:27

The victory is the Lord’s. This is the message with which the battle of Yeriho begins. The holy God who appeared to Mosheh in the burning bush (Ex 3:2–4:17) appeared to Yehoshua as the commander of the Lord’s army (Jos 5:14-15) with a message from the Lord (6:2). The city of Yeriho will fall without a siege and ensuing battle. Yisrael’s response to Yeriho’s preparedness for war (cf. 24:11) was strange, but the presence of the ark and the blowing of the trumpets symbolized that the Lord would fight for Yisrael, even as he had promised. However, Yisrael could not take any of the spoil. Because Yahweh fought for Yisrael, everything was to be devoted to him (6:17). The Lord honored the vow to Rahav, made by the spies, so that she and her family were kept alive (vv 17, 25), but they were temporarily placed outside the camp (v 23). The valuable metals were placed into the treasury (vv 19, 24), whereas everything else was burned by fire (v 24). Nothing was to be taken for personal gain; otherwise God’s judgment would rest on Yisrael (v 18). In order to emphasize God’s absolute ownership of Yeriho, Yehoshua put a curse on anyone who would attempt to rebuild the city (6:26; cf. 1 Kgs 16:34). The rumors of Yeriho’s destruction spread, and the peoples of Kena’an knew that the Lord was with Yehoshua (Jos 6:27; cf. 1:5, 9).
Tragedy and Triumph at Ay (Ai), 7:1–8:29

Victory was short-lived because Akan (Achan) defied God’s “ban,” took some of the objects, hid them in the ground under his tent (7:21), and brought God’s wrath on all of Yisrael (v 1). Yisrael was stunned by their defeat at Ay (vv 2-5). Yehoshua and the elders responded to the disaster by fasting and lamenting (vv 6-9). What a contrast between the reports of victory spread through the land and the anguished cry of God’s servant, fearful that the Kena’anim would amass strength and wipe out Yisrael (v 9). Only after the people had consecrated themselves (v 13) and Akan was exposed and his memory removed (vv 25b-26) could they renew the attack on Ay with the encouraging promise of God’s presence and victory (8:1-2). Ay, too, was taken (vv 3-19) and the population execrated (vv 20-26), but Yisrael enjoyed the spoils by direct permission from the Lord (v 27). The ruins of Ay, the pile of stones covering the body of Ay’s king (vv 28-29), and the heap of rocks over Akan’s body were sobering reminders to Yisrael that God’s faithfulness requires absolute loyalty from his people.
Renewal of the Covenant, 8:30-35

Yehoshua led Yisrael in a ceremonial covenant renewal at Shekem (Shechem), as Mosheh had instructed (Jos 8:31; cf. Dt 11:29; 27). Yehoshua took care in the proper preparation of the altar (cf. Ex 20:25) on which dedicatory and communal offerings were presented. He copied the law as a symbol of his royal leadership and his devotion to the Lord (Jos 8:32; cf. Dt 17:18). All Yisrael (officers and people, aliens and native-born Israelis) together presented themselves for the reading of the blessings and the curses (Jos 8:33-35). The whole book of Deuteronomy (i.e., “the Book of the Law,” cf. Dt 31:26) was read in their presence. Half the tribes stood on Mt Gerizim and said “Amen” to the blessings, and the other six stood on Mt Eyval (Ebal), saying “Amen” to the curses (cf. Dt 27:9-26).
Covenant with the Givonim (Gibeonites), 9:1-27

The rumors of God’s mighty acts had brought fear on the Kena’ani (Canaanite) kings (cf. Jos 2:8-11, 24; 5:1; 6:27). The first defeat at Ay had given them a ray of hope that Yisrael could be put down. Rather than submit themselves to Yisrael and suffer from humiliation as servants of Yisrael, they joined forces against Yehoshua and Yisrael (9:1-2).

The Hivim (Hivites) from Giveon (Gibeon), Kefirah (Kephirah), Be’erot (Beeroth), and Kiryat-Yearim (Kiriath-jearim) (9:7, 17) did not join with their fellow Kena’anim (Canaanites). Instead, they developed an intricate plan to deceive Yisrael (Israel) and to sue for full treaty status. The purpose of the treaty was that of friendship (namely, “peace”), promising each other to be of mutual assistance in case of attack. The concern was with the preservation of life (vv 15, 24). Their deception included a ruse about the great distance they had traveled (vv 11-14) and a false report of Yisrael’s victories in Transjordan with no mention of their crossing the Yarden (Jordan) (9:9-10; cf. 5:1). The law permitted the submissive city to subject its population to a type of suzerainty treaty, in which Yisrael defined the terms and expected the subjugated populace to serve as its forced laborers (Dt 20:11; cf. Jgs 1:28-35; 1 Kgs 9:15-21). However, the treaty permitted the Hivim to maintain their way of life with the advantage of Yisrael’s military protection.
The Southern Campaign, 10:1-43

The king of Yerushalem (Jerusalem), Adoni-Tsedek (Adoni-zedek), led the cities of Hevron (Hebron), Yarmut (Jarmuth), Lakish (Lachish), and Eglon in an alliance against Giveon as a military ploy to take a stand against Yisrael (Jos 10:1-5). The Givonim appealed to Yisrael for help based on their covenantal relationship (v 6). Yehoshua (Joshua) led Yisrael on a 25-mile (40-kilometer) hike through the wilderness from Gilgal up to Giveon during one night (vv 7-9). The Israeli (Israelite) attack surprised the Kena’anim, who were already frightened of the Israelis (Israelites). The camp of the Kena’anim was thrown into confusion, and the soldiers fled the hill country via the road of Beyt-Horon (Beth-horon) to Azekah and Makedah (Makkedah) (v 10). But while running, they were tormented with large hailstones (v 11). The victory was the Lord’s. Miraculously, Yisrael could push the Kena’anim farther from the hill country because of the long day (vv 12-14). The marvel of this day was long remembered in the Book of Jashar (cf. 2 Sm 1:18), because on it the Lord listened to a man, namely Yehoshua (Jos 10:14).

The five kings hidden in a cave at Makedah were discovered, killed, hanged on trees, and buried in the cave (10:16-27). Their foolish attempt to make war on Yisrael came to a quick end. Since the coalition of large cities had been put down, Yehoshua led Yisrael in a rapid campaign of the other southern cities (vv 29-43). The region was taken in one campaign with the Lord’s help (v 42).
The Northern Campaign, 11:1-15

The Israelis were again forced into battle, this time by the leadership of Yavin (Jabin), king of Hatsor (Hazor). Yavin rallied the kings of the northern cities who assembled their troops and horses by the waters of Merom for battle against Yisrael (11:1-5). The similarity to the southern campaign is a literary way to demonstrate that the kings of the south and north initiated the war and were consequently defeated. So it was with the northern kings, who were routed as far as the region of Tsidon (Sidon) in Foinikai (Phoenicia) (v 8). Their horses were hamstrung and their chariots burned (v 9), as the Lord had instructed (v 6). Yisrael was to depend on the Lord (cf. Ps 20:7). Hatsor, the great and ancient city, the center of Kena’ani power in the north, was completely destroyed (Jos 11:10-13). The burning of Yeriho (Jericho), Ay (Ai), and Hatsor were exceptions, because Yisrael had been promised Kena’ani houses, wells, and cities (Dt 6:10-11; cf. Jos 24:13). The campaign narrative stresses again the absolute loyalty of Yehoshua to the Lord and to Mosheh (Moses), the servant of the Lord (Jos 11:9-15).
Summary of the Campaigns, 11:16–12:24

Yehoshua led Yisrael in victory and rest because of his careful adherence to the Lord’s directions to Mosheh. Mosheh had described the land to be conquered in detail (Dt 1:7), and Yehoshua took the regions of which Mosheh had spoken. Though the cities could have sued for a peaceable arrangement under which they would have been forced laborers (Dt 20:11), none of the cities recognized Yisrael. In fear they plotted and schemed how to destroy Yisrael. They were the aggressors. God had hardened their hearts (Jos 11:20). The theological reason is a mystery, as it was in the case of Par’oh (Pharaoh). But the net result was that Kena’an (Canaan) was conquered and the population exterminated, except for the Hivim at Giveon and their surrounding cities (vv 19-20). Even the Anakim (Anakites), who had brought fear on Yisrael some 40 years before (Nm 13:33; cf. Dt 2:10, 21), were execrated (Jos 11:21). Yet it is already apparent that not every square mile of land was taken (v 22), even though in a sense the entire land was Yisrael’s, because major centers of Kena’ani resistance had been broken. The tension between fulfillment and complete fulfillment is apparent in these verses.

The listing of defeated kings (ch 12) includes the victories over Sihon and Og under Mosheh’s leadership. Their juxtaposition with the list of kings conquered under Yehoshua demonstrates the continuity of leadership and purpose—two leaders, many campaigns, but one battle. The Land of Promise is now a fulfillment. Through the campaigns the borders of the land of inheritance were now more apparent. In Transjordan the limits are from the Arnon to Mt Hermon (vv 2-5). In Kena’an the boundary extends from the region south of Tsidon to the Negev (vv 7-8).
The Division of the Land, 13:1–22:34
The Command to Divide the Land, 13:1-7

Because of Yehoshua’s advanced age, the “whole” land was not taken. Mosheh had forewarned Yisrael (Israel) that the inheritance would result from conquest as well as from gradual extension of Yisrael’s narrow boundaries. Slowly Yisrael was to inherit the whole land, lest it be overwhelmed by the size and be unable to use it properly (Ex 23:29-30; Dt 7:22). The areas still to be occupied were: the region to the north of Galil (Galilee), Mt Hermon (east of the Sea of Galil), the area occupied by the Pelishtim (Philistines), and regional Kena’ani (Canaanite) enclaves (Jos 13:2-7; cf. Jgs 1). Yisrael was not to be concerned with the future rights of occupation, because the Lord promised to help them (Jos 13:6).
Division of Transjordan, 13:8-33

Yehoshua (Joshua) did not alter the Mosaic arrangement concerning the allotments to the tribes of Menasheh (Manasseh), Re’uven (Reuben), and Gad (Jos 13:8, 32-33; cf. Nm 32; Dt 3:12-17). Their territory also excluded certain regions still occupied by Kena’anim (Canaanites) (Jos 13:13). The clans of Re’uven had received the territory from the Arnon River north to Heshbon (vv 15-23). The clans of Gad had received the territory of Gilead, south of the Yabok (Jabbok) River to Heshbon (vv 24-28). Several clans of Menasheh received the region south of the Wadi Yarmuk to the Yabok (vv 29-31). The Levitical towns are not listed here, but a reference is made to them as not receiving a patrimony, because they were to live off the offerings and sacrifices made to the Lord (Jos 13:14; cf. Nm 18:20-24; 35:1-8).
The Tribal Divisions in Kena’an, 14:1–19:51

Eleazar, the high priest, and Yehoshua together cast lots to determine the boundaries, size, and allocation for the remaining nine and a half tribes. Again the exclusion of the tribe of Levi is mentioned (Jos 14:4), because their cities will be dealt with in chapters 20–21. Another literary device is special mention of the inheritance of Kalev (Caleb) in the beginning (14:6-15) and of Yehoshua at the conclusion (19:49-50). These two were the only ones who had left Mitsrayim (Egypt) as adults, had been faithful spies, and had entered into the Promised Land (Nm 14:24, 30; Dt 1:36-38).
Yehudah (Judah), 15:1-63 (cf. Jgs 1:10-15, 20)

The boundaries of Yehudah extended from the Dead Sea westward to the Mediterranean (Jos 15:2-12). The cities of Yehudah are listed in its four regions: 29 in the Negev (vv 21-32), 42 cities in the Shefelah (Shephelah) (or western foothills) and coastal plains (vv 33-47), 38 cities in the hill country (15:48-60), and 6 cities in the desert (vv 61-62). Yehudah was unable to take Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (v 63) until David made it his capital (cf. Jgs 1:21; 2 Sm 5:6-16).
Efrayim (Ephraim) and Menasheh, 16:1–17:18

These two tribes, descended from Yosef (Joseph), were richly blessed (cf. Gn 48; 49:22-26; Dt 33:13-17) and had obtained prominence among the tribes. They received one allotment as “the allotment for Yosef” (Jos 16:1). Part of Menasheh had already received a patrimony east of the Yarden (Jordan) (13:29-31). The limits for Efrayim and the west half of Menasheh were from Beyt-El (Bethel) to Mt Gilboa in the north and from the Yarden to the Mediterranean (16:1-3). Efrayim received the smaller portion in the south (vv 5-9) but was unable to drive the Kena’anim out of Gezer. The clans of Menasheh are given, including Tselofehad (Zelophehad) (17:3-6; cf. Nm 27:1-11; 36:1-12), in order to clearly distinguish them from the clans of Menasheh in Transjordan. The region of west Menasheh extended from Shekem (Shechem) to Mt Gilboa (Jos 17:7-11); but Menasheh, also, was incapable of driving out the Kena’anim completely (vv 12-13).

Though they had received the largest portion of the land (more than a third), the tribes of Yosef complained. They knew that the Lord had blessed them (17:14), and they expected to get more cultivable land. But Yehoshua urged them to use the available land by cutting down the forests (vv 15-18). When they expressed realistic concern about Kena’ani military power, Yehoshua called on them to do their share in occupying the land.
Seven Tribes, 18:1–19:51

The Israelis (Israelites) assembled at Shiloh to set up the tabernacle (cf. 1 Sm 1). At that point seven tribes had not yet received their patrimony. Yehoshua called for each tribe to commission three men to survey the land. When they returned, Yehoshua cast lots at the tabernacle in Shiloh and divided the land (Jos 18:3-10). The territory of Benyamin (Benjamin) was between Yehudah and Efrayim (vv 11-28). Shim’on’s (Simeon’s) allotment was in southern Yehudah (19:1-9), resulting in its absorption into Yehudah (cf. Gn 49:7). Zevulun (Zebulun) (Jos 19:10-16), Yisakar (Issachar) (vv 17-23), Asher (vv 24-31), and Naftali (Naphtali) (vv 32-39) received a portion north of Menasheh in the region of Galil (Galilee). Dan received the seventh lot and suffered subsequently, when it could not maintain the allotted territory because of the pressure of Yehudah on the east and the Pelishtim (Philistines) to the west (vv 40-48). They migrated northward and found the sources of the Yarden to be a fruitful region (Jos 19:47; cf. Jgs 18).
Conclusion, 19:49-51

The conclusion is symmetric with the beginning (Jos 14:1-14) in that Yehoshua (Joshua) also received a gift. Again, mention is made that all divisions were in the presence of the Lord, witnessed to and executed by the high priest Eleazar and Yehoshua (19:51; cf. 14:1).
Cities of Refuge and the Levitical Cities, 20:1–21:45

According to the instructions of Mosheh (Moses), six Levitical cities were set apart, three on each side of the Yarden, as cities of refuge (Nm 35:9-34; Dt 4:41-43; 19:1-10). The purpose was to provide “refuge” (asylum) for those who were guilty of manslaughter but had not intentionally killed someone. This practice was not to provide a way out for someone who was guilty, but to allow for the legal process to be completed (Jos 20).

The Levites received by clan a total of 48 cities, six of which also served as cities of refuge (21:1-42). The Levites could not cultivate the soil because they were dependent on the tithes of the people (Nm 18:21-24), but they were permitted to have land for grazing. The dimensions of the land are given in Numbers 35:4-5. A special allocation is made to the descendants of Aharon (Aaron) (Jos 21:9-19), because they served as priests and their 13 cities were in the Judah-Simeon region, in proximity to the Yerushalem temple of the Solomonic era.

With the allocation of the Levitical cities, the division of the land is concluded. The promise of the land is fulfilled (21:43-45). God is faithful! This section emphasizes the fulfillment, the power, and the grace of God, by which Yisrael (Israel) entered into its rest. However, the book of Yehoshua also hints of the struggle that is still ahead of the Israelis and of the test that ultimately they will fail (cf. Ps 95:11; Heb 3:7-11).
Return of the Transjordan Tribes, 22:1-34

Yehoshua dismissed the two and a half tribes with a commendation for their loyalty to the other tribes and to the Lord (Jos 22:1-4), with a warning not to succumb to idolatry but to love the Lord in accordance with the Deuteronomic law, and with a blessing (vv 5-8). However, as they returned they set up a large altar by the Yarden (Jordan) on the western side. The other tribes heard about it and met at Shiloh (v 12). They wisely commissioned Pinhas (Phinehas), the son of the high priest, with ten representatives of the tribes, to investigate the matter. The commission charged the Transjordan tribes with treachery (Jos 22:15-20; cf. Nm 25; Jos 7).

The response of the Transjordan tribes demonstrated their concern for the unity of the tribes and for the worship of God. These tribes feared being excluded from the fellowship of God’s people and had purposefully constructed an altar, identical to that prescribed in the law, in order to demonstrate their common heritage (Jos 22:21-30). The altar was not for sacrifice or worship but functioned as a symbol of the covenantal unity of the people of God.

Pinhas and the tribal representatives were pleased with the response and left with the assurance of God’s presence (22:30-31). Their report to the tribes led to reconciliation of all the tribes on this matter. The narrative concludes with a mention of the name given to the altar: “A witness between us and them that Yahweh is our God, too” (v 34, nlt).
Epilogue: The Land Is a Sacred Trust, 23:1–24:33
The last two chapters contain Yehoshua’s farewell speeches to all the leaders and to all Yisrael.
Address to the Leaders, 23:1-16

Yehoshua (Joshua) reviews what the Lord has done for Yisrael in giving the land to the tribes. He has demonstrated his loyalty. And he will continue to be with his people so that no enemy can stand against them. He will fulfill every outstanding promise, even as he had already fulfilled promises. However, they must persevere in their loyalty to the Lord. Loyalty to the Lord is not apart from loyalty to the law of Mosheh. Apostasy will be severely punished, first by leaving the nations to ensnare Yisrael, and then by consuming them in his wrath.
Address to Yisrael, 24:1-28

The address ends with a covenant renewal at Shekem (Shechem) (Jos 24:1, 25-28; cf. 8:30-35). In the ancient Near East it was common when making a treaty (covenant) to give a brief historical summary of the relationship of the parties involved. Yehoshua reviewed Yisrael’s history from the patriarchs to their generation: patriarchs (24:2-4), exodus (vv 5-7), and conquest (vv 8-13).

The goodness, presence, and loyalty of Yahweh was evident to them. Yahweh also expected “faithfulness” from his people in the form of whole allegiance, without any form of idolatry (Jos 24:14-15). As the head of his family, Yehoshua vowed to be loyal (v 15). The people responded by giving reasons for being loyal to the Lord (vv 16-18). But Yehoshua pushed them to a deeper commitment by challenging their profession (vv 19-20), then recording their vow and setting up a stone of witness against them (vv 25-27).
End of an Era, 24:29-33

The book began with a reference to the death of Mosheh (Moses) (1:1-2) and concludes with the death and burial of Yehoshua (24:29-30) and of Eleazar the high priest (v 33). This marks the end of an era. The burial of Yosef’s (Joseph’s) bones (Jos 24:32; cf. Gn 50:25; Ex 13:19) in a plot purchased by Ya’akov (Jacob) (Gn 33:19) brings together the hope characteristic of the epoch of Mosheh and Yehoshua.
See also Cities of Refuge; Conquest and Allotment of the Land; Israel, History of; Joshua (Person) #1; Levitical Cities.
JOSIAH

1. Sixteenth king of the southern kingdom of Yehudah (Judah) (640–609 BC). A godly man, he stood in marked contrast to his grandfather Menasheh (Manasseh) and his father, Amon. In fact, Scripture declares there was no king either before or after him who was as obedient to the law of Mosheh (Moses) (2 Kgs 23:25). The Greek form of his name, Yoshiyah (Josias), appears in Matthew 1:10-11 (kjv).
The Times of Yoshiyah

When Yoshiyah became king in 640 BC, the international scene was about to change drastically. After the great Assyrian king Ashurbanipal died in 633 BC, mediocre rulers followed him on the throne, and there was considerable unrest in the empire. Nabopolassar, father of Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar), seized the kingship in Bavel (Babylon) and established the Neo-Babylonian Empire late in 626 BC. Soon Babylonians and Madim (Medes) combined forces to topple the Assyrian Empire, and in 612 BC completely destroyed the city of Nineveh. As Babylonian power rose in the east, Assyrian control over the province that had once been the kingdom of Yisrael (Israel) relaxed and Assyrian pressure on Yehudah virtually ceased. After the fall of Nineveh, the Assyrians established their capital at Haran. There they were defeated by Babylonians and Scythians in 610 BC. At that point Par’oh (Pharaoh) Nekoh (Neco) II of Mitsrayim (Egypt) decided to support Ashur (Assyria). In the late spring of 609 BC he advanced through Yehudah, defeated and killed Yoshiyah, and spent the summer campaigning in Aram (Syria).

Before Yoshiyah’s reign, Yehudah had capitulated to gross idolatry during the reign of Menasheh (697–642 BC). Baalism, Molek (Molech) worship, and other pagan religions had invaded the land, as had occultism and astrology. A false altar even stood in the temple in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), and human sacrifice to pagan deities was practiced near Yerushalem. The nation was thoroughly corrupt. Although some reform occurred in Menasheh’s latter days, conditions reverted to their former baseness during the reign of his son Amon (642–640 BC). In 640 BC officials of Amon’s household assassinated him, and the “people of the land” put Yoshiyah on the throne (2 Kgs 21:26; 22:1; 2 Chr 33:25–34:1).
Yoshiyah’s Reform Activities

Yoshiyah was only eight years old when he became king. Evidently he had spiritually motivated advisers or regents; by the time he was 16, he began of his own accord “to seek the God of his ancestor David” (2 Chr 34:3). When he was 20, he became greatly exercised over the idolatry of the land and launched a major effort to eradicate the pagan high places, groves, and images from Yehudah and Yerushalem. So intense was Yoshiyah’s hatred of idolatry that he even opened the tombs of pagan priests and burned their bones on pagan altars before the altars were destroyed.

Yoshiyah carried his reform movement beyond the borders of Yehudah, venting his fury especially on the cult center at Beyt-El (Bethel), where Yarov’am (Jeroboam) had set up his false worship. In fulfillment of prophecy (1 Kgs 13:1-3), he destroyed the altar and high place and burned the bones of officiating priests to desecrate the site (2 Kgs 23:15-18). What he did at Beyt-El he did everywhere else in the kingdom of Shomron (Samaria) (vv 19-20).

When Yoshiyah was 26, he launched a project to cleanse and repair the temple in Yerushalem (2 Kgs 22:3). Shafan (Shaphan), the king’s administrative assistant, commissioned the work; Hilkiyah (Hilkiah) the priest supervised the renovation and construction. In the process of restoring the temple, Hilkiyah found the Book of the Law, the nature and contents of which are otherwise unknown. Possibly in the dark days of Menasheh a deliberate attempt had been made to destroy the Word of God. At any rate, there was little knowledge of Scripture in Yehudah.

When Shafan read the Book of the Law to Yoshiyah, the king was devastated by the pronouncements of judgment against apostasy contained in it. He sent a delegation to Huldah the prophetess to find out what judgments awaited the land. The prophetess replied that the condemnation of God would indeed fall on Yehudah for its sin, but she sent word to Yoshiyah that because his heart was right toward God, the punishment would not come during his lifetime.

The king called together a large representative group for a public reading of the law—evidently sections especially concerned with obligations to God. The king and the people made a covenant before God to keep his commandments.

Faced with the importance of maintaining a pure monotheistic faith, the king was spurred on to even more rigorous efforts to cleanse the temple and Yerushalem. He destroyed the vessels used in Ba’al (Baal) worship, the monument of horses given by the kings of Yehudah for sun worship, the chariots dedicated to the sun, the homosexual community near the temple, and shrines built by Shelomoh (Solomon) and in use since his day. Moreover, he made stringent efforts to eliminate the pagan shrines and high places in all the towns of Yehudah (2 Kgs 23:4-14).
The Death of Yoshiyah (Josiah)

Precisely why Yoshiyah opposed Par’oh Nekoh’s advance through Yehudi (Judean) territory is unknown. He may have wanted to prevent aid from reaching the hated Assyrians or to maintain his own independence. Yoshiyah was mortally wounded in the conflict and was greatly lamented by Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) and all the people (2 Chr 35:25). Well they might weep, for their godly king was gone, and within a few years the judgment withheld during his lifetime would descend on the nation.
See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Israel, History of.
2. Son of Tsefanyah (Zephaniah), who returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) with other Yehudim (Jews) after the captivity (Zec 6:10, 14; Hebrew “Hen”).
JOSIAS*
KJV spelling of Yoshiyah (Josiah), Yehoyakin’s (Jehoiachin’s) father, in Matthew 1:10-11. See Josiah #1.
JOSIBIAH*
KJV spelling of Yoshivyah (Joshibiah), Yehu’s (Jehu’s) father, in 1 Chronicles 4:35. See Joshibiah.
JOSIPHIAH
Father of Shelomit (Shelomith), leader of a family of which 160 members accompanied Ezra back to Palestine (Ezr 8:10).
JOTBAH

Hometown of Haruts (Haruz), the father of Meshulemet (Meshullemeth), who was the mother of King Amon of Yehudah (Judah) (2 Kgs 21:19). Its location is uncertain; however, some identify it with the town later named Jotapata by the Romans, situated six miles (9.7 kilometers) north of Sepphoris (modern Khirbet Jefat).
JOTBATHAH

Temporary camping place of the Israelis (Israelites) during their wilderness wanderings, located between Hor-Hagidgad (Hor-haggidgad) and Avronah (Abronah) (Nm 33:33-34). Later, following the death of Aharon (Aaron), Yisrael (Israel) journeyed from Gudgodah to this place, noted for its streams of water (Dt 10:7).
See also Wilderness Wanderings.
JOTHAM

1. Youngest of Gid’on’s (Gideon’s) 70 sons and the only survivor of Avimelek’s (Abimelech’s) slaughter of Yotam’s (Jotham’s) brothers at Ofrah (Ophrah) (Jgs 9:5). Upon learning of Avimelek’s intrigue with the Shechemites, which led to the death of his brothers, Yotam traveled to Shekem (Shechem) and addressed its people from atop nearby Mt Gerizim. Using a parable, he portrayed Avimelek’s rise as king and concluded his denunciation by issuing a curse on both his half brother (see 8:31) and the people of Shekem for their treachery (9:7). Yotam then fled to Beer for fear of a reprisal from Avimelek (v 21). Later, God fulfilled Yotam’s curse; the people of Shekem were killed in a revolt and Avimelek was struck down at the hands of a woman (v 57).

2. Eleventh king of Yehudah (Judah) (750–735 BC). He was the son of King Azaryah (Azariah) (Uziyah (Uzziah)) of Yehudah and Jerusa, daughter of Tsadok (Zadok) (2 Kgs 15:7; 2 Chr 26:21; 27:1), and the father of Ahaz. Yotam, at 25 years of age, ascended Yehudah’s throne in the second year of King Pekah of Yisrael (Israel) (752–732 BC) and ruled for 16 years in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Initially he reigned as co-regent with Azaryah, who was stricken with leprosy for tolerating pagan worship, until his father’s death (2 Kgs 15:5).

Yotam was considered a righteous king in the eyes of the Lord. However, he also failed to cleanse the temple of its pagan influences, and subsequently the people of Yehudah continued in their evil ways (2 Chr 27:2-6). His building projects included the Upper Gate of the temple, work on the wall of Ofel (Ophel), and the fortification of numerous towns in Yehudah’s hill country (vv 3-4). Yotam also defeated the troublesome Amonim (Ammonites) in battle (v 5) and registered by genealogy the families of Gad living east of the Yarden (Jordan) (1 Chr 5:17). He was buried in Yerushalem after his death (2 Chr 27:9). The prophets Yeshayah (Isaiah) and Mikah (Micah) ministered to Yehudah, and Hoshea (Hosea) to Yisrael, during his tenure as king. Yotam is listed as an ancestor of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ in Matay’s (Matthew’s; Grk. Matthaios’) genealogy (Mt 1:9).
See also Chronology of the Bible (Old Testament); Genealogy of Jesus Christ; Israel, History of.
3. Second of Yehday’s (Jahdai’s) five sons (1 Chr 2:47).
JOT OR TITTLE*

An expression Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) used in the Sermon on the Mount. In Matthew 5:18 jot is a transliteration of the Greek letter iota. In this context it originally referred to the Hebrew letter yod, the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet. Tittle is a Middle English word referring to the diacritical dot placed over abbreviated words. The kjv translators used it to render a Greek word meaning “little horn.” The Yehudim (Jews) used that word to refer to the small marking that distinguished certain Hebrew letters from one another. Yeshua used the two terms to emphasize the importance of the law when he said not one jot or tittle would pass from the law until all was fulfilled.
JOY
Positive human condition that can be either feeling or action. The Bible uses “joy” in both senses.
Joy as a Feeling
Joy is a feeling called forth by well-being, success, or good fortune. A person automatically experiences it because of certain favorable circumstances. It cannot be commanded.

The shepherd experienced joy when he found his lost sheep (Mt 18:13). The multitude felt it when Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) healed a Jewish woman whom Satan had bound for 18 years (Lk 13:17). The disciples returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) rejoicing after Yeshua’s ascension (24:52). Joy was also the feeling of the church at Antiokeia (Antioch) when its members heard the Yerushalem Council’s decision that they did not have to be circumcised to keep God’s law (Acts 15:31). Paulos (Paul) mentioned his joy in hearing about the obedience of the Roman Christians (Rom 16:19). He wrote to the Corinthians that love does not rejoice in wrong but rejoices in the right (1 Cor 13:6; see also 1 Sm 2:1; 11:9; 18:6; 2 Sm 6:12; 1 Kgs 1:40; Est 9:17-22).

Psalms 137:1-6 shows that the emotion cannot be commanded. The Yehudim’s (Jews’) captors wanted them to sing in the land of their exile, something they were unable to do. Faraway Yerushalem was their chief joy.
Joy as an Action

There is a joy that Scripture commands. That joy is action that can be engaged in regardless of how the person feels. Proverbs 5:18 tells the reader to rejoice in the wife of his youth, without reference to what she may be like. Christ instructed his disciples to rejoice when they were persecuted, reviled, and slandered (Mt 5:11-12). The apostle Paulos commanded continuous rejoicing (Phil 4:4; 1 Thes 5:16). Ya’akov (James) said Christians are to reckon it all joy when they fall into various testings because such testings produce endurance (Jas 1:2). Joy in adverse circumstances is possible only as a fruit of the Holy Spirit, who is present in every Christian (Gal 5:22).
See also Fruit of the Spirit.
JOZABAD
1. Benyamite (Benjamite) from Gederah and one of the military men who came to David’s support at Tsiklag (Ziklag) (1 Chr 12:4).
2, 3. Leaders and mighty warriors from Menasheh’s (Manasseh’s) tribe who joined David at Tsiklag to fight against Sha’ul (Saul) (1 Chr 12:20).
4. One of the Levites who assisted with the administration of the temple contributions in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) during King Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) reign (2 Chr 31:13).
5. One of the Levitical chiefs who generously gave animals to the Levites for the celebration of the Passover feast during King Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) reign (2 Chr 35:9).

6. Levite, the son of Yeshua (Jeshua), and one who helped Meremot (Meremoth), Eleazar, and Noadyah (Noadiah) take inventory of the temple’s gifts and precious metals during the days of Ezra (Ezr 8:33).
7. Priest and one of the six sons of Pashhur who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era (Ezr 10:22).
8. One of the Levites who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife (Ezr 10:23).
9. One of the Levites who assisted Ezra with teaching the people the law during the postexilic period (Neh 8:7).
10. One of the Levites who relocated to Yerushalem and was put in charge of the work of the temple during the days of Nehemyah (Nehemiah) (Neh 11:16).
11. Alternate rendering for Shim’at’s (Shimeath’s) son in 2 Kings 12:21. See Jozacar, Jozachar.
JOZACAR*, JOZACHAR*

Son of Shim’at (Shimeath) the Amonit (Ammonitess) and one of the royal servants who conspired against the murdered King Yoash (Joash) of Yehudah (Judah) (2 Kgs 12:21). He is alternately called Zavad (Zabad) in 2 Chronicles 24:26. See Zabad.
JOZADAK*

Serayah’s (Seraiah’s) son and one of the exiles transported by Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) to Bavel (Babylonia) (1 Chr 6:14-15). He was the father of Yeshua (Jeshua) (also called Yehoshua (Joshua)), the high priest in postexilic Yerushalem (Jerusalem) during the days of Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) (Ezr 3:2, 8; 5:2; 10:18; Neh 12:26; Hg 1:1-14; 2:2-4; Zec 6:11). Yotsadak (Jozadak) is alternately called Yehotsadak (Jehozadak).
JUBAL
Son of Adah, wife of Lemek (Lamech), a descendant of Kayin (Cain). He is crredited with being the first musician, the inventor of the harp and flute (Gn 4:19-21).
JUBILEE YEAR*

Year of emancipation and restoration to be kept every 50 years. For Yisrael (Israel), the seventh year expressed at length the values of the seventh day Sabbath (Lv 25:1-7). When a series of seven years reached the perfection of seven sevens, the 50th year was heralded by the trumpet of jubilee and a whole additional year was set aside as belonging to the Lord.

The word “jubilee” simply means a ram’s horn; it came to mean a trumpet made from or in the shape of a ram’s horn. Such horns were exclusively for religious use. The sacred trumpet gave its name to the year of the ram’s horn, the jubilee year—a year to which the people of God were summoned in a striking and holy way. It was not simply a release from labor, not just a rest, but a year belonging to the Lord. In Leviticus 25 this exact expression occurs in connection with the seventh year rather than expressly with the jubilee year. Functionally such a year was a Sabbath rest for the land, and it brought enjoyment “to Yahweh” (Lv 25:4). But nothing could more directly express the implications and orientations of the 50th year.
Lordship

The first principle of the jubilee is God’s lordship over the whole earth, acknowledged by his people in their obedience to his command to set the year aside in this way. Just as the Sabbath expressed his right to order life, giving it the shape of six days’ work and one day’s rest, and just as the seventh year, linked in Deuteronomy 31:9-13 with the reading of his law, expressed his right to command the obedience of his people, so the 50th year expressed his sovereign possession of all: land, people, means of production, and life itself. Take the typical case of debtor and creditor. When God brought his people into possession of the land, he gave to each his inheritance. In a given circumstance a man might be compelled to sell his land in whole or part, but it must come back to him: “The land must never be sold on a permanent basis because it really belongs to me. You are only foreigners and tenants living with me” (Lv 25:23, nlt). In this verse “foreigners” carries the meaning “stateless persons,” “refugees,” “those who have sought political asylum”—in a word, those who have no rights except what mercy concedes. Such are the people of God and such they must acknowledge themselves to be when the jubilee year comes around. When a piece of real estate changed hands, the seller might congratulate himself on the astuteness with which he had solved his problem, and the buyer might rejoice in his skillful acquisitiveness, but in the Year of Jubilee seller and buyer alike are compelled to confess a different truth: neither is master, either of his own welfare or of the person and goods of another. Each has a Master in heaven.
Redemption

According to the ordinance, the trumpet that heralded the year was sounded on the Day of Atonement (Lv 25:9). That was the day on which the Lord proclaimed his people clean before him from all their sins (16:30). Forgiveness of sins ushered in the jubilee year. The verb “to redeem” and the noun “redemption” had a strong commercial use in the recovery of property pledged against loans of money, and in the 50th year these words would have sounded and resounded as debtors confessed that they could not “redeem” and creditors forewent their “redemption” rights, each using the very vocabulary of the Lord’s action at the exodus (Ex 6:6). This is what the Lord had done for his people, and the divine action must be the norm of the human. Brotherly generosity is urged (Lv 25:35-38), liberty is granted (vv 39-43), and slavery in perpetuity is forbidden (vv 47-55) simply because the divine redemptive act makes the redeemed into brothers, brings them into the Lord’s servitude, and cancels the bondage that would otherwise be theirs forever.
Rest

The correlative of redemption is rest. This rest is vividly illustrated and enforced as Mosheh (Moses) legislates rest from all the toil connected with promoting next year’s crop (Lv 25:4); rest from the toil of harvesting, for the people of God were to live hand to mouth, gathering only what and when need dictated (vv 5-7); rest from the anxious burden of debts incurred; and rest from slavery (v 10). Like the Sabbath, this rest would have meant exactly what it said: freedom from toil; relaxation, refreshment, and recreation. Very likely tiredness was as endemic among the people of God then as now, and grace drew near to give them a holiday. But equally with the Sabbath, release from the preoccupations of staying alive created time to be preoccupied with the Lord, his worship, his Word, and the life that pleases him. We can understand Isaiah 58 as binding the ideals of Sabbath and jubilee together. The Lord frees his people not for unbroken idleness but for the redirection of life toward himself. The jubilee year was thus a deliberate opting out of the rat race; it called a halt to acquisitiveness; it abandoned concern over the pressure to stay alive. It reordered priorities, giving a chance to appraise the use of time and the selection of objectives. For a whole year the people of God stood back, rested, ceased from the good in order to attain the best.
Faith

But this standing back from life was not in the style of a dropout. It was the action of responsible faith. No one on earth can escape questions such as “What shall we eat?” The Lord foresees and provides (Lv 25:20); grace provides so that God’s people can enjoy the ordinances of grace (cf. Ex 16:29). When he commands a year off, he enables them to take it. The 50th year was a living testimony to his faithfulness. The last season of sowing and reaping would have been the 49th year; in the final 7th year in the series the people would live off the casual growth; and in the 50th year nothing but the sheer attentive faithfulness of their God could provide for them (Lv 25:21). Here indeed their faith would be put to the test, for God spoke a word of majestic promise and called on them to believe. At the heart of their jubilee they took God at his word and found him faithful.
Obedience

Biblically, it is a central characteristic of the people of God that they do what he commands for no other reason than that he commands it. In the ordinance of the 50th year the people of God must show themselves as his obedient ones, and in fact their obedience is the guarantee of continuance in the land he has granted to them. Thus, for example, Leviticus 26:34-35 teaches that loss of tenure and loss of liberty is directly related to contravention of the principle of the Sabbath, found on the seventh day, seventh year, and jubilee year. Refusal to obey goes hand in hand with loss of possession, leaving behind an empty land, which then enjoys the Sabbath rest it never received from its disobedient inhabitants.
Hope

In the 50th year the people lived in the light of the forgiveness of sins, walked by obedience in harmony with the God who redeemed them, and in freedom from toil, received from the ground its life-sustaining benefits without any sweat on their brows (Gn 2:16; 3:19). It was a sort of Eden restored, the curse momentarily held in abeyance—but also a prolonged foretaste of the coming day when the promises would all be fulfilled, the blood of the covenant efficacious without hindrance, the prisoners of hope (i.e., who had waited in hope for their release) freed, and the trumpet of liberation heard throughout the world (Is 27:13; Zec 9:11-14). The Year of Jubilee in a limited but real way foreshadowed what would yet be the eternal inheritance and bliss of the people of God.
See also Feasts and Festivals of Israel.

Alternate name for Yehukal (Jehucal), Shelemyah’s (Shelemiah’s) son, in Jeremiah 38:1 (nlt mg). See Jehucal.

JUDAEA*
